favorable D23 result and perform D16 activation after every current fence passes.
D23 creates no Page, Navigation, Communications, task, reminder, email, Giving,
Legal Entity, Stripe, settlement, bank, currency, contribution, receipt, ledger,
or accounting authority.

Staff see consequence-led language: **You can complete this review**,
**Someone else must review this version**, or **We couldn't confirm the review
requirements**. The page states what remains live and shows the next lawful
action. It never relies on a disabled button, tooltip, permission code, peer
engagement, red danger treatment, or the phrase “self-approve.”

The full corrected contract, staff UX, source ownership, database/RLS boundary,
22-category adversarial review, 56 acceptance criteria, monitors, rollout, and
traceability are recorded in
[phase-24-d23-source-owned-proportional-independence-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d23-source-owned-proportional-independence-adversarial-review.md).
The current primary-source and repository evidence is recorded separately in
[phase-24-d23-source-owned-proportional-independence-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d23-source-owned-proportional-independence-primary-research.md).

## D24 — Which protected participants are unable to perform independent review?

### Why this needs your decision

The D23 research found a real repository contradiction:

- the active outbound-communications OpenSpec excludes only the **latest
  material editor**; but
- the Phase 17 PRD and traceability record exclude **every substantive author
  or editor** of the exact protected candidate.

That is not wording trivia. It changes whether someone who contributed to a
protected version can become its “independent” reviewer after another person
makes the last edit.

### Concrete Hope Ministries example

Maria changes protected Navigation. Ana later fixes the final protected label.
Maria is no longer the latest editor, but Maria's change remains in the exact
candidate.

Should Maria now be allowed to review the combined protected version?

### Option 1 — exclude only the latest material editor

Maria may review because Ana made the latest material edit.

**Impact:** more people remain eligible and small teams need fewer handoffs.
However, two participants can rotate the final edit and review each other's
combined work. Independence no longer covers the whole candidate.

### Option 2 — exclude every substantive participant

**Recommended.** Maria and Ana are both unable to review that exact protected
candidate. A third currently authorized human must review. Reading, commenting,
routing, or requesting changes does not disqualify; only a source-defined
material contribution does.

**Impact:** staff get one predictable rule: **If you materially change protected
work, another person reviews it.** If a reviewer fixes protected content, Core
warns before save that review must hand off. The cost is that small teams need
the later candidate-scoped reviewer recovery when no internal person remains.

### Option 3 — exclude only each participant's protected subgraph

Maria could review protected areas she did not edit, while another person
reviews Maria's subgraph.

**Impact:** theoretically most proportional, but one atomic Plan now needs
partial approvals, graph attribution, combination rules, and a difficult staff
explanation. This is the most brittle option.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 2 — exclude every substantive participant for the
exact protected candidate.** It matches the primary Phase 17 decision, prevents
last-editor laundering, and gives staff the clearest rule before they edit.

Do you choose **Option 2**, or would you amend it toward **Option 1** or
**Option 3**?

### Founder answer

**Option 2 — exclude every substantive participant.**

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

D24 now resolves the repository contradiction in favor of the governing Phase
12/17 rule: when D23 returns **different human required**, the successful
reviewer's stable human identity must be absent from the complete substantive-
participant set for the exact protected candidate and review epoch. The
weaker active OpenSpec phrase **latest material editor** is a wording defect,
not the permanent rule, and must be corrected before implementation or key
activation.

A **Protected candidate participant** is a stable human whose trusted,
source-owned accepted command introduced a material effect into that exact
candidate lineage. The set is the append-only union over the candidate's
included source heads and protected dependencies. A later overwrite, revert,
last edit, role/account change, identity relink, copy, squash, rebase, import,
restore, or new review request cannot erase participation. Only a genuinely
new candidate built from an independently proved clean basis and carrying none
of the discarded unreviewed material may begin a new lineage.

Each source owns a closed, versioned materiality classifier. Reading,
previewing, testing without mutation, generic comments, requesting changes,
routing, item engagement, rejected proposals, and source-proved semantic no-
ops do not add a participant. An accepted tracked material suggestion adds
both its provable human proposer and accepter. A human accepting material AI or
imported work participates; AI, automation, service/shared identities,
support, impersonation, and **View as** can never supply an independent human.
Unknown, incomplete, contradictory, incompatible, or corrupt provenance is
indeterminate and blocks.

D24 applies only to the exact still-unsatisfied source obligation selected by
D23. It does not pull the historical authors of already-reviewed Page,
Navigation, publication, or dependency versions into a duplicate Plan review,
and a Plan review never satisfies another source's review. One atomic
candidate has one complete participant set and one independent review; D24
creates no partial approvals, subgraph votes, generic workflow engine, or
authorship-surveillance system.

The final server command re-proves the exact candidate, included heads,
participant digest, source/evaluator/policy generations, stable-human identity
epoch, current authorization and step-up, expected heads, and semantic
idempotency inside one short expected-head/CAS transaction. Browser callers
cannot submit actor, author, materiality, participant, scope, or result truth.
Normalized append-only evidence, composite same-scope constraints, restrictive
deletion, explicit grants, RLS `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, privileged-path
parity, and body-free audit evidence are required. Any race, projection gap,
or audit failure produces no favorable review and no public effect.

The staff rule is intentionally simple: **If you materially change protected
work in this version, another person reviews it.** Review opens read-only.
Before a reviewer enters a potentially material edit path, Core says **Editing
will hand off this review** and explains that saving a material change requires
another reviewer. **Request changes** remains available without
disqualification. After a material save, work is preserved, the old review is
stale, the participant-safe routing projection is recomputed, and the live
website remains unchanged.

A participant sees **Another person must review this version**, one privacy-
safe reason, what remains live, and one lawful next action. A qualified person
sees **You can review this version** and the exact consequence-led action. If
no eligible internal reviewer exists, Core shows **Another reviewer is
required** and the safe current state; it does not show a disabled unexplained
button, send recurring reminders, promise an invitation before D25, reveal a
participant roster without separate authority, or create a same-human/admin
bypass.

D24 only subtracts reviewer eligibility. It grants no permission, assignment,
route, delegate, reminder, email, public mutation, or deadline and has no
Giving, Legal Entity, Stripe, settlement, bank, currency, contribution,
receipt, ledger, or accounting effect. Existing public content remains active
while a candidate is blocked.

The complete corrected D24-R1–D24-R14 contract, staff journey, source-of-truth
matrix, database/RLS boundary, 22-category adversarial review, acceptance
proof, monitors, rollout order, and traceability are recorded in
[phase-24-d24-every-substantive-participant-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d24-every-substantive-participant-adversarial-review.md).
The current primary-source and repository evidence is recorded separately in
[phase-24-d24-every-substantive-participant-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d24-every-substantive-participant-primary-research.md).

## D25 — What happens when no qualified internal reviewer remains?

### Why this needs your decision

D24 deliberately protects the meaning of independent review. In a one-person
ministry—or when every currently authorized person helped prepare the exact
protected candidate—that can leave nobody inside the Tenant who may review it.
Core needs a lawful recovery path without silently weakening D24, granting a
broad permanent role, or leaving staff unsure whether the live website is at
risk.

This question does **not** decide who is independent; D24 already did that. It
decides whether an applicable source may authorize a narrowly bounded outside
human for one exact candidate. Phase 17 already has a source-specific
candidate-scoped pattern, but D25 must not assume every Page, Navigation, or
default-change source can safely expose the same evidence.

### Concrete Hope Ministries example

Maria is Hope's only Website staff member. She materially changes protected
Navigation in the French default Plan, so D24 correctly prevents her from
reviewing it. The current English website remains live and unchanged. What
should Maria be able to do next?

### Option 1 — invite one candidate-scoped external reviewer — recommended

Where **every applicable source explicitly supports delegation**, Maria may
invite one verified, distinct human for only the immutable candidate and
participant/dependency digest. The delegate receives a synthetic, minimized,
read-only comparison and one review action—not standing Tenant membership.
Access binds the Tenant, Site, source, candidate, safe reason, identity,
step-up, expiry, and revocation and ends on decision, cancellation,
supersession, revocation, or expiry. The delegate cannot edit, re-delegate,
export, browse unrelated data, approve a successor, or touch Giving/finance.
They must also pass D24. If any source cannot provide a safe complete
projection, the candidate stays honestly blocked.

**Staff impact:** Hope gets one clear **Invite a reviewer** recovery action and
does not create a fake permanent staff account. The cost is a carefully
verified invite and source-by-source evidence contract.

### Option 2 — internal qualified staff only

Maria must add and fully onboard another permanent staff member through Phase
12 before the candidate can be reviewed.

**Staff impact:** this has the smallest special review surface, but it is heavy
for a one-time review and can deadlock one-person ministries or tempt them to
over-grant a lasting role merely to publish.

### Option 3 — emergency same-human or administrator exception

Allow Maria or a super administrator to review after a warning, reason, and
step-up.

**Staff impact:** fastest in the moment, but it destroys D24's independent-
human guarantee and makes administrator status a safety bypass. A real
emergency should restore a compatible, previously independently reviewed safe
version—not approve novel protected work.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — one source-authorized, exact candidate-
scoped external reviewer.** It gives solo ministries a clear way forward while
keeping review genuinely independent, private, expiring, and non-transferable.
It is allowed only when every applicable source proves the delegate can see
enough to review safely without receiving broader Tenant access.

Do you choose **Option 1**, **Option 2 — internal staff only**, or **Option 3 —
an emergency same-human exception**? You may amend any option.

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — one source-authorized, exact candidate-scoped external reviewer,
without making the staff or Tenant experience inflexible.**

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

D25 resolves the no-internal-reviewer recovery without weakening D23/D24. In
the D25 recovery posture, the external action appears only after every
applicable source and the current Phase 12 resolver completely prove that the
exact different-human obligation has no eligible internal reviewer. Partial,
stale, timed-out, incompatible, or unknown evidence is not zero and never
releases external access. D26 separately decides whether a Tenant may also
choose external review when an internal reviewer is eligible.

Every applicable Page, Navigation, Communications, Site/default, or other
source must affirmatively allow external review, declare any internal-officer
or qualification restriction, and provide a complete minimum-sufficient
external-review projection for the exact candidate. One nondelegable or
indeterminate source blocks the combined external path. The Plan coordinates
the result but never invents source permission, copies source content into an
authorization record, or treats a partial projection as enough.

Phase 4 owns the authority-free invitation, intended-human binding,
credential, scanner-safe deliberate redemption, expiry, replacement,
revocation, and invitation audit. Phase 12 must add one server-derived
**Candidate Review Authorization Context** to its closed context union. That
context binds the exact Tenant, environment, Site, source contracts, immutable
candidate and dependency/participant/projection digests, stable human,
operation ceiling, assurance profile, expiry, revocation, and governance
epochs. It is never an Active Tenant Assignment, membership, role, group,
internal responsibility route, or reusable capability.

The source owner retains the candidate, materiality, D24 participant set,
external-projection contract, review eligibility, final decision, and any
explicitly combined publication or activation effect. Phase 17/6 prepare and
deliver the branded invitation and record provider outcomes. Invitation
creation, message dispatch, provider acceptance, inbox delivery, email open,
identity acceptance, projection access, review decision, and public effect are
distinct facts. None implies the next.

One exact candidate has at most one current external invitee or accepted grant.
D22's up-to-three rule governs internal attention and is not copied into
external disclosure. Staff are nevertheless not locked to one person: they may
**Send again** without extending authority, **Cancel invitation**, **Replace
reviewer** immediately, or explicitly **Invite this reviewer for the new
version** after a candidate changes. Replacement revokes the old path before
the successor is released. Pending, failed-delivery, declined, expired,
canceled, revoked, replaced, superseded, ambiguous, or indeterminate
invitations grant nothing.

A private **Saved reviewer contact** makes repeated work fast. It is an
optional Tenant convenience reference to a previously verified stable human,
not an “approved reviewer” or pool. Selecting it only prefills a new invitation.
It conveys no access, capability, qualification, eligibility, assurance,
independence, route membership, or authority. Removing a saved contact changes
only future selection; revoking an active invitation remains a separate
explicit action, and neither operation rewrites history.

The delegate remains a distinct, authenticated, stepped-up human and must pass
the complete D24 participant comparison on invitation acceptance, every
projection read, and the final source command. Shared mailboxes, groups, AI,
bots, services, support, impersonation, **View as**, or a second account for the
same human cannot qualify. Verified contact-point possession alone is not
claimed as KYC or proof against collusion; uncertain or contradictory stable-
human correlation blocks. Each source owns a bounded assurance profile so Core
does not force government-ID proof for every website review or accept email
possession where stronger assurance is required.

The external review surface is focused, authenticated, no-store, first-party,
and read-only. It shows the exact organization, Site, locale, candidate effect,
access end, and text-first **Current**, **Proposed**, and **Unchanged** evidence.
It may expose only the source-certified minimum needed to decide, using
synthetic facts in place of donor, missionary, recipient, payment, credential,
member-care, restricted, or other operational data. It provides only
**Request changes**, **Complete review** or the source's exact effect-led action,
and **Decline**. It provides no editor, Mission Control navigation, unrelated
Site/locale, export/download feature, participant roster, re-delegation, route
management, successor access, Giving, or finance.

The ordinary staff journey is one Base Maia sheet: search **Previously used
reviewers** or enter a new person, review exactly what the person can see/do and
what remains Live, then **Send invitation**. Do not ask for a job title, role,
due date, priority, justification essay, permission bundle, or recurring
reminder. The result distinguishes **Invitation created**, **Invitation sent**,
**Accepted**, **Review completed**, and the source's public outcome. Delivery
failure says the reviewer has not been told and offers **Send again** or
**Choose another reviewer**; decline, expiry, source prohibition, and candidate
change each provide a safe next action without deleting valid source work.

Invitation and accepted-grant expiry are security boundaries, not D18 Plan
target dates or schedules. A source/Phase 4 code-owned bounded expiry policy
must have exact manifest values before Live; Tenant policy may shorten but
never lengthen past the source/platform maximum. The UI shows one absolute
localized date, time, and zone. Viewing or resend never extends it; after
expiry, staff issue a fresh invitation. Core provides accessible authentication
choices, permits password-manager/autofill and OTP paste, and never requires an
inaccessible cognitive puzzle.

The authoritative model uses immutable invitation and grant/context versions,
stable Party/principal references, exact source/candidate/projection digests,
one current head, append-only lifecycle and decision evidence, a separate
Phase 6 communication identity, and a non-authoritative saved-contact
reference—not a mutable JSON guest row. Same-scope composite constraints,
unique current-candidate invitation state, restrictive deletion, indexed
foreign keys and resolution paths, explicit grants, `ENABLE` plus `FORCE RLS`,
operation-correct `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, fixed-search-path functions,
trusted server attribution, and identical RPC/worker/service/Payload/support/
repair/migration checks are release requirements. External reviewers receive
no direct table/PostgREST access.

Invitation acceptance and exact context creation commit through one local CAS;
external message delivery remains recoverable outbox work. The final source
command re-proves source support, candidate/heads, projection and participant
digests, stable identity, current context/assurance, source/policy/evaluator/
governance epochs, expiry/revocation, expected head, and semantic idempotency in
one short transaction with no provider call. Candidate or dependency change,
identity merge, participant change, policy/projection change, authorization
loss, decision, cancellation, replacement, revocation, or expiry denies future
access immediately. Failure leaves the current Site unchanged.

D25 creates one deliberate invitation message only. It does not create a D19/
D20 internal item for the nonmember, recurring reminder, SLA, timer-driven
fallback, standing external route, marketplace, chat product, reviewer rating,
workflow language, or generic guest workspace. It grants no Page/Navigation
editing and has no Giving, Legal Entity, Stripe, settlement, bank, currency,
contribution, receipt, ledger, accounting, or public effect by itself.

The complete corrected contract, staff and external-reviewer journeys, source-
of-truth matrix, database/RLS boundary, 22-category adversarial review,
acceptance proof, monitors, rollout order, and traceability are recorded in
[phase-24-d25-candidate-scoped-external-reviewer-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d25-candidate-scoped-external-reviewer-adversarial-review.md).
The current repository and primary-source evidence is recorded separately in
[phase-24-d25-candidate-scoped-external-reviewer-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d25-candidate-scoped-external-reviewer-primary-research.md).
The cross-source authorization boundary is recorded in
[ADR-0181](../../../docs/adr/0181-source-authorized-candidate-scoped-external-review.md).

## D26 — When may staff choose an external reviewer if an internal reviewer is eligible?

### Why this needs your decision

D25 establishes a safe exact-candidate external-review capability for the
small-team dead end. It does not yet decide whether that capability should stay
hidden unless Core proves no internal reviewer exists. This matters because a
ministry may have an eligible internal Website reviewer but deliberately want a
bilingual board member, legal adviser, accessibility specialist, or other
trusted outside human for one source-approved protected change.

The choice changes disclosure and staff freedom, but it never changes D25's
scope: every external reviewer still receives one fresh candidate grant, one
minimum safe projection, no membership, and no standing access. No option
creates automatic external routing.

### Concrete Hope Ministries example

Ana is an eligible internal reviewer for Hope's French protected candidate.
Hope also uses Eli, a bilingual board member saved as a reviewer contact. Every
applicable source permits external review and can expose a safe complete
comparison. Should Maria be allowed to choose Eli instead of Ana?

### Option 1 — Tenant chooses a bounded availability posture — recommended

The platform default is **Only when no internal reviewer is eligible**. An
authorized Tenant Website administrator may instead enable **Allow external
review as an option for source-approved protected changes**. A Site may narrow
that Tenant choice but cannot widen it. Every source restriction, D23/D24 check,
and D25 projection/identity boundary still wins.

**Staff impact:** small ministries get recovery automatically, while Tenants
that routinely use board, language, legal, or accessibility reviewers can make
that choice without pretending those people are staff. It adds one bounded,
plain-language setting—not a policy builder.

### Option 2 — recovery only

External review appears only after a complete current resolver proves zero
eligible internal reviewers. If Ana is eligible, Maria must use Ana or change
the internal route; Eli cannot be chosen.

**Staff impact:** least external disclosure and the fewest settings, but it is
rigid for ministries with legitimate outside-review practices and makes Core
prove “zero internal” before the action appears.

### Option 3 — always offer external review whenever every source permits it

Every authorized staff member sees **Invite external reviewer** beside the
internal path for every source-approved protected candidate.

**Staff impact:** maximum immediate choice and no setup, but it exposes a
privacy-sensitive option to every Tenant by default and may encourage
unnecessary external sharing when the organization never asked for it.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — a bounded Tenant posture with recovery-only
as the safe default.** It best honors Tenant control and staff flexibility
without automatic disclosure, standing access, or another workflow product.

Do you choose **Option 1**, **Option 2 — recovery only**, or **Option 3 — always
offer external review when source-permitted**? You may amend any option.

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — bounded Tenant choice, provided it follows modern practice and
fits Core's staff UX/UI clearly.** Broad verification gates are deferred until
the end of the Grill-with-Docs session.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

The smallest complete policy has three explicit Tenant postures, not the
initial two:

1. `external_review_prohibited` — **Do not allow external review**;
2. `recovery_only` — **Only when no internal reviewer is eligible**, the
   platform and migration default; and
3. `source_permitted_choice` — **Allow external review as an option for
   source-approved changes**.

The third, stricter posture is necessary because capability and policy answer
different questions. A capability decides **who may manage or use an allowed
action**; the posture decides **whether the organization permits the external
disclosure at all**. Treating an absent capability as prohibition would make a
later role edit silently change policy and would leave staff and audit unable
to explain the organization choice.

Each Site inherits the current Tenant posture and may explicitly narrow to
recovery-only or prohibited. It never stores the permissive posture as an
override and can never widen its Tenant. The current effective result is the
strictest applicable platform, source, Tenant, Site, qualification, D23/D24,
and D25 result. Unknown, partial, stale, timed-out, or contradictory proof is
not zero internal reviewers and never releases the recovery path.

Saving policy creates no invitation, notification, saved-reviewer selection,
grant, guest, membership, route, task, Needs attention item, review,
publication, or public effect. Internal review remains the ordinary primary
path. Optional external review appears as a deliberate secondary action only
after a fresh exact-candidate evaluation, and every invitation still uses
D25's one-human, minimum-projection, expiring, non-transferable boundary.

Tenant staff see one **External review** card under Website **Review &
publishing** settings. It uses three descriptive radio cards—not an ambiguous
enable switch—with **Only when no internal reviewer is eligible** visibly
marked **Recommended**. Choosing a radio only changes the local form; an
explicit save shows the exact effect. Widening says **This does not send an
invitation**. Narrowing names how many current external reviews will lose
access, shows only rows the manager may already view, and uses a privacy-safe
aggregate for hidden rows. No typed phrase, justification essay, target date,
custom rule, or second confirmation is added.

A Site setting always shows **Organization choice**, **Site choice**, and
**Effective for this Site** separately, using the organization's actual display
name rather than the word Tenant. **Use Hope Ministries setting** is a real
inherit action, not a copied value. A stricter Site is labeled **Site setting**
and offers **Restore Hope Ministries setting**. When the organization prevents
a broader choice, Core explains why instead of displaying a broken disabled
control.

The posture is current authorization truth. A narrowing policy-head/epoch
change immediately denies pending or accepted D25 paths that no longer pass;
idempotent reconciliation then records **Ended by policy** without delaying
denial or changing the current website. Widening requires a fresh current
evaluation and never resurrects an expired, canceled, replaced, revoked,
superseded, ended, or completed invitation, credential, grant, session, or
link. Completed history remains immutable. New, cloned, imported, transferred,
or retired Sites cannot copy or carry an override or active grant across the
destination Tenant/environment boundary.

Tenant and Site policy management require distinct Phase 12 registry-owned
capabilities, trusted server-derived scope and actor, appropriate fresh
assurance, immutable policy versions, one current head, expected-head compare-
and-swap, purpose-limited audit, force-RLS parity, and current policy fencing on
every protected request. Core must not reuse the current hard-coded default-
Tenant/broad-role organization-settings implementation or treat browser input,
an app cache, a service role, support impersonation, or a generic settings JSON
document as authority.

The result is deliberately not a generic sharing center, role system, source
matrix, Page/locale/reviewer/domain rule builder, reviewer marketplace,
allowlist, workflow, reminder, SLA, schedule, or Giving/financial policy. Site
identity remains a behavior-neutral presentation-and-attribution context and
does not own this policy, Legal Entity, Stripe, settlement, bank, currency, or
accounting identity.

The modern-practice comparison supports the shape, not invented customer
demand: SharePoint and Google demonstrate organization ceilings with narrower
resource settings and visible inheritance; Microsoft Entra and Slack separate
external-collaboration availability from invitation authority; OWASP supports
least privilege, default deny, and authorization on every request; and W3C
supports explicit labeled radio choices, predictable save behavior, reflow,
status announcements, and accessible targets. Core intentionally improves on
general collaboration products by never leaving dormant candidate credentials
that silently reactivate.

The complete corrected D26-R1–D26-R18 contract, current/intended/permanent
distinctions, staff journeys and exact copy, source-of-truth and RLS boundary,
22-category adversarial review, 100 acceptance outcomes, monitors, rollout, and
unresolved assumptions are recorded in
[phase-24-d26-bounded-tenant-external-review-availability-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d26-bounded-tenant-external-review-availability-adversarial-review.md).
The current repository and primary-source evidence is recorded separately in
[phase-24-d26-bounded-tenant-external-review-availability-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d26-bounded-tenant-external-review-availability-primary-research.md).
The D25–D26 architecture boundary is recorded in
[ADR-0181](../../../docs/adr/0181-source-authorized-candidate-scoped-external-review.md).

## D27 — What happens to internal review attention when staff choose an external reviewer?

### Why this needs your decision

D26 now lets an organization deliberately choose an external reviewer even
when an internal reviewer is eligible. D21/D22 may already have given internal
staff personal **Needs attention** items. D25 guarantees that only one external
person can hold the candidate-scoped path, but it does not decide whether the
internal and external review lanes remain actionable together.

This is a staff-clarity decision, not a permission shortcut. Eligible internal
people keep their underlying Website capabilities under every option; the
choice decides who is visibly responsible and what action Core presents while
external review is in progress.

### Concrete Hope Ministries example

Ana has **Needs attention — Review the French default version**. Maria chooses
Eli, a bilingual external reviewer, and sends him the exact-version invitation.
Should Ana still be able to complete the same review while Eli is working?

### Option 1 — one visible lane with deliberate internal takeover — recommended

Sending Eli's invitation hands visible responsibility to **External review —
Eli Martin**. Ana's actionable item ends as **Reassigned**, while her read state
and underlying source permission remain truthful. Authorized internal staff see
**Eli is reviewing this version** and, when needed, **Take over review**. Taking
over first ends Eli's pending or accepted access and then creates the fresh
internal responsibility leg as one safe transition. A stale internal completion
cannot race through; Core explains that staff must take over first.

**Impact:** staff see one accountable reviewer, Eli is not asked to do work that
Ana may silently finish first, and Hope can recover immediately if Eli is slow,
unreachable, or invited by mistake. This adds one explicit handoff state but
reuses D21's differential handoff and D25's revoke-before-replace behavior.

### Option 2 — internal and external remain actionable; first valid review wins

Ana keeps her item while Eli receives the invitation. Either may complete the
exact current review; one server compare-and-swap wins and the other sees the
completed result.

**Impact:** this is mechanically simple and gives the fastest fallback, but it
creates duplicate work, unclear ownership, and potentially unnecessary external
disclosure. “Choose Eli” would not truly assign Eli the review.

### Option 3 — external review is exclusive until it ends

Ana's item ends and no internal reviewer can intervene until Eli completes,
declines, expires, loses access, or an authorized staff manager cancels the
external path.

**Impact:** ownership is very clear, but an invitation becomes an avoidable
operational lock. Staff can be stranded behind an unavailable external person.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — one visible review lane with deliberate
internal takeover.** It provides the clearest, least wasteful staff experience
without revoking anyone's underlying permission or making the external reviewer
an inflexible lock. It also gives failures an obvious recovery: **Send again**,
**Choose another external reviewer**, or **Return review to Hope Ministries**.

Do you choose **Option 1**, **Option 2 — parallel first-wins**, or **Option 3 —
external exclusive until it ends**? You may amend any option.

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — one visible review lane with deliberate takeover.**

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

The chosen experience is the best permanent direction, but **lane** must mean a
source-owned coordination posture—not an assignee, claim, lock, permission,
task, or notification row. One exact protected candidate and review epoch has
one current **Candidate review responsibility lane**: internal, external,
reassignment needed, or terminal. It selects one visible responsibility/action
path and grants no capability, qualification, membership, invitation access,
review result, or public effect.

The external handoff occurs when Core successfully commits the authority-free
D25 invitation in its own database—not when email dispatch succeeds, an inbox
receives it, Eli opens it, or Eli verifies and accepts. The consequence-led
action is **Send invitation and hand off**. If that local command fails, the
internal lane and items remain current. If it succeeds, the source advances the
lane externally, ends the current D21 internal routing occurrence as
`responsibility_reassigned`, records the D25 invitation, and appends the
delivery outbox obligation in one authoritative local transaction.

Provider acceptance, delivery, open, link activity, verified invitation
acceptance, projection access, review completion, and public effect remain
separate facts. Before verified acceptance, staff see **Waiting for Eli to
accept** and Eli has no candidate access. A proved or ambiguous delivery failure
keeps the one selected external lane and truthfully offers **Send again**,
**Replace external reviewer**, or **Return to internal review**. Core never
creates a parallel internal lane merely because email is uncertain.

Internal D21/D22 personal items end as **Reassigned to external review** where
the viewer may know that reason. Their unread/read history is neither copied nor
fabricated, nobody is marked as having reviewed, the saved internal route stays
unchanged, and old items never revive. External reviewers receive the focused
D25 invitation/review surface, never a staff bell, internal route membership,
generic Mission Control dashboard, or Tenant membership.

D27 explicitly narrows D22's ordinary current-action behavior without turning
the route into an allowlist. Internally qualified people retain their underlying
source capabilities, but while the external lane is current the candidate's
state fence replaces a competing final action with **Return to internal review**
or a source-admitted takeover action. Any currently source-authorized,
D23/D24-independent internal reviewer may initiate that transition even when
they are not a D21 recipient. A separately authorized manager may return
responsibility without gaining review authority. The command actor is never
silently assigned as the reviewer.

Returning internally atomically makes the invitation, grant, Phase 12 context,
and current external session inert before or with advancing the lane internally.
It then resolves the current D21 Site/Tenant route and appends one successor
routing occurrence. Newly selected qualified recipients receive fresh personal
items with fresh engagement. A completely proved zero-recipient route still
permits an internal lane with no items; the source remains discoverable and
performable by independently authorized staff. Indeterminate route resolution
does not revoke an otherwise-valid external path merely to attempt return;
independent current policy/security revocation may still end access and leave
**Review needs reassignment**.

One source compare-and-swap remains the completion authority. External
completion first makes takeover stale; takeover first makes external completion
stale; internal completion first prevents external handoff; and external
handoff first requires deliberate return before internal completion. Semantic
retry returns the same receipt. No provider/network call occurs while source,
lane, invitation, or review heads are locked.

Decline, expiry, cancellation, identity failure, policy loss, source withdrawal,
and candidate supersession are not review completion. They preserve immutable
history, deny incompatible external access immediately, revive nothing, and
either follow source terminal truth or enter **Review needs reassignment** until
the next-lane behavior is ratified by D28. The current public Site remains
unchanged.

The staff surface uses Base Maia status cards, sheets/dialogs, semantic tokens,
consequence-led buttons, explicit localized expiry, polite status announcements,
predictable focus, full keyboard operation, 320-CSS-pixel/400% reflow, shared
touch targets, RTL/long-Unicode resilience, and honest weak-network recovery.
It exposes no presence, email-open, time-spent, unfinished-note transfer,
countdown pressure, automatic reminder, or hidden reviewer identity.

The authoritative model requires immutable source-owned lane revisions, one
current head, mutually exclusive internal/external reference arcs, same-scope
Tenant/environment/Site/candidate/review-epoch relationships, restrictive
deletion, expected-head CAS, semantic idempotency, body-free receipts,
transactional outbox, indexed reverse/reconciliation paths, direct browser-
write revocation, `ENABLE` plus `FORCE RLS`, operation-correct `USING` and
`WITH CHECK`, trusted server-derived scope/actor, and identical RPC/view/worker/
service/support/Payload/import/repair/migration enforcement.

Current broad staff-role mappings, mutable Mission Control task assignees,
queues, reminders, the legacy `mission_control_attention_items` row, Payload,
email/provider events, and UI hiding are explicitly unsafe authorities for D27.
No current runtime implements this lane.

Modern products validate the trade-off dimensions rather than Core's exact
answer: HubSpot makes pending content approval explicit and supports cancel/
reassign; Salesforce exposes in-progress approval reassignment; Contentful
separates task assignment from permissions; Adobe distinguishes replacement
from parallel alternate recipients; Blackbaud supports explicit reviewer
reassignment while preserving submitted history; Power Automate distinguishes
first-response, all-response, and sequential approvals; and GitHub/GitLab make
parallel review explicit. Their standing users, super-admin bypasses, multiple
reviewers, due dates, reminders, and generic workflow machinery are not imported.
Core's one external lane remains a product judgment grounded in D21–D26.

The architecture trade-off is recorded in
[ADR-0182](../../../docs/adr/0182-one-current-candidate-review-responsibility-lane.md),
and the domain term is recorded in `CONTEXT.md`. The complete corrected
contract, current/intended/permanent distinctions, staff and reviewer journeys,
database/RLS boundary, 22-category adversarial review, acceptance proof,
monitors, rollout, and unknowns are recorded in
[phase-24-d27-one-visible-review-lane-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d27-one-visible-review-lane-adversarial-review.md).
The primary-source and repository evidence is recorded separately in
[phase-24-d27-one-visible-review-lane-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d27-one-visible-review-lane-primary-research.md).

## D28 — What happens if the selected external reviewer declines or their access expires?

### Why this needs your decision

D27 now guarantees one visible lane and no hidden parallel fallback. If Eli
declines or his invitation/grant expires before review, he has no access and no
review was completed. Core must decide whether to surprise the internal route
with automatically restored work or ask an authorized person to choose the next
lane.

Delivery failure is different: the invitation still exists and staff can send
it again. Policy/security loss and candidate supersession follow their own
current source rules. D28 is only about a declined or expired external path for
a still-current candidate that still needs review.

### Hope Ministries example

Maria deliberately chose Eli because he is bilingual even though Ana could
review internally. Eli later declines. Ana's old item cannot simply reopen;
D21/ADR-0027 require a fresh successor occurrence if responsibility returns.

Core shows:

```text
External review needs a next step

Eli declined this review.
Eli no longer has access. Nothing changed on hope.org.

What should happen next?
```

### Option 1 — one state-driven next-lane choice — recommended

Core does not notify internal reviewers automatically. It creates one
deduplicated **Needs attention** item only for the people currently authorized
to choose the next lane. Reading clears unread state but not the actionable
condition. The source page offers:

- **Invite another external reviewer**;
- **Return to internal review**; or
- **Keep the current version**.

The item ends when a successor lane commits or the source episode ends. It
creates no email or recurring reminder.

**Impact:** Maria may choose another bilingual reviewer instead of unexpectedly
routing the work to Ana. The unusual failure needs one explicit recovery step,
but the normal invitation flow gains no extra question.

### Option 2 — automatically return to the current internal route

Decline or expiry immediately resolves D21 and creates fresh internal items for
the currently qualified route members.

**Impact:** least staff effort and fastest continuation, but it silently reverses
Maria's deliberate choice, can surprise or re-notify internal staff, and must
invent behavior for zero or indeterminate routes.

### Option 3 — remain unassigned with no attention item

Core shows **Review needs reassignment** only when an authorized person happens
to revisit the candidate.

**Impact:** creates no notification noise, but the required review can be
forgotten indefinitely and staff may reasonably assume somebody else owns it.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — one state-driven next-lane choice.** It
preserves the meaning of choosing an external expert, avoids hidden routing,
and uses the already selected D19/D20 attention model only for the exceptional
recovery state. It is the clearest balance of staff control and discoverability.

Do you choose **Option 1**, **Option 2 — automatic internal return**, or
**Option 3 — remain unassigned without an item**? You may amend any option.

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — one explicit next-lane choice.** The experience must be excellent
for every user and consistent with Core's product and repository contracts.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

The explicit recovery choice is the safest and clearest permanent direction.
Automatic internal return would silently reverse a deliberate external handoff,
possibly surprise or re-notify staff, and invent unsafe behavior when route
proof is zero or unknown. Leaving the candidate unassigned without attention
would make required review easy to forget. The chosen answer therefore stands,
but its informal item/action wording must be narrowed before it is safe to
implement.

D28 applies only when the still-current candidate still requires review and its
current external path authoritatively becomes **declined** or **expired**.
Delivery failure remains in the external lane with resend/replace/return
recovery. Candidate or Plan terminality wins. Policy, identity, and security
loss follow their separately governed current rules.

Decline or expiry advances the source-owned Candidate review responsibility
lane to `reassignment_needed` and opens one immutable **Candidate review
reassignment episode** inside the existing candidate and review epoch. It does
not create a new D20 review-required episode. Duplicate expiry jobs, callbacks,
refreshes, retries, or permission revisions produce the same semantic episode;
a later fresh external lane that separately ends without review may produce a
new episode only after the prior one ended.

The phrase **one item** means one producer-proved episode and one semantically
idempotent Phase 6 occurrence, followed by one independently engaged Phase 17
item for each exact Tenant+Party+role+surface recipient. Core never creates one
shared Tenant row or shared read state. The occurrence identity derives from
trusted Tenant, environment, Site, source/candidate, review epoch, recovery
meaning, and reassignment-episode identity—not timestamp, email address, worker
attempt, UI session, or permission revision.

The compact notification preview is deliberately private:

```text
External review needs a next step

hope.org · French (Canada)
The external review ended before completion.
English (United States) remains live. Nothing changes automatically.

[Choose next review path]
```

Reviewer identity, contact, exact reason, candidate details, and feedback appear
only in a separately authorized source detail. Opening the item clears only the
viewer's unread engagement. The item remains in **Needs attention** while the
episode is actionable; it cannot be dismissed, archived, snoozed, aged out, or
converted into a task. Closing the Card, Sheet, or Dialog is a no-op and leaves
the item visible. No email, digest, push, recurring reminder, due date,
countdown, escalation, or age-derived urgency is created.

After a decline, an authorized detail may show:

```text
Choose how review should continue

Eli Ramos declined this review.
Eli no longer has access.

hope.org still opens English (United States).
The planned change is private. Giving is unchanged.

[Choose another external reviewer]
[Return to internal review]
```

After expiry, the same surface shows an absolute localized date, time, and time
zone and normally makes **Invite Eli again** primary, followed by **Choose
another external reviewer** and **Return to internal review** where currently
lawful. Every external choice creates a fresh D25 invitation after current
source, D26 posture, identity, eligibility, projection, and authority proof; no
expired or declined grant is revived. A stale or offline client can inspect only
safe current status and must reconnect before any lane mutation.

The action list is current-state driven rather than a fixed menu. If external
review is no longer permitted, external actions disappear and internal recovery
becomes primary. Under D26 recovery-only posture, a fresh external invitation is
available only under its accepted zero-internal-recovery proof. If the current
internal notification route proves zero but independently eligible internal
reviewers exist, **Return to internal review** may proceed with an explicit
warning that nobody will receive a notification and that the work remains
discoverable in **Site → Languages**. If internal eligibility proves zero, the
useless return action is omitted. If route or eligibility proof is stale,
partial, contradictory, timed out, over limit, or otherwise indeterminate, Core
does not label it zero and does not commit that return.

The original **Keep current version** button is rejected. The current Live
version already remains unchanged; a no-op cannot end required attention, and
silently treating the label as cancellation could destroy staff intent. The UI
instead states that Live and Giving remain unchanged. If an independently
authorized person wants to end the Plan, Core may expose D17's separate
**Cancel planned change** action with its exact consequence preview and
source-owned terminal command. That action is not a lane choice and never
deletes source-owned content or review evidence.

The reassignment episode ends exactly once when a fresh external invitation and
external lane commit, the D27 internal return commits, or an accepted
source-terminal disposition ends the candidate. Failed invitation creation,
failed route proof, read state, elapsed time, or a closed panel cannot end it.
Two staff choosing different paths race through one expected-head source/lane
compare-and-swap; one wins and the loser receives current truth without a
second invitation, route occurrence, item, or effect. A decline/expiry race
likewise records one truthful terminal result according to authoritative source
time and head state; late events cannot flap or reopen it.

Access and engagement remain recipient-specific. Every shown recipient must
currently see the exact private recovery context and be able to perform at
least one shown action. Losing access removes active/recent presentation
immediately. Gaining access later never revives an old item or inherits another
person's read state. A completely proved zero-recipient resolution releases a
zero-member occurrence and creates no guessed item; the source recovery state
remains permanently discoverable. Partial or indeterminate resolution releases
nobody and reconciles the same occurrence.

The source owns immutable reassignment episodes, lane revisions, one current
head, terminal reason, source end, and recovery command receipts. Phase 6/17
owns only occurrence, recipient item, and personal engagement projections. The
permanent storage boundary uses same-scope Tenant/environment/Site/source/
candidate/review-epoch keys, restrictive deletion, unique semantic occurrence
and per-recipient item slots, expected-head CAS, semantic idempotency,
transactional outbox reconciliation, body-free audit, direct-browser-write
revocation, `ENABLE` plus `FORCE RLS`, operation-correct `USING` and `WITH
CHECK`, trusted server-derived actor/scope/recipient/authority facts, and the
same poison matrix for RPCs, views, workers, service-role, support, repair,
cache, realtime, import, export, and migration paths.

Current runtime implements none of D25–D28. Its broad MVP permissions, mutable
Mission Control tasks, Tenant-shared `mission_control_attention_items`, donor/
email `notification_queue`, CMS state, and provider delivery state are unsafe
authorities and must not be reused or dual-written. The D28 notification key
remains Reserved until the next decision specifies its exact responsibility
route, recipient role, cardinality, and bounded resolver. Active OpenSpec must
also be reconciled from its obsolete latest-editor independence wording to
D24's every-substantive-participant contract before any D28 key can become
Live.

The staff surface reuses Core's Base Maia Card and responsive Sheet/Dialog
vocabulary, semantic tokens, ordinary buttons, consequence-led confirmations,
stable focus, polite status announcements, full keyboard operation, minimum
important target size, 320-CSS-pixel/400% reflow, forced-color and reduced-
motion support, long-name/CJK/RTL resilience, absolute localized expiry, and
truthful weak-network recovery. It does not create a workflow builder, queue,
claim, SLA, new task center, or reviewer-performance score.

Current first-party product evidence supports the useful pattern but not Core's
authority model: Blackbaud exposes review decline/reassignment; HubSpot keeps
content approval visible and explicitly cancelable/reassignable; Salesforce
limits reassignment to an ongoing assigned work item and an approval-admin
action; Power Automate separates pending approvals from explicit cancel/
reassign actions; Contentful keeps assigned work discoverable; GitHub permits
explicit re-request; and Linear distinguishes inbox read state from underlying
issue state. Their standing users, broad admins, parallel reviewers, task
assignment, due dates, reminders, email defaults, snooze, and generic workflow
machinery are negative evidence and are not imported.

This closes the recovery behavior in
[ADR-0182](../../../docs/adr/0182-one-current-candidate-review-responsibility-lane.md)
and adds the reassignment-episode term to `CONTEXT.md`. The complete corrected
contract, current/intended/permanent distinctions, UX journeys, database/RLS
boundary, all 22 adversarial categories, acceptance proof, monitors, rollout,
and unknowns are recorded in
[phase-24-d28-explicit-next-lane-choice-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d28-explicit-next-lane-choice-adversarial-review.md).
The primary-source and repository evidence is recorded separately in
[phase-24-d28-explicit-next-lane-choice-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d28-explicit-next-lane-choice-primary-research.md).

## D29 — Who should receive “External review needs a next step”?

### Why this needs your decision

D28 establishes the recovery episode and what an authorized person may do, but
permission does not prove responsibility. Core must not silently notify every
admin/capability holder, assume that internal reviewers manage external
handoffs, or make the original inviter a permanent owner. This decision chooses
the small, resilient group that Core should actively bring back to the work;
current authorization is still re-proved separately for every view and action.

### Hope Ministries example

Maria invited Eli, but Maria later leaves Hope Ministries. Eli's invitation
expires. Ana is qualified to review French internally, Joel manages Website
access, and Priya coordinates Hope's website reviews. Who should receive the
new personal **Needs attention** item?

### Option 1 — 1–3 explicit Website review coordinators — recommended

Hope selects one to three people under **Settings → Websites → Reviews**, with
a Tenant default and optional Site override. This is a distinct responsibility
meaning from “who reviews”; the editor asks **Who chooses the next step?** and
explains:

> These people choose what happens when an external review ends. This does not
> give them permission to review, invite, or change the website.

The picker shows visible active same-Tenant staff and presents current
qualification as a separate warning rather than a permission grant or rigid
admission rule. It explains the effect before save, preserves inheritance
explicitly, and uses the same bounded route/version/zero/unknown patterns as
D21/D22. At event time Core sends personal items only to selected coordinators
who can then see the exact candidate and perform at least one lawful next
action.

**Impact:** clearest ownership, least noise, resilient when one person leaves,
and consistent with Core's rule that permission and responsibility are
different. It adds one small setup choice, but not a workflow builder or a
per-candidate assignment step.

### Option 2 — every holder of the exact recovery capability

Core sends the item to every currently bounded person who may perform at least
one recovery action.

**Impact:** no new setting and good theoretical coverage, but permission changes
silently change responsibility, larger Tenants may receive noisy fan-out, and
staff cannot answer “why was I notified?” from an intentional route.

### Option 3 — original inviter first, then current managers

Core initially routes to the staff person who sent the external invitation and
falls back to current recovery managers if that person is no longer eligible.

**Impact:** low initial noise and intuitive in the simplest case, but it couples
future responsibility to a historical actor, fails awkwardly during leave or
turnover, and introduces a hidden fallback hierarchy that is difficult to
explain and test.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — 1–3 explicit Website review coordinators.**
It gives Hope a small, visible owner group without granting new authority,
reuses Core's proven Tenant/Site responsibility-route UX, and avoids both noisy
broadcasts and brittle original-inviter coupling.

Do you choose **Option 1 — explicit coordinators**, **Option 2 — every exact-
capability holder**, or **Option 3 — original inviter with manager fallback**?
You may amend any option.

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — one to three explicit Website review coordinators.** The result
must create more clarity than confusion and provide excellent, modern UX/UI for
everyone who configures, receives, or encounters the follow-up state.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

The chosen direction is stronger than capability broadcast or original-inviter
fallback, but the bare phrase “1–3 coordinators” is not implementable safely.
It must be recorded as one distinct, versioned **Website review follow-up
route**, whose user-facing members are **Review coordinators**. The route owns
only deliberate responsibility intent. It is not a permission role, reviewer
roster, team, shared task, queue, availability model, or action allowlist.

One person is the recommended ordinary setup. A Tenant may deliberately add up
to two more only when responsibility is genuinely shared. The one-to-three
members are distinct, stable, same-Tenant Parties, unordered and co-equal. No
primary, backup, rank, round robin, quorum, claim, escalation, workload,
presence, leave, or time-based behavior exists. A duplicate or fourth member
rejects atomically; the previous route remains current. Three is a code-owned
v1 product bound—not a universal external best practice or a Tenant setting—and
can change only through a versioned decision with new comprehension, noise,
privacy, scale, migration, and rollout proof.

D29 remains completely separate from D21. Core may reuse D21/D22's typed route
revision, bounded resolver, personal-item, handoff, and audit machinery, but it
never copies, aliases, synchronizes, suggests, or dynamically uses the Website
reviewer roster. A person may be deliberately selected in both routes, but the
memberships, route purposes, recipient roles, revisions, occurrences, and audit
meanings remain independent.

A new or migrated Tenant starts visibly **Not configured**; Core infers nobody
from the current user, creator, editor, inviter, prior actor, reviewer, admin,
capability holder, role, group, team, support user, AI, or legacy task. Ordinary
Sites inherit the Tenant posture by reference without copied member rows. An
authorized manager may deliberately turn Tenant follow-up off; **off** remains
distinct from never configured and is not an empty configured route. A Site may
inherit, deliberately send no Site follow-up item, or choose one to three
different coordinators. A Site member route also records exactly one visible
outcome if no Site coordinator can currently act:

- **Use Hope Ministries review coordinators** — recommended; or
- **Send no follow-up item**.

If even one Site coordinator is currently qualified, the qualified Site set is
the only recipient set; Tenant coordinators do not join it. Tenant fallback may
run only after complete proof that zero Site members qualify. Partial, stale,
timed-out, contradictory, corrupt, over-limit, or otherwise indeterminate proof
releases nobody and never widens the audience. A healthy routing leg remains
stable; later access recovery does not bounce responsibility back or revive an
old item.

The picker searches only visible active same-Tenant staff. It binds stable Party
identity, not name or email text, and shows current qualification as a separate
plain-language status. At Site scope it says either **Can currently receive
follow-up for hope.org** or **Cannot currently receive — selecting this person
does not grant access**. At Tenant scope it may show only a privacy-safe coverage
summary over Sites the manager may enumerate. An active person may still be
selected as prospective responsibility intent despite a current qualification
warning; only independently qualified people receive an event item. This keeps
the setting flexible without pretending that responsibility grants authority.

At each D28 reassignment episode, the server intersects the winning explicit
route with exact current Tenant Assignment, stable Party, Site/candidate
visibility, Phase 12 policy and authorization epochs, the fixed D29 recipient
role/surface, and at least one lawful successor-lane action: issue a fresh
external invitation or return to internal review. **Cancel planned change**
alone does not qualify a coordinator because cancellation is a separate
source-terminal authority. Different coordinators may see different lawful
actions; item possession never unions their permissions. An independently
authorized non-coordinator may still act from the source page.

One D28 episode creates one semantic Phase 6 occurrence and one personal Phase
17 item for each exact qualified Party+role+surface. There is no shared item or
read state. Opening clears only that person's unread engagement and never
claims, assigns, completes, or hides the work. The item remains in **Needs
attention** until one successful source command chooses the next lane or the
source becomes terminal. One source compare-and-swap winner ends every
applicable sibling item. Access loss removes protected presentation; later
access never revives old engagement. D29 creates no recurring reminder, email,
push, SMS, due date, countdown, task, comment thread, public change, Giving
effect, or financial effect.

Unconfigured, deliberately no-item, configured-but-proved-zero, or indeterminate
D29 coverage never blocks an independently authorized D25 external handoff. At
the consequential confirmation, Core uses distinct truthful copy. For an
unconfigured posture it says:

```text
External review follow-up isn't assigned

If this review ends without a decision, no one will receive a Needs attention
item. Authorized staff can still find it in Languages.

[Set follow-up coordinators]   [Send invitation and hand off]
```

Only a separately authorized route manager sees setup. Deliberate no-item says
**External review follow-up is off**; configured-but-proved-zero says **No
coordinator can currently receive follow-up**; indeterminate says **We couldn't
confirm follow-up coverage** and that Core will not guess or broaden. The
authorized source action remains available when its own D25/D26/source proofs
pass.

The staff information architecture is one coherent **Settings → Websites →
Reviews** page titled **Website reviews**:

```text
Website reviews

Review responsibilities

Review notifications
Who normally receives private attention when a Website Plan is ready for
review, changed since review, or affected by a current-default change.

External review follow-up
Who receives attention to choose the next path when an outside review ends
without a decision.

External review
When authorized staff may invite one outside person.
```

**Review responsibilities** is a section, not the page title, because D26's
availability posture is policy rather than a roster. The D29 card asks **Who
chooses the next step?**, names decline and invitation expiry, displays the
current coordinators and safe Site usage summary, and repeats that selection
grants no permission. **Change coordinators** opens a responsive shared Base
Maia Sheet with one searchable combobox and selected-person rows outside the
listbox. One person is visibly “usually clearest”; **Add coverage** progressively
reveals the second and third choice; at three the UI says **3 people selected ·
maximum** and explains how to replace someone. There are no empty quota slots,
avatars-as-status, flags, drag ordering, select-all, groups, or hidden defaults.

Ordinary prospective save is one step and needs no confirmation dialog. It says
that future follow-up will use the saved route and that current follow-ups kept
their recipients. If current D28 episodes exist, an independently authorized
**Review current follow-up** action opens a fresh privacy-filtered impact
preview. Unchanged recipients keep their item and engagement with no new unread;
removed recipients leave active attention without fabricated read or revoked
permission; newly admitted qualified recipients receive one successor item.
Stale impact changes nothing and requests a fresh preview.

An empty configured route is impossible. Removing the final Tenant coordinator
requires the deliberate action **Stop follow-up notifications** with the Site
and current-work consequence; the resulting **External review follow-up is
off** posture is not **Not configured**. Removing the final Site coordinator
requires an explicit choice to inherit the Tenant posture or send no Site item.
Neither ordinary save nor removal silently reassigns current work, changes
access, alters source state, or affects the public Site or Giving.

The responsive Sheet, last-person Dialog, radio groups, combobox, selected rows,
status messages, and errors use shared `@asym/ui` Base Maia/Base UI primitives
and semantic tokens. The flow requires visible labels, stable focus and focus
return, keyboard and screen-reader support, 44-by-44 important targets,
320-CSS-pixel/400% reflow, forced colors, reduced motion, long Unicode/CJK names,
RTL/bidi isolation, localized plurals, mobile safe areas, on-screen-keyboard
reachability, cancelable paginated search, persistent non-toast-only results,
and truthful offline/conflict/lost-response recovery. Avatars are decorative;
color, icon, order, position, or motion never carries decisive meaning alone.

The permanent data boundary is relational and typed: append-only Tenant/Site
route revisions, one current head per exact Tenant+environment+scope+purpose,
normalized stable-Party members, a canonical unordered-set digest, closed
inherit/override/fallback modes, immutable receipts and body-free audit, and
separate D28 source, Phase 6 occurrence, Phase 17 item, and engagement owners.
No mutable JSON roster, CMS collection, generic workflow engine, task row, or
read model becomes authority. The protected command validates the whole 1–3 set,
releases the revision last, and advances one expected head atomically.

Browser business writes are revoked. Exposed relations use least grants plus
`ENABLE` and `FORCE RLS`; `USING` proves the existing row and `WITH CHECK` the
resulting row, so an allowed mutation cannot move Tenant, environment, Site,
purpose, Party, role, actor, or head. Tenant, actor, scope, route purpose,
qualification, recipient set, and audit attribution are server-derived.
Security-definer, owner, service-role, worker, RPC, view, support, repair,
import, export, cache, realtime, clone, transfer, and migration paths pass the
same authorization and cross-Tenant poison matrix. Same-key/same-meaning retries
return one receipt; changed meaning rejects; slow enumeration and provider work
never run under route/source locks.

The shared Mission Control task requirement applies to independently lifecycle-
owned staff tasks and its contribution-facing Needs Attention view. It does not
reclassify ADR-0027 recipient-specific, source-actionable items as tasks. The
dedicated OpenSpec pass must add that clarification; this Grill does not mutate
OpenSpec prematurely.

The modern external evidence supports explicit named responsibility, targeted
notification to reduce noise, separate assignment and permission, deliberate
reassignment, accessible people selection, deny-by-default authorization, and
RLS plus grant/privileged-path parity. It does not prove that three is universally
optimal, that every ministry needs D29, or that Tenant inheritance matches every
ministry. Those remain explicit Core product judgments gated by representative
nonprofit comprehension/task testing and named launch monitors.

All 22 required adversarial categories contain a material concern under an
unamended or incorrectly implemented answer; none invalidates the explicit-route
direction. The amendments above resolve the decision-level concerns. The full
current/intended/permanent analysis, exact concern structures, 25 corrected
rules, 130 independently testable acceptance criteria, 24 named signals with
threshold/owner/response, rollout, rollback, and evidence limits are recorded in
[phase-24-d29-explicit-website-review-coordinators-adversarial-review.md](./phase-24-d29-explicit-website-review-coordinators-adversarial-review.md).
Primary repository and external evidence is recorded in
[phase-24-d29-explicit-website-review-coordinators-primary-research.md](./phase-24-d29-explicit-website-review-coordinators-primary-research.md).
The accepted architecture is amended in
[ADR-0182](../../../docs/adr/0182-one-current-candidate-review-responsibility-lane.md),
and the canonical **Website review follow-up route** term is added to
`CONTEXT.md`.

D29 closes the founder-level recipient-responsibility decision. The D28/D29 key
remains **Reserved**, not Live, until Phase 12, D19/Phase 6/17, D21–D29, source
adapters, OpenSpec, schema/RLS, migration, accessibility, production-shaped
tests, canary, monitors, and release evidence implement the same contract.

## D30 — What feedback must accompany Request changes?

### Why this needs your decision

D25 already makes **Request changes** a terminal result for the exact external
review, and any corrected successor candidate must receive fresh review. What
is still unresolved is the minimum feedback needed to make that result useful.
A bare result is fast but may leave staff with no idea what to repair. A large
structured form could burden a simple correction and accidentally create a
comments, task, checklist, or quality-assurance product.

### Hope Ministries example

Eli reviews Hope Ministries' French (Canada) candidate and discovers that its
**Contact us** link still opens the English page. He selects **Request changes**.
Maria needs to know what to fix before creating the successor candidate. What
must Eli provide before the review ends?

### Option 1 — one required concise explanation — recommended

The focused review surface asks **What needs to change?** and requires one
bounded private explanation tied to this exact candidate and result. Eli may
optionally anchor it to a visible source section. Core adds no required category,
checklist, assignee, due date, attachment, comment thread, mention, or suggested-
edit system.

**End-user experience:** Eli writes “The Contact us link opens the English page”
and submits. Maria sees that private explanation alongside the returned
candidate and can fix the exact issue.

**Impact:** this is the smallest dependable amount of actionable context and
keeps reviewer friction low. The spec must still define safe length, privacy,
retention, display, localization, source-anchor behavior, and successor-
candidate lineage.

### Option 2 — optional note

Eli may submit **Request changes** without any explanation.

**End-user experience:** the quickest possible submit, but Maria may see only
“Changes requested” and must inspect the whole candidate or contact Eli outside
Core.

**Impact:** lowest reviewer friction, highest ambiguity and rework risk. A
helpful placeholder cannot guarantee actionable context.

### Option 3 — required structured checklist

Each affected source defines categories and required fields before **Request
changes** can submit.

**End-user experience:** Eli classifies the issue and completes prescribed
fields, giving Maria consistent detail when the taxonomy fits.

**Impact:** potentially useful for mature repeatable programs, but likely
disproportionate for ordinary Website review. It freezes unproved categories,
adds translation/accessibility/configuration burden, and risks a second form or
workflow engine.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — one required concise explanation, with
optional source anchors.** It is the smallest permanent rule that makes
**Request changes** genuinely actionable without importing comments, tasks,
checklists, assignments, or a collaboration system.

Do you choose **Option 1 — required concise explanation**, **Option 2 — optional
note**, or **Option 3 — structured checklist**? You may amend any option.

### Founder answer (D30)

**One required concise explanation; optional source anchor.**

### D30 adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.**

The root decision is correct and follows a strong current pattern, but it is
not a universal industry rule. GitHub's current review API requires a body for
`REQUEST_CHANGES`; HubSpot requires requested-changes text in a comparable
approval flow; and Contentful proves that one bounded, version-bound feedback
body can remain much smaller than a conversation product. GitLab and Microsoft
Power Automate also show legitimate optional-comment models, so Core records
the requirement as a source-specific product judgment: an external reviewer who
asserts that this exact candidate must be repaired must provide the smallest
useful context before losing access. Core does not import code-review threads,
CRM workflow builders, or a grant-review taxonomy.

The phrase “concise explanation” was unsafe until the count, normalization,
privacy, lifecycle, UI, and authority boundaries were made exact. The final v1
ceiling is **1,000 Unicode code points after NFC, line-ending normalization,
and surrounding-whitespace trimming**. Five hundred is unnecessarily tight for
several related corrections and international text. Two thousand is cheap to
store and appears in a different Blackbaud nonprofit rejection context, but it
permits roughly a mini-specification, increases staff scanning and sensitive-
paste exposure, and weakens the founder's explicit “concise” choice without
evidence that 1,000 is insufficient. The UI lets reviewers paste over the
ceiling and edit down; it never silently truncates. A named limit-pressure
monitor requires review if more than 2% of at least 100 nonempty sessions hit
the ceiling in 30 days, with a versioned increase—not abbreviation advice,
attachments, or external email—when legitimate original-language evidence
requires it.

The corrected permanent decision is:

> Every valid external-review **Request changes** result contains exactly one
> private Unicode plain-text **Request-changes explanation** answering **What
> needs to change?** for the exact immutable candidate and review epoch. The
> accepted canonical body contains 1–1,000 Unicode code points. It accepts
> ordinary international scripts, punctuation, emoji, combining marks, and
> line breaks; it has no word, sentence, category, sentiment, language, secret,
> payment, or AI “quality” heuristic gate. It is inert plain text, never
> Markdown, HTML, rich text, an auto-link, command, or prompt.
>
> The reviewer may attach zero or one **Review source anchor** offered by the
> exact source projection. It is an opaque source-owned identity bound to the
> Tenant, environment, Site, source, candidate, review epoch, adapter version,
> and projection digest. It is never caller text, a URL, path, DOM/CSS/XPath
> selector, array index, selected quote, copied content, or permission. Absence
> never blocks submission; an invalid supplied anchor rejects without silently
> dropping it. A committed anchor opens only the retained original projection
> under current authorization and never retargets to Live or a successor.
>
> One source-owned expected-head command re-proves the current external-review
> context, stable human, D23/D24 independence, D26 posture, D27 lane, source
> admission, candidate/projection heads, assurance, expiry, revocation,
> explanation, and optional anchor. It atomically appends the terminal result,
> protected readable-body reference, anchor, immutable receipt, source/lane
> transition, trusted attribution, body-free audit, and authorization-context
> end. Same key and same canonical meaning returns the original receipt;
> changed meaning rejects; stale or concurrent losers write nothing.
>
> Request changes is terminal for that exact external review but is not
> approval, decline, expiry, rejection, cancellation, D28 reassignment,
> publication, source editing, successor creation, or notification delivery.
> The candidate, current Live Website, and Giving remain unchanged. Any
> corrected successor is a new candidate requiring fresh participation,
> policy, lane, and review proof; prior feedback may be referenced read-only but
> is never copied as successor authority.
>
> The explanation is visible only through current purpose-specific source
> authorization. It never appears in notifications, email, SMS, push, webhook
> previews, logs, traces, metrics, analytics, cache keys, session replay,
> search, AI, generic exports, CMS fields, tasks, comments, public surfaces,
> Giving, or finance. It follows the source's named records schedule. A narrow
> audited privacy/security command may quarantine and dispose of sensitive text
> without rewriting the result, actor, protected keyed non-enumerable
> fingerprint, or body-free history. Raw or unsalted body hashes are forbidden
> and fingerprints never enter telemetry.
>
> D30 creates no reply, thread, reaction, mention, category, severity,
> checklist, assignee, due date, attachment, suggested edit, resolution state,
> machine translation, or generic workflow engine.

### D30 reviewer UX/UI

The final action uses a responsive **in-flow Base Maia decision Card**, not a
modal, Sheet, popover, or comments sidebar. The exact Current/Proposed/Unchanged
evidence remains scrollable while the reviewer writes or adds the one location.
On narrow screens the same Card stacks immediately after the action; it does
not trap focus or make evidence inert. Opening the Card has no business effect.

```text
Request changes

Tell Hope Ministries what must be corrected. This ends your review of this
version. The current Website and Giving stay unchanged.

What needs to change? (required)
Visible only on this review to authorized Hope Ministries staff.
Be specific enough for staff to act. Do not include passwords, payment or donor
details, or private personal or ministry-location information. Up to 1,000
characters.

[The Contact us link opens the English page.                         ]

Related section (optional)
Contact us link · French (Canada)                     [Change] [Remove]

[Keep reviewing]                              [Request changes]
```

The textarea begins at a useful multi-line height and grows without obscuring
errors or actions. The visible count stays quiet below 80% while the limit is
programmatically available on field entry; meaningful, throttled announcements
