## D38 — Who should initially hold and grant the Tenant-wide application capability?

### Why this needs your decision

Hope Ministries lets Ana configure **Returned Website work** for future
occurrences. Jordan is responsible for organization-wide operational changes
across restricted Sites. D37 correctly prevents Ana's policy-edit permission
from silently authorizing Tenant-wide current adoption, but Core still needs a
safe and understandable way for Jordan to receive that authority—and must
decide whether a Tenant can deliberately leave it unassigned.

This is not just implementation wiring. The choice determines least privilege,
small-ministry setup friction, audit/revocation ownership, who can change many
people's Tasks Hub work at once, and whether the “separate capability” remains
real or quietly collapses back into a broad role.

### Option 1 — explicit Tenant governance grant; zero holders allowed — recommended

A separately authorized Tenant access administrator deliberately grants
**Apply Website recovery settings to current work** to a trusted active staff
member through Core's intended Phase 12 authorization system. The grant is Tenant-scoped,
visible to authorized access administrators, audited, revocable, and grants no
source detail, policy edit, coordinator qualification, task administration, or
source assignment. A Tenant may have zero holders; prospective saving and the
complete Needs assignment lane still work.

**User/Tenant UX:** policy editors see a clean prospective save; capable
operators see the quiet current-work action; access administrators manage one
plain-language permission in the future product-backed People & access UI. No Website-specific
holder roster, title inference, disabled-control clutter, or artificial minimum
holder count is needed.

**Impact:** strongest least privilege and separation of duties with modest
one-time setup. It requires a precisely governed bootstrap administrator and
clear grant/revoke history.

### Option 2 — automatically grant every Tenant administrator

Every current Tenant administrator receives the capability by default.

**User/Tenant UX:** no setup, but administrators responsible for unrelated
areas silently gain authority to add or end personal coordinator work across
restricted Sites.

**Impact:** lowest friction and broader blast radius; current broad role labels
become product authorization and are harder to narrow safely later.

### Option 3 — automatically grant every recovery-policy editor

Anyone who can save the prospective D35 policy can apply it to current work.

**User/Tenant UX:** setting and action always appear together, but a Tenant
cannot separate ordinary future configuration from high-impact current backlog
mutation.

**Impact:** directly collapses the D36/D37 separation and should be rejected.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — explicit Tenant governance grant with zero
holders allowed.** It follows least privilege, preserves a fully usable
zero-holder fallback, avoids a new Website-specific role/roster, and keeps
granting and revocation clear, auditable, and reversible.

Do you choose **Option 1 — explicit Tenant governance grant; zero holders
allowed**, **Option 2 — every Tenant administrator by default**, or **Option 3
— every recovery-policy editor by default**? You may amend any option.

### D38 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — explicit Tenant governance grant with zero
holders allowed, after a complete Core UX/UI and modern-practice review.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> Core registers **Apply Website recovery settings to current work** as one
> narrow Tenant-scoped, `explicit_only` Phase 12 capability. It authorizes only
> D37 preparation, exact complete aggregate review, acceptance, safe status/
> result, and retry/reconciliation. It grants no policy edit, source record,
> Site, D30/D34 context, correction action, coordinator qualification, Tasks
> Hub administration, public Website, Giving, finance, export, or other
> authority.
>
> It is seeded nowhere and implied by nothing. Tenant Owner, administrator,
> staff role, Content/Web Studio group, policy editor, Site/source visibility,
> coordinator membership, task authority, previous application, support
> context, and `super_admin` label do not grant it. Migration infers no holder.
>
> Zero **effective** holders is valid and quiet. Prospective D35 save, the
> source-owned Needs assignment lane, and ordinary authorized source assignment
> continue to work. Zero creates no fallback holder, setup error, warning,
> Needs-attention item, email, reminder, recurring task, SLA, escalation, or
> health failure.
>
> Grant authority is separate from application authority. Only a current same-
> Tenant principal resolving `permissions.manage_grants` within a live delegated
> scope and capability ceiling may grant or revoke. The grantor need not hold
> D38. Current `admin`/staff/role checks, route visibility, and service-role
> access are insufficient. Phase 12's existing quorum-aware self-grant,
> separation-of-duties, last-permissions-manager, delegation, and recovery
> rules apply; D38 creates no duplicate approval or break-glass system.
>
> Phase 12's registry coverage becomes `registry = bundled-map capabilities ∪
explicit-only catalog`. Bundled capabilities remain covered by the reviewed
> None/View/Manage/Admin map; explicit-only capabilities remain deliberately
> assignable but absent from every ladder and seed. D38 is explicit-only, and
> its presence in Owner, Web Studio, a role, or default group is a build
> failure.
>
> Every human grant resolves through one exact active same-Tenant staff Active
> Tenant Assignment, never bare profile, Party, email, title, invitation,
> donor/missionary identity, external reviewer, support operator, service
> account, AI, or cross-Tenant group. Assignment end prevents attachment to a
> later/recreated assignment. D39 permits typed direct assignment and protected
> flat Access-group sources through one Phase 12 EffectiveAccess model.
>
> The grant/revoke command derives Tenant, actual/acting actor, grantor
> assignment, subject, capability, source/provenance, delegation, and time from
> trusted server context. One visible duration choice—**Until removed** or an
> optional expiry—and one concise business reason are reviewed with exact
> ability/non-effects. The reason is governed audit evidence and may contain no
> protected ministry, person, Site, care, donor, correction, or source detail.
>
> Every mutation uses Phase 12's expected-head, semantic-idempotent, advisory-
> locked command and atomically commits grant state, Tenant governance epoch,
> append-only audit, and durable receipt. Exact replay returns the receipt;
> changed meaning conflicts. No Website grant table, roster, JSON list, role,
> local expiry, approval, PIM, access-review, or notification engine is added.
>
> Current EffectiveAccess—not a row, role, token, badge, cache, or historic
> event—determines exercise and the deduplicated holder count. Authorized
> access UX explains every direct/group/expiry/delegation path. Removing one
> path never claims access ended when another survives; a group change states
> its full authorized member consequence.
>
> Removing the final effective D38 holder is allowed after one proportionate
> consequence review. It explains that no one can start a Tenant-wide current-
> work update until a grant is added, while new work and Needs assignment
> remain usable. It requires no typed phrase, forced second approver, or alarm
> styling.
>
> Revocation, expiry, Active Tenant Assignment end, suspension, or applicable
> delegation end advances/invalidates the Phase 12 governance boundary and
> fences every uncommitted D37 member. Permission managers may see only whether
> the subject has an active application and that remaining work will stop;
> source identities/counts/results remain hidden. Committed D37 history stays
> immutable, and regrant requires a fresh D37 review/application.
>
> The durable UX belongs in Phase 12 **People & access** and **My Access**, not
> a Website roster and not the current seed-backed **Teams & Users** demo. D38
> appears under **Additional permissions → Website operations** with plain
> organization-wide scope, exact non-effects, duration, current provenance, and
> audit. A holder can reach a focused safe **Current-work update** route without
> receiving policy-edit authority. A non-holder policy editor sees only the
> quiet prospective-save result and no disabled action, holder/backlog oracle,
> request dead end, or nag.
>
> The review is one responsive, non-nested, receipt-backed Core Base Maia flow.
> It preserves semantic labels, 44-pixel targets, keyboard/focus behavior,
> programmatic status, 320-pixel/400-percent reflow, forced colors, reduced
> motion, international names, RTL, localized expiry, and low-bandwidth lost-
> response recovery. A toast is supplementary.
>
> Same-Tenant constraints, immutable scope, restrictive deletes, indexed
> current heads, `ENABLE` plus `FORCE RLS`, operation-correct `USING`/
> `WITH CHECK`, least grants, pinned functions, and owner/service/RPC/worker/
> support/repair/import/export/cache/Realtime/AI parity preserve the boundary.
> Inngest may later reconcile identifier-only Phase 12 effects but never owns a
> grant, holder, expiry, epoch, or revocation fence.

## D39 — Which central assignment surfaces may carry D38?

### Why this needs your decision

Hope Ministries has one operations lead, so a direct grant is easiest. Larger
Mission Network has six rotating Website operations staff already managed
through a governed Phase 12 group. Direct-only can drift at scale; group-only
creates ceremony for a one-person ministry; both is safe only if Core explains
every path and a revoke never falsely claims access ended.

This chooses the grant subject/source. It does not change who may administer
grants, who can edit recovery policy, or who can see source work.

### Option 1 — direct Active Tenant Assignment and governed flat group — recommended

Permit both through one Phase 12 EffectiveAccess/provenance/epoch model. Create
no seeded Website group; permit no nesting, dynamic/external membership, role
mapping, or Website-local roster. `permissions.manage_grants` attaches D38 to
the group; the separate scoped `permissions.manage_membership` command manages
people and must show the D38 consequence.

**User/Tenant UX:** small ministries grant one person directly; larger
ministries manage a stable job-function group. Person detail always says
**Direct grant** and/or **Through [group]** and shows the real post-revoke
result.

**Impact:** best permanent flexibility with no second authorization engine;
group changes require complete consequence review and audit.

### Option 2 — direct Active Tenant Assignment only

Every holder receives an individual grant.

**User/Tenant UX:** simplest provenance for the expected small holder set.

**Impact:** larger organizations repeat grants/offboarding and may drift; group
support later changes the source model.

### Option 3 — governed flat group only

Every holder receives D38 through one or more managed groups.

**User/Tenant UX:** centralized rotation for larger teams.

**Impact:** needless group creation and maintenance for a one-person or
two-person ministry.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — both direct and governed flat-group
assignment through Phase 12, with no seeded group and one complete provenance
model.** It matches mature IAM's direct-for-one-off/group-for-job-function
pattern and supports small and larger ministries without permission sprawl.

Which mode should D39 record: **Option 1 — both direct and governed flat
group**, **Option 2 — direct only**, or **Option 3 — group only**?

### D39 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — both direct Active Tenant Assignment and
governed flat-group assignment through one Phase 12 EffectiveAccess model,
after deeper modern-practice and Core UX/UI review.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> Phase 12 permits D38 through exactly two central sources: (1) one direct,
> typed capability grant to an exact active same-Tenant staff Active Tenant
> Assignment, and (2) one capability grant to a governed flat **Access group**
> whose current active members each bind an exact active same-Tenant staff
> Active Tenant Assignment. Direct assignment serves a specific person or
> exception; an Access group serves a stable job function. Neither source is
> required, seeded, inferred, or created automatically.
>
> Both sources enter the same `resolveProjection` union, authorization floor,
> provenance model, expiry evaluation, governance epoch, audit, and
> EffectiveAccess result. A holder is counted once even when direct and one or
> more group paths coexist. One path has no precedence over another, and
> removing one source removes only that source. Core computes the post-change
> result before review and commit; a surviving path prevents effective revoke
> and prevents D37 from being stopped.
>
> The direct relation is a typed Phase 12 **assignment capability grant**. It
> is not a record-scoped `named_person_grant` and no Website-local grant table
> is created. The group relation is one group-to-capability edge plus current
> membership edges, never N copied direct grants. Any materialized per-person
> view is derived, disposable, and non-authoritative.
>
> A group carrying D38 is a protected authorization group. It is manual,
> static, flat, same-Tenant, human-staff-only, and assignment-bound. Nested,
> dynamic, external/IdP/SCIM, cross-Tenant, role-derived, task-derived,
> coordinator-derived, invited/pending-person, service, AI, API-key, support,
> and silently activating memberships cannot confer D38. The current seeded
> **Teams & Users** demo, organizational teams, Tasks Hub groups, Mobilize
> cohorts, and Website rosters are not Access groups or authorization truth.
>
> Attaching, renewing, or removing D38 on an Access group is a
> `permissions.manage_grants` operation within the actor's current live
> assignable-capability ceiling. Adding, activating, or renewing a member is a
> separate `permissions.manage_membership` operation whose exact group scope
> and live protected-group administrative ceiling cover the group's complete
> current capability bundle and bundle revision. Possessing D38 is neither
> necessary nor sufficient for either operation. Widening a bundle invalidates
> stale membership-administration authority until it is reauthorized.
>
> An actor cannot add, activate, or renew the same human Party through the same
> or another assignment, and cannot use ordinary group ownership or an Admin
> label to create another self-preserving path. Phase 12's existing
> quorum-aware self-grant/recovery and last-permissions-manager invariants are
> the only exception machinery. A scoped membership manager may still perform
> a purely subtractive removal after a later bundle widening, subject to those
> invariants and truthful full-bundle consequence review.
>
> Every direct-grant, group-capability, and membership mutation re-proves the
> trusted Tenant, actual/acting actor, assignment, group, complete capability
> bundle, target eligibility, administrative scope/ceiling, self/SoD rules,
> relevant source heads, and post-change EffectiveAccess under Phase 12's one
> advisory-locked mutation boundary. State, one Tenant epoch advance,
> append-only audit, and durable receipt commit atomically. Exact semantic
> replay returns the receipt; changed meaning or stale relevant heads require
> fresh review.
>
> Each source path retains independent state, expiry, revocation, delegation,
> and audit provenance. A group path is effective only while the group grant,
> membership, delegation, capability, assignment, and Tenant context are all
> current. The earliest applicable authoritative UTC instant ends the path;
> timers, caches, projections, Realtime, Tasks Hub, and Inngest never own or
> delay authorization. Terminal edges never resurrect through rehire, group
> restore, regrant, import, clone, or environment promotion.
>
> Loss of the final effective D38 path fences every later uncommitted D37
> effect. Earlier committed effects and history remain immutable; regrant does
> not resume a stopped application. Core supplies no per-member deny, mute,
> exclusion, hidden `remove all paths` shortcut, or automatic source
> conversion. Staff change the authoritative direct grant, group grant, or
> membership and review every affected capability and person.
>
> The permanent UX lives in Mission Control **People & access**, **People**,
> **Access groups**, permission history, and **My Access**. A person detail page
> is the direct path; an Access-group detail page is the group path. D38 appears
> once with accessible provenance such as **Granted directly — until removed**
> and **Through Website Operations — membership ends 31 August 2026**. The UI
> never exposes `EffectiveAccess` or `Active Tenant Assignment` as ordinary
> product vocabulary.
>
> Adding a member reviews the group's complete capability bundle. Attaching or
> removing D38 reviews exact current deduplicated counts: current active
> members, newly gaining or losing, and retaining through another source. It
> also states that later governed active members receive the group's
> permissions and whether bundle widening invalidates any membership manager's
> ceiling. Reviews reveal no protected Website source, Site, person, task, or
> correction detail.
>
> Person and My Access views show one permission with all current sources.
> Direct removal says **Direct permission removed. Jordan still has this
> permission through Website Operations** when a group path survives. Group
> archive/removal never uses the current prototype's false permanent-delete
> promise. Zero direct grants, zero groups, zero members, and zero holders stay
> valid quiet states with no warning, unread item, task, email, reminder, or
> escalation.
>
> The production UI uses Core Base Maia semantic components and tokens, one
> focused page/inline review rather than nested Team sheets or a wide module
> matrix, durable receipt-backed outcomes, at least 44-pixel targets, keyboard
> and screen-reader completeness, visible focus and associated errors/status,
> 320-pixel/400-percent reflow, forced colors, reduced motion, international
> names, RTL/bidirectional isolation, localized times, and low-bandwidth lost-
> response recovery. D38 holders see only their safe provenance; access-
> governance authority is required to enumerate other holders, reasons,
> memberships, or history.
>
> Every authorization relation has `tenant_id NOT NULL`, composite same-Tenant
> foreign keys, immutable scope, restrictive deletion, current-edge
> uniqueness, indexed resolver predicates, `ENABLE` plus `FORCE ROW LEVEL
SECURITY`, operation-correct `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, browser-write revoke,
> pinned privileged functions, and owner/service/RPC/worker/support/repair/
> import/AI parity. Group writes remain O(1) authoritative relationship writes
> plus one epoch, with set-based paginated consequence calculation and no
> synchronous per-member authority fanout.

The hybrid direction is modern practice only with this asymmetry and protected-
group boundary. Entra, Google Cloud, Salesforce, GitHub, Contentful, and
Blackbaud all support direct and group/team assignment for different operating
scales; Entra and AWS also show why privileged groups require stronger
membership controls and why direct-only remains safer than a weak group
implementation. No evidence proves a typical ministry holder count, so group
usage remains optional and must be validated through scenario-based usability
research rather than assumed.

## D40 — When group-derived access already exists, may staff add a redundant direct grant?

### Why this needs your decision

Jordan already receives D38 through **Website Operations**. A temporary
rotation or uncertain upcoming group change makes an access administrator want
to add a direct grant too. That second source may be intentional continuity,
but it also makes later group removal look successful while Jordan retains the
capability. Automatically blocking it can make legitimate coverage brittle;
allowing it as a routine one-click action creates sticky privilege and confusing
reviews.

This decides only whether Core may create a second direct source when the same
Active Tenant Assignment already resolves D38 through one or more Access
groups. It does not change additive EffectiveAccess, source-aware revoke, or
the authority required to grant.

### Option 1 — deliberate exception with explicit warning, fresh reason, and independent duration — recommended

Core shows the existing group source first, recommends keeping the group as the
single source, and makes **Add a separate direct grant** a secondary action. If
chosen, the administrator must provide a new concise reason, make an explicit
unpreselected duration choice for this source, and review that Jordan will keep
access if group membership ends. The direct source remains independently
revocable and auditable.

**User/Tenant UX:** the normal path stays uncluttered, legitimate continuity is
possible, and the sticky-access consequence is impossible to miss. Later
reviews can distinguish an intentional exception from accidental duplication.

**Impact:** strongest balance of flexibility, clarity, and least privilege;
adds one proportional review only when creating overlap.

### Option 2 — block the direct grant while any group source exists

Core requires staff to remove or end every group source before granting the
person directly.

**User/Tenant UX:** simplest provenance and no redundant paths, but legitimate
handoff or continuity changes become multi-step and may introduce an access
gap or risky source churn.

**Impact:** safest strict model, but inflexible for ministries and can force a
group-wide change to solve one person's temporary need.

### Option 3 — allow redundant direct grants as an ordinary action

Core permits the same direct grant flow without a distinct warning or
exception treatment.

**User/Tenant UX:** fewest immediate steps, but the administrator may not
realize that group removal will not revoke access.

**Impact:** high risk of sticky privilege, confusing recertification, and false
revocation expectations; reject.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — allow a redundant direct path only as a
deliberate exception with existing-source warning, a fresh reason, and an
independent explicit duration.** It preserves Tenant flexibility without
making duplicate authority a silent default, and it fits the source-first
People & access UX established by D39.

Which D40 rule should Core record: **Option 1 — deliberate documented
exception**, **Option 2 — block while a group path exists**, or **Option 3 —
ordinary redundant grants**? You may amend any option.

### D40 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — deliberate continuity exception. Show the
existing source first; expose a secondary **Add separate direct grant** action;
require a fresh concise reason and an independent unpreselected duration; and
warn explicitly that group removal will not end access.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D40 permits one deliberate **separate direct grant** only when the exact
> active same-Tenant staff Active Tenant Assignment currently receives D38
> through at least one complete protected Access-group path and has no current
> direct D38 source. This is a future-access persistence change, not a current
> capability gain.
>
> The ordinary person-access surface first shows every current group-derived
> D38 source and its current end condition. It states: **Jordan already has this
> permission through Website Operations. Adding a separate direct grant will
> not change what Jordan can do now. Jordan will keep this permission if every
> listed group source ends.** Keeping one group source is presented as the
> simplest path when it meets the need.
>
> **Add separate direct grant** is a discoverable secondary action. It is never
> preselected, promoted from holder count, hidden in an icon-only menu, offered
> as the ordinary Grant permission action, created during group membership,
> copied from another source, or folded into a generic Save command. Product
> copy avoids **redundant**, **duplicate permission**, and **exception access**
> as current user-facing labels.
>
> Review requires a newly entered, bounded, Unicode-safe, privacy-safe reason
> explaining why independent access is needed. Fresh means independently
> entered and not prefilled or copied; it is not a brittle text-uniqueness test.
> D40 reuses Phase 12's one canonical grant-reason normalization and exact
> Unicode/storage/display bounds, defines no local limit, and remains Reserved
> until OpenSpec declares that shared contract precisely.
> The reason records governance need only and may not solicit protected
> ministry, personnel, missionary, member-care, donor, Site, location,
> correction, or source detail.
>
> The administrator explicitly chooses an independent duration with neither
> option selected initially: **Ends on…**, described as proportionate for a
> planned handoff or temporary coverage, or D38's **Until removed**, described
> as ongoing independent responsibility. Selecting **Until removed** adds the
> persistent explanation that every listed group may end while the direct
> source continues until authorized removal or another Phase 12 terminal
> condition. No typed phrase, acknowledgement checkbox, or duplicate
> confirmation is added.
>
> D40 creates the same typed Phase 12 `assignment_capability_grants` source as
> any direct D38 grant, under the same unique current Tenant/assignment/
> capability head. It adds no exception table, backup relationship, permission
> kind, holder Boolean, priority, deny, group override, or second resolver.
> Server-derived creation intent and immutable audit/receipt evidence preserve
> that the source was deliberately added for continuity; creation intent never
> affects exercise authorization.
>
> At review and commit, the server derives and proves the Tenant, actual/acting
> actor, grantor assignment, target assignment, D38 capability, current grant-
> manager authority, live assignable-capability ceiling, self/alternate-hat/
> SoD/quorum rules, absence of a direct source, and every complete current
> contributing group capability/membership/delegation/expiry path. Caller-
> supplied actor, Tenant, capability, creation classification, source basis,
> effective result, or audit attribution is rejected.
>
> Review binds one canonical complete group-source-set digest and every
> authorization-relevant head that was shown. If any contributing source is
> added, removed, expires, changes its authorization-relevant capability,
> membership, delegation, or expiry meaning, or becomes ineffective, if a
> direct source appears, or if actor/target authority changes before commit,
> nothing is written. A display-label rename alone does not invalidate the
> review; Core uses the current safe label in the receipt. For a material
> change, Core persistently reports **Access changed while you were reviewing.
> Nothing was changed. Review the current access.** It never silently converts
> the continuity command into an ordinary direct grant that newly restores or
> widens access.
>
> The direct source receives its own identity, reason, duration, grantor and
> delegation provenance, semantic idempotency identity, terminal history,
> audit, and durable receipt. The immutable overlap-creation basis retains the
> stable reviewed group source identities/heads or a constraint-complete typed
> source-set proof. That basis explains creation intent but is never a live
> dependency: later group rename, removal, archive, expiry, membership end, or
> delegation end does not cascade into or terminate the independent direct
> source.
>
> Grant state, overlap basis, audit, receipt, and exactly one Tenant
> authorization-epoch advance commit atomically under Phase 12's locked
> command. The epoch advances even though the current capability set is
> unchanged, because provenance, cache explanation, and future revocation
> behavior changed. Exact semantic replay returns the original receipt;
> changed target, reason, duration, intent, source set, or expected head
> conflicts. Concurrency produces at most one current direct D38 source.
>
> Same-Party self-grant protections apply even when the actor already exercises
> D38 through a group, because the new path preserves access after later group
> removal. D38 possession, group membership authority, Admin/Owner labels,
> task authority, policy edit, Website access, route visibility, service role,
> or support state does not authorize D40.
>
> If continuity commits first, later group removal reports that the direct
> source survives and names its end condition. If group removal commits first,
> D40 conflicts and a later ordinary direct grant requires its own current-
> state review. Removing/expiring the direct source while a group survives
> reports that group-derived access remains. Every successful source mutation
> advances the epoch, but only final post-change EffectiveAccess loss fences
> later uncommitted D37 effects. Regrant never resumes a stopped D37
> application.
>
> Success says: **Separate direct grant added. Jordan's current abilities did
> not change. This grant remains [until date/until removed] even if Website
> Operations access ends.** It is persistent, route-addressable, receipt-
> backed, and programmatically announced. A toast is supplementary.
>
> Person detail and My Access continue to show D38 once with all current
> sources. Access administrators may inspect the minimized reason and creation
> history; ordinary holders see only their safe source and duration. D41 must
> decide how prominently the historical continuity origin remains visible
> after every group path has ended.
>
> D40 creates no scheduled handoff, future-start state, automatic conversion,
> cleanup, deduplication, approval graph, PIM/JIT system, access-review
> campaign, notification, unread item, email, reminder, task, D37 application,
> Website write, coordinator change, external synchronization, or Inngest
> authority.

The deliberate exception is modern practice when described as independent
source persistence: Entra, Google, Salesforce, GitHub, Contentful, and AWS all
demonstrate additive direct/group paths, source-specific removal, independent
duration, or temporary-access justification. Google PAM's stricter refusal of
same-scope active grants is the strongest counterevidence and confirms why the
ordinary direct flow must remain unavailable during overlap. No source proves
that missions ministries commonly need this exact workflow, so frequency and
terminology remain product hypotheses—never automatic grant criteria.

## D41 — After every group path ends, how should the surviving direct grant be presented?

### Why this needs your decision

Jordan receives D38 through Website Operations and a D40 separate direct grant.
Later, Jordan leaves the group. The direct grant is already authoritative and
no data transition is required, but the interface must decide whether daily
access views should continue emphasizing its historical continuity origin.

A permanent **Continuity exception** badge may help auditors but can become
stale, noisy, or stigmatizing once nothing exceptional remains. Automatically
“converting” the row would fabricate a lifecycle event and invite unnecessary
state. Hiding origin entirely would weaken explanation history.

### Option 1 — current source label with historical origin in provenance — recommended

Current access shows **Granted directly** with duration. Expanded provenance
and immutable history say **Added for continuity** and retain the original
overlap basis, reason, actor, and receipt. No write, conversion, notification,
or new task occurs when the last group path ends.

**User/Tenant UX:** ordinary access stays calm and current; governance staff can
still explain exactly why and how the source was created.

**Impact:** cleanest separation of current truth from historical provenance and
no derived-state synchronization risk.

### Option 2 — keep a prominent continuity badge until the direct grant ends

Current person and access-manager views continue to label the source
**Continuity grant** even after all group sources have ended.

**User/Tenant UX:** maximum ongoing visibility, but the badge becomes noisy and
can imply the grant is temporary, second-class, or still dependent on a group.

**Impact:** no authority error if derived correctly, but greater terminology
and projection burden.

### Option 3 — automatically convert it into an ordinary direct grant

When the final group path ends, Core writes a conversion event or mutates the
grant into another state.

**User/Tenant UX:** the label becomes ordinary, but the same result can be
presented without a write.

**Impact:** creates fake lifecycle, race, idempotency, rollback, and audit
complexity; reject.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — show current direct access plainly and keep
Added for continuity in expanded provenance/history.** It gives administrators
complete explanation without burdening ordinary users or inventing a state
transition.

Which D41 presentation should Core record: **Option 1 — current label plus
historical origin**, **Option 2 — prominent continuity badge**, or **Option 3 —
automatic conversion**? You may amend any option.

### D41 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — present the surviving source as the current
direct grant and retain its continuity origin in expanded provenance/history.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> When the final current group-derived D38 path ends and the D40-origin direct
> D38 grant remains current, Core presents one deduplicated current capability
> row with **Direct grant · [current end condition]** in People & access and
> **Granted directly to you · [current end condition]** in My Access. It does
> not present **Continuity grant**, **Continuity exception**, **Former group
> access**, or another current source class or badge.
>
> Current source and historical origin are different facts with different
> owners. Phase 12's current assignment-capability grant, assignment/floor/
> delegation/expiry state, current EffectiveAccess, and Tenant authorization
> epoch own current truth. D40's immutable overlap creation basis and append-
> only access history own **Added for continuity**. Audit provenance, cached
> explanation, search indexes, exports, badges, Tasks Hub, analytics, and UI
> state never authorize or reclassify access.
>
> Authorized **Why this person has access** in administration, **Why you have
> access** in My Access, and durable history say \*\*Added for
> continuity on [localized instant] while access also came through [authorized
>
> > historical group summary]\*\* and may show when the final group-derived path
> > ended. It preserves stable source identity, event-time safe label, actor,
> > minimized reason, receipt, and ordered history only to the extent allowed by
> > D42. Ordinary current presentation never promotes the governance reason.
>
> Ending the last group path performs no D41 mutation. It does not convert,
> reissue, renew, retag, copy, or update the direct grant or its D40 basis. The
> authoritative group-source mutation already advances the Phase 12 epoch; the
> next current read derives the direct-only presentation. Core stores no post-
> overlap Boolean, continuity status, conversion event, shadow source kind, or
> second invalidation system.
>
> If a group path later returns, the current source list again shows both
> **Granted directly** and **Through [current Access group]**. The immutable
> D40 origin remains expanded history only; group return neither erases nor
> promotes it. Direct expiry, revoke, applicable delegation loss,
> recertification denial, assignment suspension/end, or the subtract-only
> floor removes an ineffective direct source from current presentation while
> preserving its terminal history. A later direct successor has its own
> provenance and never inherits D40 origin automatically.
>
> A group display-name change never changes authority or rewrites event-time
> provenance. Authorized history retains stable identity plus the minimized
> safe label at the event and may show \*\*formerly [event label], now [current
>
> > label]\*\* when both are permitted and useful. Archived or terminal sources
> > are non-interactive historical entries. Ordinary group deletion cannot
> > cascade into or erase retained grant/basis/audit history.
>
> Current access renders from the canonical Phase 12 read at one current
> Tenant epoch before optional history. If the authorized history projection
> is unavailable, stale, rebuilding, or times out, current direct access still
> renders truthfully and the expanded panel says **Access history is
> temporarily unavailable. Current access is not affected.** If canonical
> current access itself cannot be proven, Core shows no stale current claim,
> disables access mutations, and provides a persistent retry/recovery state.
> History, Realtime, a search index, analytics, or Inngest never fills that gap.
>
> Current-list and operational-export semantics classify the source as
> **direct**. Only a separately authorized governance/audit query may filter by
> D40 creation origin. Ordinary People search, current-holder reports, My
> Access, Website, donor, missionary, Tasks Hub, notifications, performance
> analytics, and staff/Tenant scoring receive no continuity-origin field,
> reason, historical group roster, or internal source identity.
>
> Current access caches bind at least the validated Tenant Authorization
> Context, exact Active Tenant Assignment, capability, current governance
> epoch, and viewer/purpose projection. Historical projections additionally
> bind the immutable provenance revision/version. Cross-Tenant, cross-hat,
> cross-viewer, or cross-purpose cache reuse is forbidden. Stale or out-of-
> order responses cannot overwrite a newer epoch.
>
> Current list/card reads remain set-based and do not scan or fetch history per
> visible person. Authorized provenance loads deliberately from a Tenant-
> indexed, paginated read model. The current summary appears first on slow or
> unreliable connections; optional history failure never blocks it. Exports
> bind an authoritative snapshot instant/epoch or fail rather than silently
> mixing current and historical versions.
>
> The interaction reuses Core's shared Base Maia/Base UI disclosure or
> equivalent existing person-detail composition. **Why this person has access**
> / **Why you have access** is a
> text-labeled keyboard/touch control with programmatic expanded state; it is
> never hover-only, icon-only, color-only, or a badge. It preserves visible
> focus, at least 44-by-44 CSS-pixel important targets, logical focus order,
> forced colors, reduced motion, 320-CSS-pixel/400-percent reflow, RTL/CJK/
> bidirectional names, localized absolute date/time/zone, screen-reader event
> order, and explicit loading/unavailable/retry states. No nested modal is
> introduced in the seed-backed Teams demo, which is not the permanent People
> & access surface.
>
> D41 creates no authorization write, direct-grant update, D37 start/stop/
> resume, conversion worker, cleanup, notification, unread item, email,
> reminder, task, review campaign, recertification timer, report score,
> external synchronization, Website/CMS write, or Inngest authority. Phase 12
> risk-based recertification remains the only recertification owner.

Current official evidence supports the corrected split without dictating
Core's domain model. Microsoft Entra shows whether a current role was assigned
directly or through a group; Salesforce consolidates a permission and exposes
**Access Granted By** through a row-level action; GitHub exposes mixed-source
detail on demand; Google Policy Analyzer explains current access but documents
best-effort freshness; Blackbaud separates user management from user-history
audit; W3C defines a keyboard-operable disclosure with programmatic expanded
state. These products prove the usefulness of current-source explanation and
separate audit history. They do not prove missions-ministry frequency or the
safe audience for historical group/reason detail, so D42 owns that disclosure
decision.

Option 1. The corrected decision resolves them through 30 requirements, 120

## D42 — Who may see the historical continuity origin and governance reason?

### Why this needs your decision

Jordan's current My Access row can safely say **Granted directly to you**.
Expanded D41 provenance may additionally contain an old Access-group name, the
fact that group access ended, Morgan's grant decision, a minimized governance
reason, and receipt history. Those facts help explanation and audit, but a
group label or reason can reveal internal staffing, Member Care, security,
location, or ministry context that the current holder or a membership manager
does not need.

D42 decides the read audience only. It does not change the direct grant,
EffectiveAccess, D40 basis, retention, or recertification.

### Option 1 — tiered provenance by viewer and purpose — recommended

- The subject sees a safe **Added for continuity · [date]** summary
  in **Why you have access**, but no historical group label, governance reason,
  actor, basis, receipt, other member, or protected detail.
- Authorized grant managers and security/audit readers see the minimized
  reason, actor, stable/event-time source evidence, current rename context,
  terminal events, and receipt within their exact Tenant/scope.
- A membership manager reviewing removal sees only the current surviving
  direct source and end condition needed to understand that action.
- Everyone else sees no continuity origin or reason.

**User/Tenant UX:** the holder can understand that direct access was deliberate
without being exposed to governance-sensitive context; administrators retain
complete explainability; group managers get the consequence needed for their
one action without gaining grant-administration visibility.

**Impact:** requires one centralized viewer/purpose projection policy and
negative authorization tests, but best matches Core's role-scoped surfaces and
data minimization.

### Option 2 — show the full origin and reason to the subject

The holder sees event-time group names, grant actor, governance reason, and
history alongside their current direct source.

**User/Tenant UX:** maximum transparency and self-correction, but internal group
names and rationales may expose unnecessary personnel, care, security, or
location context and may be confusing without administrator vocabulary.

**Impact:** simplest subject/admin content model but materially weakens least-
privilege disclosure.

### Option 3 — governance-only history

The subject sees only **Granted directly to you** and duration. Only authorized
grant managers/security auditors may see **Added for continuity**, historical
groups, reason, actor, and receipt.

**User/Tenant UX:** strongest minimization and quietest My Access surface, but
the holder cannot tell why an apparently unexpected direct grant exists or
report a mistaken continuity decision with useful context.

**Impact:** lowest disclosure surface, but weaker transparency and self-service
correction.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — tiered provenance by viewer and purpose.** It
keeps current access understandable for the person, gives each administrator
only the explanation needed for their operation, and protects potentially
sensitive ministry/staff context without hiding the governance trail from
authorized reviewers.

Which D42 disclosure policy should Core record: **Option 1 — tiered
provenance**, **Option 2 — full origin to the subject**, or **Option 3 —
governance-only history**? You may amend any option.

### D42 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — tiered provenance by viewer and purpose.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D42 defines four code-owned, server-derived, field-allowlisted projections
> over the one immutable D40/D41 history. A caller never supplies or upgrades a
> tier. Phase 12 derives the exact Tenant Authorization Context, current Active
> Tenant Assignment, subject, registered surface purpose, current capability/
> scope, floor/clearance/residency posture, and authorization epoch before any
> field leaves the server.
>
> `access.self_explanation` is available only to the exact current subject in
> My Access. Current source appears first. Expanded **Why you have access** may
> show **Added for continuity · [localized date]** and the fixed explanation
> **Direct access was added so your access could continue if group access
> changed.** It exposes no historical group identity/label, reason, actor,
> authority/delegation, basis/hash, receipt, other member, or protected detail.
>
> `access.membership_change_review` exists only inside one currently authorized
> exact-group membership-change review/receipt. It may show that the target
> will retain the capability through a direct source and that source's current
> end condition. Membership authority exposes no D40 origin/date, historical
> group, reason, actor, receipt, direct-grant edit control, or audit chronology.
>
> `access.grant_governance` requires current exact-scope
> `permissions.manage_grants` authority or separately authorized Phase 12
> access-review authority. **Why this person has access** may show only the
> current direct source/end, continuity origin/date, current-floor-permitted
> event-time source summary, bounded reason and safe actor attribution, and the
> relevant chronology/remediation context. A source label withheld by the
> current floor renders exactly **Protected access group**; protected reason or
> actor values are omitted. Raw IDs/hash, complete membership/delegation chain,
> receipt internals, unrelated events, and protected domain content remain out.
>
> `access.security_audit` requires the distinct current
> `permissions.audit.read` capability, registered audit purpose, exact Tenant/
> scope, and every Phase 12 floor/clearance/residency and existing risk control.
> It may return the complete typed authorization-governance basis, actual and
> acting actors, authority/delegation, receipts, warning version, and authorized
> chronology, but never unrestricted Website, worker, care, donor, location,
> credential, secret, or cross-Tenant data. Bulk export additionally requires
> current `permissions.audit.export`; read permission alone cannot create a
> downloadable copy.
>
> One request uses one purpose projection. My Access stays self-minimized even
> when the same human is a grant manager or auditor; richer fields require
> deliberate navigation to that separately authorized surface. Historical
> participation, Owner/Admin/staff labels, D38 possession, route visibility,
> support, impersonation, service role, Tasks Hub, notification, Website,
> analytics, search, AI, cached data, or URL knowledge grants no provenance.
>
> Every disclosure load, page/cursor, export chunk, worker execution, and retry
> reauthorizes current viewer/subject/Tenant/purpose/scope/floor/epoch. Losing
> authority prevents every later response. Responses and caches bind Tenant,
> viewer and subject assignments, purpose/projection version, source/basis
> revision, scope, and epoch; a richer payload is never fetched and hidden in
> the client or reused for a lower purpose. Realtime carries no protected
> provenance.
>
> Raw basis/audit relations have no browser grants. Purpose-built server
> projections preserve forced-RLS, security-invoker or hardened pinned-RPC,
> table-owner/service/`BYPASSRLS`/worker/support/export parity, and correct
> operation policies. Full protected reads and exports create identifiers-only
> durable read-audit evidence without copying group/reason text or recursively
> auditing each audit row. Unknown fields/classifications fail closed.
>
> Phase 12 remains source of truth for authorization, retention,
> anonymization, read audit, risk/step-up, and export controls; D40 remains
> source of truth for immutable creation evidence. Current D41 access stays
> usable when optional provenance is unavailable. D42 creates no grant write,
> role-name check, Tenant-configurable field tiers, local approval/step-up,
> task, notification, email, timer, AI summary, conversion worker, scoring, or
> Inngest authority.
>
> The UI reuses Core Base Maia/Base UI disclosure and detail composition with
> current source before history, semantic headings/lists, no raw JSON, 44-CSS-
> pixel important controls, visible focus, programmatic state/status, 320-CSS-
> pixel/400-percent reflow, forced colors, reduced motion, localized time zones,
> RTL/CJK/bidirectional-safe text, and a calm low-bandwidth unavailable/retry
> state. Missing fields are omitted rather than shown as noisy empty rows.

Current official evidence supports the pattern without dictating Core's exact
model. Microsoft separates My Access from designated audit readers and exports;
GitHub can grant audit-log viewing without full ownership; Google separates
policy, group-expansion, private-log, field-view, and export authority;
Salesforce separates current **Access Granted By** from Setup Audit Trail;
Contentful separates a member's team visibility from Owner/Admin audit access;
and Blackbaud places attributable access history in Security/Audit history.
NIST least privilege, OWASP per-request authorization, and W3C disclosure
semantics reinforce the corrected server and interaction boundaries.

## D43 — What should a holder be able to do when continuity access looks wrong?

### Why this needs your decision

Jordan opens **Why you have access** and sees:

```text
Granted directly to you · Ends 15 October 2026
Added for continuity · 29 August 2026
Direct access was added so your access could continue if group access changed.
```

Jordan believes the direct access is no longer appropriate. D42 intentionally
does not reveal the internal group, reason, actor, or receipt. The product now
needs one safe next action. Immediate self-revocation could interrupt active
recovery work or race another source change; explanation-only sends a field or
small-ministry user hunting for an unknown administrator.

D43 decides only the holder's correction path. It does not change D42 fields,
grant authority, D37 consequences, Phase 12 revocation, or Tasks Hub ownership.

### Option 1 — governed request to review or remove — recommended

Show one secondary **Request access review** action in the expanded My Access
detail. A compact Core sheet asks for one concise, safe explanation and states
**Your access will not change until an authorized reviewer decides.** Core
creates one deduplicated, source-owned request against the exact current direct
grant/head. The holder sees durable status; current authorized grant governance
reviews current sources and D37 consequence, then retains or removes the grant
through the existing source command.

The request may project recipient work into the shared Tasks Hub under
ADR-0183, so CMS, Mobilize, and later source domains can reuse one task shell
without making a task the request, authorization, or completion truth. Inngest
may later deliver identifier-only projection/retry work; it never decides,
revokes, or owns the request.

**UX:** clear self-service correction with no destructive surprise, no need to
know an administrator, and a visible outcome on mobile or low bandwidth.

**Impact:** adds a small governed request lifecycle and source-to-task
projection seam, but avoids a one-off CMS workflow and preserves Phase 12 as
the only authorization owner.

### Option 2 — immediate holder self-revoke

Show **Remove my direct access** with a consequence review and confirmation.

**UX:** fastest way to reduce access and strongest sense of control.

**Impact:** gives the holder a mutation they otherwise lack; a mistake can stop
current work, surviving sources complicate the result, and undo cannot be
promised. It weakens the deliberate grant-governance boundary.

### Option 3 — explanation only; contact an administrator

Show provenance with no in-product correction action.

**UX:** quiet and mechanically simple.

**Impact:** creates off-platform work, unclear ownership, poor auditability,
and disproportionate friction for small or distributed ministries.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — a governed Request access review flow.** It
lets holders flag stale access in one clear step without granting accidental
self-revocation, and it establishes the reusable source-owned request/Tasks Hub
projection seam the broader product will need.

Which D43 action should Core record: **Option 1 — governed review/removal
request**, **Option 2 — immediate self-revoke**, or **Option 3 — explanation
only/contact an administrator**? You may amend any option.

### D43 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — governed review/removal request.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D43 is one typed Phase 12 `permission_change_request`, not a Website-local
> table, generic approval workflow, support ticket, notification, task, or
> Inngest human process. Its stable request kind is
> `holder_direct_grant_review`, with contract version 1. Initial activation is
> deliberately narrow: the exact current subject may ask to review one exact
> current D40 continuity-created direct D38 assignment-capability source shown
> under D42's self-explanation projection. A Tenant, subject, assignment,
> target grant, requester, actor, state, or audit attribution supplied by the
> client is ignored or rejected.
>
> In **My Access**, the current source and end condition remain first. The quiet
> secondary action is **Ask for an access review**. It expands one inline
> Base Maia/Base UI form below the source—not a modal, nested sheet, wizard, or
> separate route. The form says **Someone authorized to manage access will
> decide whether to keep or remove this direct access. Sending this request
> will not change your access.** It asks exactly **Why should this access be
> reviewed?** and requires trimmed 1–500-code-point plain text. The helper says
> **Briefly explain what changed. Do not include confidential ministry, donor,
> member-care, personnel, location, or security details.** Submit is **Submit
> review request**; cancel writes nothing and
> returns focus. A committed response becomes the persistent status **Review
> requested. Your access has not changed.**, never a toast-only or optimistic
> access result.
>
> One exact `(Tenant, Active Tenant Assignment, direct source, request kind)`
> has at most one `pending_review` episode. The closed lifecycle is
> `pending_review`, `withdrawn`, `resolved_kept`, `resolved_removed`, and
> `no_longer_applicable`; only pending may transition. The holder may
> **Withdraw request** while pending, which changes no access. Exact semantic
> replay returns the original receipt; a different explanation while pending
> returns that current request without overwriting it. Requests, submitted
> explanations, terminal events, trusted actor evidence, and receipts are
> immutable in ordinary UX. A later concern creates a successor episode only
> while the same exact source remains current.
>
> Submission uses Core's ordinary authenticated same-origin mutation/request-
> forgery boundary plus an opaque command idempotency key; D43 adds no custom
> single-use form-intent subsystem. The client may send only that key, the
> bounded explanation, and an untrusted source locator/expected head. The
> server re-resolves the exact source and derives every authorization and
> attribution field from current trusted context.
>
> The authoritative administrator surface is the permission-filtered Phase 12
> **Access requests** lane, where D43 appears as **Review current access**.
> **Access reviews** remains reserved for periodic recertification campaigns.
> Lane enumeration, actionable detail, D44 recipient eligibility, and both
> decisions require current same-Tenant `permissions.manage_grants` within the
> exact live scope and assignable-capability ceiling plus every Phase 12 floor,
> self/SoD/quorum, last-authority, and risk control. D42 audit or review-read
> authority, a role name, original grantor, task assignment, notification,
> deep link, support status, or service role grants no decision authority.
>
> Review reloads the current request and grant heads, current direct/group
> sources, independent end condition, and freshly computed D37/post-removal
> consequence. It offers only **Keep direct access** and **Remove direct
> access**, never generic Approve/Deny or Complete. Keep requires one new
> holder-safe 1–500-code-point explanation and changes no grant, duration, or
> authorization epoch. Remove asks for no duplicate prose: the reviewed
> consequence and authoritative source receipt provide the safe outcome. It
> invokes the one advisory-locked Phase 12 grant-state command and atomically
> commits the exact direct-source end, request decision, audit evidence,
> semantic receipt, one authorization-epoch advance, and identifier-only
> projection intent. Any stale head or failed invariant writes neither the
> decision nor revocation. Other sources remain independent; the result says
> whether access survives through another current source and never claims all
> access ended without proof.
>
> If expiry, assignment end, ordinary revocation, or another authoritative
> event ends the exact source first, it is immediately non-actionable from
> current source truth and converges to `no_longer_applicable`, shown to the
> holder as **Direct access ended before review**. Current access never retains
> a dead source. A quiet subject-only **My access requests** section, backed by
> the same Phase 12 aggregate and retention policy, preserves the safe pending
> or terminal outcome for the same current Active Tenant Assignment. It is not
> a current-access list, task list, audit log, or second source of authority.
>
> Same-Tenant composite foreign keys bind request, subject assignment, direct
> source, actors, decision, and source receipt; pending uniqueness, closed-kind/
> state checks, append-only history, non-cascading deletion, indexed source-
> lane queries, raw-browser denial, forced RLS, correct `USING`/`WITH CHECK`,
> hardened pinned-function grants, and owner/service/`BYPASSRLS` parity enforce
> the boundary. Request and decision text is protected governance data: Tasks
> Hub, notifications, email, logs, traces, search, analytics, AI, Realtime,
> ordinary exports, and caches receive no copy.
>
> D43 registers the pending request as one ADR-0183 source-work occurrence.
> Phase 12 owns actionability, status, decision, and closure. Tasks Hub may
> later project at most one shared task identity plus recipient-specific
> engagement; generic Complete/Reopen/Reassign/Dismiss/Delete/comment/bulk/
> import/AI/support/worker mutations reject. D44 decides personal attention
> only. The **Access requests** lane and holder status work when no personal
> route exists or Tasks Hub is unavailable. If used, Inngest receives only a
> versioned identifier-only post-commit event through Core's dispatch ledger,
> reauthorizes at fire time, and may materialize or reconcile; it owns no
> request, reviewer, human wait, decision, access, idempotency, or completion.
>
> The flow uses semantic headings/labels, associated hint/error/count/status,
> visible focus, keyboard order, 44-CSS-pixel important controls, 320-CSS-pixel/
> 400-percent reflow, forced-color and reduced-motion support, Unicode/RTL/CJK/
> bidirectional-safe wrapping, localized timestamps, server validation, and
> receipt recovery after an ambiguous network response. It adds no deadline,
> SLA, auto-removal, reminder/escalation engine, comment thread, attachment,
> configurable form/status DSL, or AI summary.

This resolves the external-practice conflict deliberately. Microsoft Entra
supports self-review with governed later application; SailPoint supports
holder-initiated removal requests with required comments and reviewer
decisions; Okta separates request status, assignees, cancellation, and
provisioning. Some products also permit immediate self-removal. Core does not
copy that behavior because D40 intentionally created an independent continuity
source and D37 proves that final access loss can fence uncommitted work. The
one-field governed request retains user control without turning a generic task
or a mistaken click into authorization truth.

All 22 adversarial categories contain a material concern under the unqualified
option. The corrected decision resolves them through 30 normative
requirements, 120 continuous acceptance criteria, 120 continuous primary-

## D44 — Who should receive personal responsibility for a holder access request?

### Why this needs your decision

Jordan's request is already safe and discoverable in the permission-filtered
**Access requests** lane. Suppose six people currently have exact grant-
decision authority, but only Maria and Arjun routinely handle access requests.
Maria is away next week; another eligible manager may cover a different scope.
D44 decides personal Tasks Hub attention only—not who may see or decide the
source request.

All options keep the authoritative **Access requests** lane and current
command-time authorization. Personal assignment never grants request detail or
decision power. The requester is never assigned their own personal review task;
that routing rule does not change Phase 12's existing self/SoD/quorum decision
rules at the source. Proved-zero or indeterminate routing never guesses a role,
original grantor, requester-selected reviewer, or administrator fallback.

### Option 1 — optional one to three Access request coordinators — recommended

The Tenant may name one to three unique, unordered, co-equal **Access request
coordinators**. Core resolves the complete current configuration, excludes the
requester, and personally projects the one source-backed task only to configured
people who independently remain eligible for that exact request. An inactive or
ineligible configured person is a known exclusion; an incomplete resolver
projects nothing. No configuration or no eligible coordinator means lane-only
operation, not broadcast or fallback.

**UX/impact:** clear bounded accountability for small or distributed teams,
quiet personal task lists, and continuity through the shared lane without
making one historical person a brittle owner. Coordinator status grants no
authorization and imports no Website/D35 coordinator meaning.

### Option 2 — every currently eligible grant manager

Project recipient engagement for every current exact-scope grant manager except
the requester.

**UX/impact:** no coordinator setup and high visibility, but duplicated personal
work, diffuse ownership, membership-churn fanout, notification fatigue, noisy
counts, and wider exposure of even the safe task envelope.

### Option 3 — shared Access requests lane only

Create no personal task projection. Authorized staff deliberately work from the
shared source lane.

**UX/impact:** strongest no-build routing alternative and no fanout, but nobody
receives explicit responsibility; requests can age unless staff remember to
check the lane.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — optional one to three Access request
coordinators.** It follows the modern separation between request authority and
work assignment, provides deliberate accountability without an all-admin
broadcast, and remains fully operable with no configuration.

Which D44 personal routing policy should Core record: **Option 1 — optional one
to three Access request coordinators**, **Option 2 — every currently eligible
grant manager**, or **Option 3 — shared Access requests lane only**? You may
amend any option.

### D44 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — optional one to three **Access request
coordinators**. Tasks Hub is not their only notification path.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> A Tenant may deliberately use the complete permission-filtered **Access
> requests** lane alone or name one to three unique, unordered, co-equal current
> same-Tenant Active Tenant Assignments as **Access request coordinators**.
> Newly selected members must independently satisfy current D43 grant-decision
> eligibility in at least one live Tenant scope; each request then re-proves
> its exact-scope `permissions.manage_grants` recipient checks. Configuration grants no
> capability, visibility, decision authority, task administration, notification
> preference, or other access. A recreated assignment never inherits the
> selection. Each request re-proves current authority and excludes its requester
> from personal responsibility without changing separately lawful source-lane
> action.
>
> The policy is exactly **Use the shared Access requests lane only** or **Also
> give specific people personal responsibility**. Lane-only is a complete safe
> mode, not **Off**, **Not configured**, or failed coverage. Named mode contains
> one to three current eligible assignments; zero or four is invalid. The
> complete resolver returns a released bounded set, proved zero, or indeterminate.
> Proved zero and indeterminate route nobody and never fall back to every grant
> manager, an Owner/Admin, original grantor, requester-selected reviewer,
> manager, group, prior recipient, support operator, AI, or service role.
>
> The D44-governed future **People & access → Access requests** area shows one compact
> **Access request coordinators** summary and **Change coordinators** action; D44
> adds no top-level page or coordinator dashboard. One responsive Base Maia
> Sheet explains that every request remains in Access requests and that choosing
> a person gives responsibility, not permission. Named mode progressively
> reveals a server-filtered, paginated Base UI picker containing only current
> eligible people. Previously configured members who later become ineligible
> remain visible to authorized policy managers as **Not currently eligible** and
> receive nothing. Members are co-equal; there is no primary/backup, ordering,
> group, round-robin, workload, schedule, delegation, manager, escalation, or
> fourth-member control.
>
> Before save, Core computes a fresh permission-safe aggregate consequence
> review against the current policy, authorization, and pending-request heads.
> It shows current open requests plus continuing, newly assigned, no-longer-
> assigned personal responsibilities and requests remaining shared-lane-only,
> with clear request-versus-responsibility units and without per-person workload
> or protected request detail. Copy says **This updates personal responsibility for open and
> future requests. Access and request decisions do not change.** Stale, partial,
> timed-out, contradictory, corrupt, or indeterminate impact writes nothing.
> A confirmed save appends one immutable policy revision, audit, semantic
> receipt, trusted cutover, and identifier-only reconciliation intent; it applies
> to every current and future pending D43 request.
>
> Continuing recipients preserve engagement; newly admitted recipients receive
> a fresh source-backed personal task and required in-product attention; removed
> recipients end as **Coordinator responsibility changed**. An unchanged
> effective set creates no recipient-generation, task, bell, unread, or audit
> churn. D43 withdrawal, keep/remove, or no-longer-applicable remains the only
> business closure. Routing changes no request, decision, grant, duration, or
> authorization epoch.
>
> Tasks Hub is not the only attention path. A newly opened request creates one
> safe, source-actionable `holder_access_review_requested_v1` Phase 17 item for
> each newly admitted coordinator. A route or eligibility change admitting one
> coordinator to existing pending work creates individual Tasks Hub assignments
> but only one safe `access_request_responsibility_updated_v1` in-product item
> for that recipient and responsibility-application generation, not one bell
> item per existing request. The generation pins the route revision, current
> eligibility/authorization basis, admission cause, and sealed child set so
> later re-admission under the same route cannot collide.
> Both use `presentation.source_actionable_then_recent_90d@1`, deep-link to the
> authenticated People & access source, copy no request/decision explanation,
> D40 reason, capability/group provenance, raw ID, or qualification detail, and
> offer no inline Keep/Remove action.
>
> Phase 12 owns the route, current recipient generation, D43 request, grant, and
> authorization. ADR-0183 owns task presentation and engagement only. ADR-0027/
> Phase 17 owns notification presentation and engagement only. Phase 6 owns any
> external delivery. Their identities, engagement, retries, and receipts remain
> independent; none derives truth from another. Current authorization and source
> state win every race. Inngest, if used, receives identifier-only post-commit
> work and may reconcile projections; it owns no policy, recipient, task,
> notification, human wait, idempotency, request, decision, or access truth.
>
> Same-Tenant composite relationships, one current policy head, closed mode and
> cardinality checks, append-only revisions/generations, restrictive deletion,
> expected heads, semantic receipts, raw-browser denial, `ENABLE`/`FORCE RLS`,
> correct `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, hardened pinned-function grants, and owner/
> service/`BYPASSRLS`/worker/support parity enforce the boundary. Protected D43
> detail remains behind fresh Phase 12 authorization and is never copied into
> route, task, notification, email, search, analytics, logs, AI, Realtime, or
> workflow payloads.

The modern pattern is supported but deliberately narrowed. Microsoft Entra
uses assigned reviewers and keeps its review portal independently available
from email; Okta separates request/task assignees and multiple notification
channels; SailPoint uses email plus in-app notices and a distinct approval
surface; Jira separates queues, assignees, and internal notifications. None
proves that three coordinators is universally correct, so 1–3 remains a
versioned Core v1 product judgment with named monitoring rather than an
external “best practice” claim.

option. The corrected decision resolves them through 30 normative requirements,

## D45 — Should external email supplement the required in-product attention?

### Why this needs your decision

Jordan submits a D43 access review request. Ana is an eligible configured
coordinator. D44 already guarantees that Ana receives one personal Tasks Hub
assignment and one source-actionable Notification Center item; either opens the
same freshly authorized People & access detail. D45 decides only whether Core
also sends Ana an external email.

Email can reach staff who are away from Mission Control, including people in
field or low-frequency administrative roles, but it also adds deliverability,
privacy, preference, duplication, and notification-fatigue costs. It must never
carry Keep/Remove buttons or protected request detail, and failure must never
change the D43 source, Tasks Hub assignment, or required in-product item.

### Option 1 — optional immediate email, default off — recommended

The Tenant may enable the contract-approved initial email step, and Core sends
it only when the admitted coordinator's own recipient preference also permits
it. The safe email contains the Tenant brand, **Access review needs attention**,
and an authenticated link to People & access—no reason, capability/provenance
detail, peer names, sensitive preview, or decision button. One new request may
produce one email. Backlog adoption may produce at most one grouped email for
the matching responsibility-update occurrence, never one email per historical
child request.

**UX/impact:** useful reach for ministries whose coordinators do not keep
Mission Control open, while keeping the default quiet and privacy-minimizing.
The settings must distinguish Tenant enablement from personal preference and
must say delivery is not guaranteed.

### Option 2 — mandatory immediate email

Every admitted coordinator gets a required safe initial or grouped-update email
step in addition to task and in-product attention, with no recipient opt-out.
Current destination, suppression, source-fence, and provider-safety checks may
still block delivery, and the UI must not claim receipt.

**UX/impact:** maximizes nominal reach, but creates avoidable noise, privacy and
deliverability burden, and a brittle mandatory expectation for users who work
primarily in Mission Control.

### Option 3 — no external email

Keep the required Tasks Hub and Notification Center experience only.

**UX/impact:** smallest and most private implementation, but coordinators who do
not open Mission Control regularly may miss new responsibility.

All options exclude SMS, push, Slack, Teams, email decision buttons, protected
email content, automatic escalation, and reminders. Reminder/escalation policy
would be a later separate D46 decision.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — optional immediate email, default off.** It
adds a useful reach channel without making email mandatory or authoritative,
preserves recipient control, and follows Core's contract → Tenant enablement →
recipient preference → current authorization order.

Which D45 policy should Core record: **Option 1 — optional immediate email when
the Tenant enables it and the coordinator preference permits it**, **Option 2 —
mandatory immediate email**, or **Option 3 — no external email**? You may amend
any option.

### D45 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — optional immediate email, default Off. Core
must preserve clear future seams for push, Slack, Teams, Google Chat, reminders,
digests, Tasks Hub, in-product notification, and escalation without pretending
they are one interchangeable channel.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D45 adds exactly one optional immediate `staff_email` sibling to each of
> D44's two exact Phase 17 contracts:
> `holder_access_review_requested_v1` for a newly admitted coordinator on one
> new request and `access_request_responsibility_updated_v1` for a newly
> admitted coordinator across one deliberate current-responsibility
> application. Both keep required `staff_in_product`; Tasks Hub and the complete
> **People & access → Access requests** lane remain independently available.

This deliberately takes only the parts of modern systems that fit Core.
Microsoft Entra separates initial email from reminders and keeps the review
surface available; Okta names exact audiences and supports distinct email,
Slack, and Teams paths; HubSpot exposes separate channel/topic preferences and
lets an individual's choice narrow defaults; Contentful pairs durable tasks
with assignment email. None proves Core should enable email by default, use an
email address as identity, import a vendor's workflow engine, or expose every
future channel now. Tenant-default-Off plus a self-owned opt-out is a
proportionate Core product judgment because it avoids both surprise universal
mail and a confusing second hidden opt-in; the D44 lane, Tasks Hub, and required in-product item already
provide durable recovery and D43 concerns sensitive authorization.
