## D46 — Should a still-pending access review receive an automatic reminder?

### Why this needs your decision

Hope Mission enables D45 email. Ana receives the initial task, required in-app
item, and—because she has not turned that personal email off—one email on Monday. The request is
still pending the next Monday. D43 currently has no due date, SLA, expiry,
urgency transition, or evidence-backed expectation for how quickly a ministry
must decide. D46 decides whether Core should create a second source-owned timed
occurrence anyway.

A reminder can help a coordinator who missed the initial attention, but an
arbitrary timer can nag volunteers, imply a deadline that does not exist, create
duplicate channel noise, and become an accidental workflow/escalation engine.
All options keep the complete source lane unchanged; for every current D44
personal recipient, that recipient's source-backed Tasks Hub item and required
in-product item remain durable, while D45 initial-email policy is unchanged. A
reminder, if adopted, would be a distinct
source occurrence with fresh recipient/source proof—not a resend or a timer
inside Phase 17.

### Option 1 — no automatic reminder in v1 — recommended

Create no timed reminder until the governing access-request source defines a
real due date, expiry, risk transition, or another separately ratified temporal
requirement. Pending
work remains continuously visible in **Access requests**; every current D44
personal recipient retains their source-backed Tasks Hub item and source-
actionable Notification Center item. Staff may follow up deliberately.

**UX/impact:** no invented urgency, duplicate unread items, arbitrary calendar
math, or reminder configuration. The cost is that a coordinator who overlooks
all durable surfaces receives no second nudge.

### Option 2 — one fixed product-wide reminder after seven calendar days

For every still-current request, create one reminder occurrence seven calendar
days after initial admission. It re-proves the exact source and recipient and
never repeats or escalates automatically.

**UX/impact:** predictable and simple, but seven days is an unsupported product
number, ignores weekends/time zones/ministry rhythms, and visually implies a
service expectation Core has not established.

### Option 3 — one Tenant-selected reminder from bounded choices

Let an authorized Tenant select Off, 3 days, 7 days, or 14 days in the exact
contract-bounded plan. At most one reminder occurs while the source remains
pending; changing the choice is future-only.

**UX/impact:** adapts to different ministries, but adds configuration, temporal
semantics, impact review, scheduling/repair states, and choice complexity before
Core has evidence that any cadence is useful.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — no automatic reminder in v1.** Current
official access-governance and CMS examples tie reminders to a real review
duration, expiry, or due date. D43 has none. The durable lane/task/in-product
item plus optional initial email provide recovery without inventing urgency;
Core can add a reminder when a source-owned temporal fact makes it truthful.

Which D46 policy should Core record: **Option 1 — no automatic reminder in v1
until a source-owned temporal requirement exists**, **Option 2 — one fixed
seven-day reminder**, or **Option 3 — one Tenant-selected reminder from Off,
3, 7, or 14 days**? You may amend any option.

### D46 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — no automatic reminder in v1. Preserve a
clean, modern path to add reminders later without speculative implementation or
technical debt now.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D46 creates no automatic reminder for a D43 Holder-initiated direct-grant
> review request while Phase 12 owns no truthful due instant, expiry, risk
> transition, SLA, or other separately ratified temporal requirement. Whether
> cadence alone can qualify remains D47. A request may remain
> `pending_review` for any duration its authoritative source permits. Elapsed
> request age, `created_at`, the independent grant end, Tasks Hub fields or
> engagement, Phase 17 presentation/retention, D45 delivery time or outcome,
> provider evidence, Tenant configuration, and executor wall time create no
> reminder occurrence, deadline, urgency, or access consequence.
>
> The complete permission-filtered **People & access → Access requests** lane
> remains the source-owned recovery read model over authoritative D43 records.
> When D44 assigns personal
> responsibility, the exact source-backed Tasks Hub item and required
> source-actionable Notification Center item remain continuously discoverable;
> D45 may add only its independently gated initial email. Age never clones,
> reopens, re-unreads, rebadges, reprioritizes, reassigns, or extends any of
> them, and valid shared-lane-only operation is not an ownerless failure.
> Source withdrawal, a lawful keep/remove decision, or the exact source becoming
> inapplicable alone ends D43 work.
>
> “No reminder” is an affirmative negative contract, not a dormant Off state.
> D46 adds no reminder key, meaning, profile, Delivery Step, plan choice,
> recipient preference, content, due/reminder column or relation, enum, API or
> event field, outbox/queue member, provider template, feature flag, cron,
> scheduled function, Inngest function/event/sleep, generic scheduler/workflow,
> analytics trigger, or hidden/disabled UI control. Unknown attempts to express
> those meanings fail closed. Core adds no generic **Send reminder** command;
> deliberate human follow-up through another independently governed channel is
> not an automatic D46 occurrence.
>
> Current UX stays quiet and reuses the established Base Maia source, task,
> notification, and settings surfaces. Tenant administrators see only D44
> routing and D45 initial-email delivery. Recipients see current work and its
> authoritative destination. Holders see their existing source-owned status
> and date. No screen, accessible name, sort treatment, badge, color, icon,
> toast, email, or empty state invents **Due soon**, **Overdue**, **Urgent**,
> **Reminder**, **Reminders off**, **Snoozed**, a countdown, or a response
> promise. Existing authorized timestamps remain historical facts; D46 gives
> them no temporal-policy meaning. Mobile, low-bandwidth, keyboard, screen-
> reader, zoom/reflow, forced-color, localization, RTL/CJK, and time-zone states
> retain the same truthful no-reminder semantics.
>
> A future reminder can be admitted only by a new evidence-backed source
> decision that first ratifies one **Source-owned temporal requirement** and one
> stable reminder meaning. Before any executable artifact exists, that contract
> must define the exact source and policy revision; clock owner; absolute
> instant and human time-zone/calendar/tzdb interpretation when applicable;
> current actionability and usefulness predicates; recipient generation and
> authorization; bounded cardinality; semantic occurrence identity; atomic
> source occurrence plus identifier-only product dispatch/projection handoff;
> permanent product uniqueness and claims;
> cancellation, supersession, rescheduling, and terminal paths; privacy and
> safe content; late/missed/outage/catch-up behavior; rollout, kill, rollback,
> repair, audit, observability, and proof. Rescheduling creates an explicit
> successor generation rather than silently mutating historical meaning.
>
> A future reminder is a new source-owned occurrence, not a retry or resend of
> D44/D45 and not a Tasks Hub, Phase 17, provider, or workflow fact. Its in-
> product, email, push, Slack, Teams, Google Chat, or later transports are
> independently reviewed Delivery Steps; D45 email enablement never authorizes
> reminder email, and reminder, digest, escalation, recurrence, and transport
> remain separate decisions. No generic channel payload, preference map,
> cadence preset, reminder table, scheduler, or rules DSL is prebuilt.
>
> Inngest is a valid optional future executor only after product truth exists.
> The source transaction must atomically commit the temporal occurrence fact
> plus an identifier-only product dispatch/projection handoff. Phase 17 then
> compiles the permitted plan and Phase 6 owns recipient communication intents,
> preparation, provider handoff, and delivery evidence. An identifier-only
> workflow wake may later sleep, scan, or reconcile,
> then claim the exact product occurrence and freshly re-prove current source,
> Tenant, EffectiveAccess, recipient, authorization, cancellation, and
> usefulness before any presentation or submission. Inngest's event/run
> idempotency windows, cancellation, clock, trace retention, replay, and status
> are secondary safeguards, never the clock, source, permanent uniqueness,
> audit record, or outcome. A cancellation event cannot replace fire-time
> source proof.
>
> Aggregate age, route coverage, support, and attention evidence may trigger
> product research only. It cannot send a reminder, classify an individual as
> late, score staff, label a request overdue, or silently activate code. Any
> production monitor must name its aggregate signal, threshold, accountable
> owner, and human response; no monitor becomes product policy without a later
> founder/source decision.
> Monitor names in the D46 evidence package are acceptance/evidence labels, not
> authorization for a v1 telemetry pipeline, table, event, job, dashboard, or
> alert. Zero-artifact invariants use CI and release audit. Product discovery is
> deliberate, privacy-reviewed, time-bounded research using already permitted
> source facts unless a separate instrumentation decision authorizes more.

This deliberately adopts the boundary—not the feature breadth—of current
systems. Microsoft Entra binds reminders to a review duration and due-date
context; Contentful reminds before an optional task due date; HubSpot separates
due-time reminders from independently opted-in digests; Inngest supplies useful
durable wake-ups but documents bounded idempotency and cancellation/visibility
limits. Those products support source time, explicit channel separation, and
durable task visibility; they do not justify inventing seven days, importing a
task reminder as access truth, or reserving a generic reminder engine in Core.

All 22 adversarial categories contain a material concern under the unqualified
“no reminder, but make it future-ready” answer. The corrected decision resolves
them through 30 normative requirements, continuous acceptance criteria,
continuous primary-research assertions, named monitors, explicit UX/access/
data/executor boundaries, and a no-placeholder rollout in:

## D47 — Can a Tenant cadence alone become the source clock for an access-review reminder?

### Why this needs your decision

Suppose interviews and aggregate product evidence show that Hope Mission's
coordinators want one nudge after five working days. Nothing is due on day five,
the request does not expire, access risk does not change, and no action occurs
if staff respond later. D46 correctly creates no reminder now, but its future
admission gate still needs to decide whether that validated preference could
itself become Phase 12 business time.

This is not merely a notification setting. Treating cadence as source truth
would require an exact calendar and time zone, version/effective-date rules,
future-versus-current impact, rescheduling, recipient changes, cancellation,
outage catch-up, audit, and plain-language UX that does not falsely imply an
SLA. Rejecting cadence alone keeps those costs out until a real lifecycle fact
exists, but may delay a useful nudge for ministries whose workflow has no formal
deadline.

All options describe a possible later feature. None creates a reminder,
setting, key, schema, worker, or placeholder through D47, and none decides
whether a later policy applies only to new requests or may include current
work; a later feature decision would still need D46's complete source,
authorization, timing, idempotency, privacy, channel, rollout, and proof
contract.

### Option 1 — a bounded, independently validated Tenant cadence may qualify — recommended

After sufficient ministry research, Phase 12 may define an Off-by-default,
versioned, bounded Tenant attention policy even without a due/expiry/risk
transition. It may create at most one source-owned reminder while the exact
request remains current; it creates no SLA, Due/Overdue status, no-response
action, escalation, or access change. Exact choices, calendar/time-zone model,
and impact rules require a later decision rather than being frozen now.

**UX/impact:** gives ministries useful flexibility without pretending a
deadline exists. A later compact source setting could say **If a review is
still waiting after [bounded choice], create one courtesy reminder** and
immediately explain **This does not set a due date or change access. How it is
delivered is managed separately.** It must preview the exact cohort effect
selected later and keep channel delivery separate.

### Option 2 — cadence alone is insufficient

A future automatic reminder requires an independently meaningful source
lifecycle fact, such as a due instant, expiry, or risk/state transition. Once
that fact exists, a reviewed Tenant choice may narrow or choose among bounded
offsets inside the source-owned window, but it cannot create the window.

**UX/impact:** produces the strongest temporal clarity and smallest settings
surface. It can also make a useful courtesy reminder impossible for ministries
whose work has no formal deadline, or pressure product design to invent a fake
deadline merely to create a nudge.

### Option 3 — one evidence-backed product-wide cadence

After aggregate validation, Core chooses one product-wide source cadence with
no Tenant control. The source owns it and every future reminder still passes
the D46 contract.

**UX/impact:** avoids configuration and creates predictable behavior, but one
cadence is unlikely to fit both small volunteer ministries and staffed global
organizations and can become a hard-coded policy number that is costly to
change truthfully.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — a bounded, independently validated Tenant
cadence may qualify as Phase 12 source policy.** Microsoft Entra and Contentful
show the clearest due-window model; Okta and SailPoint also demonstrate that
timing remains sound when the source explicitly owns its versioned timeout/
cadence policy. Many ministries may have a legitimate courtesy-attention rhythm
without a formal SLA. Requiring a terminal consequence could make that useful
workflow impossible or incentivize a fake deadline. The safe modern boundary
is not “every reminder needs a due date”; it is “the business source—not Tasks,
notifications, delivery settings, providers, or Inngest—must own one bounded,
truthfully explained temporal policy.” Default Off, one reminder, code-owned
choices, explicit no-deadline copy, explicit cohort impact, and the full D46
admission contract keep that flexibility from becoming a rules engine or
accidental urgency; request-cohort impact remains a separate decision.

Can a validated Tenant cadence ever create access-review reminder time while
D43 still has no due date, expiry, risk transition, or other lifecycle
obligation: **Option 1 — yes; a bounded, independently validated, Off-by-default
Tenant cadence may become Phase 12 source policy**, **Option 2 — no; cadence may
only narrow a real source window**, or **Option 3 — only one evidence-backed product-wide
cadence**? You may amend any option.

### D47 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — an independently validated, bounded,
Tenant-default-Off cadence may later qualify as Phase 12 source policy for at
most one D43 courtesy reminder, even without a due date, expiry, risk
transition, or other consequence-bearing lifecycle fact. It must be modern,
clear, reliable, and free of brittle or speculative implementation.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D47 is a future **admission rule**, not feature approval. It permits Core to
> consider an **Access-review attention cadence policy** only after a
> preregistered, representative, privacy-reviewed evidence package demonstrates
> a real missed-attention problem, compares the complete D46 no-reminder
> baseline and strongest no-build alternative, and shows that affected users
> understand one courtesy nudge without inferring Due, Overdue, an SLA,
> escalation, no-response action, performance judgment, or threatened access.
> Vendor defaults, raw request age, one Tenant request, support volume,
> click/open data, or a plausible ministry story cannot qualify it.
>
> The possible future policy is a separate versioned Tenant-wide Phase 12
> source policy, absent/Off by default. If later evidence and decisions admit
> non-Off values, an authorized Tenant may select only one value from a small,
> code-owned, evidence-backed set. D47 chooses no number, unit, calendar, time
> zone, send time, channel, content, or preset. Free-form duration/date, cron,
> RRULE, recurrence, custom calendar, per-request/per-person override, branching
> condition, recipient query, channel list, reminder text, and Tenant-authored
> rule/workflow are prohibited.
>
> One exact D43 request episode may create at most one future courtesy reminder
> source occurrence. The permanent occurrence slot excludes mutable policy
> revision, recipient count, route revision, channel, task/item identity,
> provider key, executor run, retry, repair, and replay, so none can mint a
> second reminder. The admitted policy revision and temporal inputs become
> immutable comparison/audit evidence, not another uniqueness dimension.
> Reminder, digest, repeat, escalation, reassignment, snooze, timeout, manual
> nudge, and no-response action remain different undecided meanings.
>
> The only possible source meaning is that one exact access review is still
> waiting at an admitted courtesy-attention point. The request remains equally
> valid before and after it. Crossing the cadence never creates Due/Overdue,
> urgency, priority, compliance or staff-performance state; changes no D43
> lifecycle, grant, capability, EffectiveAccess, assignment, authorization
> epoch, decision default, or access; and never supplies evidence that a person
> read, understood, or acted.
>
> Phase 12 alone owns whether the future source policy applies, its temporal
> interpretation, the exact request episode, source occurrence, cancellation/
> supersession, and current-usefulness proof. D44 alone owns personal
> responsibility. ADR-0183 Tasks Hub retains the existing source-backed task
> and gains no due/reminder field or second task. Phase 17 owns only a later
> stable message meaning plus bounded presentation/Delivery Steps; Phase 6 owns
> recipient communication intents, preparation, provider handoff, delivery
> evidence, and ambiguity repair. Providers own provider evidence. Inngest may
> later wake, claim, and reconcile identifier-only product work, but never owns
> source time, recipient authority, permanent idempotency, cancellation truth,
> audit history, or outcome.
>
> The cadence policy is not a D44 coordinator-policy field, Phase 17 Delivery
> Plan, personal Notification setting, task property, automation, or Inngest
> configuration. A Delivery Plan or preference cannot create, delay,
> reschedule, cancel, or repeat Phase 12 source time. D45 initial-email plan,
> recipient preference, intent, provider retry/outcome, or later channel
> enablement authorizes no reminder occurrence or transport.
>
> A future policy writer must use the established D44 management boundary: a
> current same-Tenant actor independently authorized for Tenant-wide
> `permissions.manage_grants` administration and the registered source-policy
> purpose, through an expected-head server command. Coordinator/recipient/task
> status, Owner/Administrator labels, group membership,
> `system_messages.plan.manage`, provider access, support, AI, and service role
> alone grant nothing. Tenant, actor, time, policy/source heads, and audit
> attribution are trusted-server-derived; no browser/client caller supplies
> authority facts.
>
> If later persistence is earned, it must use a separate immutable/versioned
> Phase 12 policy aggregate and source occurrence/receipt, not cadence fields on
> D43/D44/tasks/Phase 17, mutable `last_reminded_at`, raw interval, generic
> `remind_at`, polymorphic scheduler, provider schedule, or JSON rule blob.
> Tenant-composite relationships, non-null closed choice identity, restrictive
> deletion, forced RLS, matching mutation `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, browser
> revocation, narrow privileged-path parity, permanent product uniqueness,
> expected-head commands, claims, append-only evidence, and identifier-only
> events are mandatory. No policy revision can retarget another Tenant/request
> or transform a permitted row into a forbidden state.
>
> D47 activates no source policy, reminder, stable message key, catalog/manifest
> row, schema, enum, preset, preference, event, queue, outbox member, job, cron,
> Inngest function/sleep, provider template, telemetry pipeline, feature flag,
> migration, setting, or UI placeholder. Phase 17 census counts remain 20
> Target Live candidates and 20 Reserved keys. Current generic task reminders,
> contribution approval timers, Support automation, and demo/broad-role UI are
> migration hazards, not precedents.
>
> A later source-policy experience belongs in **People & access → Access
> requests**, not System Messages, Tasks, Notifications, Automations, or
> provider settings. Its durable mental model is **one courtesy reminder while
> a request is still waiting**, **This does not set a due date or change
> access**, and **How it is delivered is managed separately**. Off is the safe
> default. It must use shared Base Maia/Base UI patterns and eventually prove
> concise source context, local draft, explicit save/cancel, persistent result
> and stale-head recovery, mobile/low-bandwidth operation, keyboard/screen-
> reader behavior, 400-percent reflow, forced colors, localization/RTL/CJK, and
> non-color semantics. D47 chooses no exact component, copy, schedule preview,
> current-work impact statement, recipient wording, or recovery flow before the
> remaining policy decisions.
>
> D47 deliberately leaves unresolved: whether a later non-Off policy applies
> only to new requests or may include current pending work; policy-change/Off/
> reschedule and rollback semantics; recipient-generation binding, route churn,
> zero-member and backfill behavior; elapsed versus civil/working-day clock,
> IANA zone, DST/tzdb, holidays, lateness/catch-up; exact presets; stable Phase
> 17 message key/presentation; and every channel. D48 decides request-cohort
> application first, D49 recipient binding next, and D50 clock/calendar after
> those ownership inputs are fixed.
>
> The active outbound-communications OpenSpec's generic Tenant-enabled reminder
> scenario is not access-reminder authority. Before later activation, a source-
> specific scenario must state that Phase 12 selects cadence and commits the
> current source occurrence before Phase 17 compiles delivery; no plan or
> preference owns source time. Canonical workflow OpenSpec already keeps product
> records, authorization, dispatch ledger, and product claims authoritative and
> Inngest replaceable, so its ownership model does not change.

The strongest alternative remains **cadence alone is insufficient**. It is
technically smaller and semantically stricter. Option 1 survives only because a
truthfully labelled one-time courtesy-attention rhythm may solve a validated
ministry problem without manufacturing a deadline. If representative evidence
never clears the gate, the correct permanent result remains D46's no reminder.

Modern evidence supports the amended boundary rather than a copied feature.
Microsoft Entra anchors reminders to review windows and recommends controlled
pilots; Okta ties warnings to source expiry/duration; Contentful, HubSpot, and
Blackbaud commonly attach reminders to due source work. SailPoint additionally
demonstrates a source-owned cadence with explicit count, timing, time zone,
schedule preview, and policy versions that affect requests according to source
rules. WCAG warns that non-emergency interruptions should be suppressible and
that status feedback must not become unnecessarily chatty. None establishes a
Core cadence value or authorizes enterprise workflow breadth.

## D48 — Which requests may a later non-Off cadence policy include?

### Why this needs your decision

Hope Mission has twelve D43 requests already waiting when it later enables an
activated reminder cadence. Whether those requests enter the policy is
not a small implementation detail. It determines whether Core needs a current-
cohort transaction, baseline time, consequence preview, recipient snapshot,
backfill controls, migration, rollback, and protection against a reminder storm.

All options remain future-only and activate nothing through D48. D48 chooses
only the request cohort. Recipient-generation binding remains D49 and the
clock/calendar model remains D50.

### Option 1 — new requests only — recommended

A future non-Off cadence policy applies only to D43 request episodes committed
after its trusted effective boundary. Existing pending requests receive no
catch-up reminder. Their complete Access requests lane, existing source-backed
task for each current D44 personal recipient, and required initial in-product
attention remain the recovery paths.

**UX/impact:** the eventual impact review can say **New access requests only**
and **Existing requests will not be reminded**. This is predictable, low-noise,
rollback-friendly, and requires no historical-age interpretation or current-
cohort backfill machinery. The tradeoff is that older overlooked requests do
not receive the new courtesy nudge.

### Option 2 — separate deliberate application to current requests

Ordinary policy publication still affects new requests only. A separately
authorized **Apply to current requests** operation may later admit a complete
current cohort after a fresh aggregate consequence preview and confirmation.
The cohort receives a new source-owned baseline at confirmation; original
request age never creates an immediate reminder.

**UX/impact:** helps ministries address an existing backlog without surprise,
and follows Core's explicit-current-work precedent. It adds another consequential
operation, capability/authorization question, cohort identity, concurrency and
idempotency rules, partial-failure recovery, audit, preview freshness, and
rollback path before any reminder can be useful.

### Option 3 — automatically include current requests using original age

When the policy becomes non-Off, every pending request is evaluated from its
original creation time. Requests already beyond the chosen threshold may create
reminder work immediately.

**UX/impact:** reaches the backlog with no second action, but can cause an
irreversible burst, treat historically valid waiting as lateness, surprise
coordinators, and couple rollout safety to old timestamps and route history.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — new requests only.** It matches Core's
future-only attention-widening safety, makes the user impact explainable in one
sentence, prevents retroactive notification storms, and avoids building a
backfill/current-cohort lifecycle before evidence shows it is needed. Option 2
is the strongest alternative if later ministry evidence proves current backlog
adoption is necessary; D44's deliberate current-work application is the right
pattern then, but D48 should not prebuild it. Option 3 is unsafe.

Which D48 request-cohort policy should Core record: **Option 1 — new requests
only**, **Option 2 — new requests plus a separate deliberate Apply to current
requests operation with a fresh baseline**, or **Option 3 — automatically
include current requests using original age**? You may amend any option.

### D48 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — the first later non-Off access-review cadence
applies only to genuinely new D43 request episodes. It must be modern,
reliable, quiet, and free of a brittle timestamp classifier, surprise backlog
effect, or speculative implementation.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D48 selects **new request episodes only** for the first transition from source
> policy Off to a later activated non-Off cadence. Every D43 request
> episode already pending before that trusted first-activation boundary is
> permanently outside that activation. It cannot age in because it stays open,
> gains a coordinator, is viewed, edited, restored, replayed, migrated,
> reprojected, reindexed, or observed by a task, notification, worker, cache, or
> analytics process. A genuinely new successor episode created after a lawful
> terminal predecessor is evaluated as new work; it never reclassifies the old
> episode.
>
> **New** is an authoritative Phase 12 source-order fact, not
> `created_at >= enabled_at`, browser/server/worker time, HTTP arrival or response
> order, row insertion, deployment, task creation, notification creation, UUID
> order, or a later scan. First non-Off policy publication and D43 request
> creation must share one stable Tenant/environment/policy-kind serialization
> namespace that exists even when the optional policy row is absent. Locking a
> missing row, only one grant, or only one request is insufficient. The future
> design may use an advisory lock, compare-and-swap, serializable transaction, or
> another proven database mechanism, but D48 freezes the required behavior, not
> SQL, schema, or a vendor executor.
>
> A D43 creation may record cadence admission only when its trusted source
> mutation linearizes after the committed first non-Off policy boundary, freshly
> proves the exact server-observed policy head, and atomically commits the request
> episode, evaluated policy input/disposition, immutable source receipt/audit,
> and identifier-only durable handoff. A creation ordered before activation is
> excluded even when its response or projection appears later. A command begun
> before activation but ordered after it may use the winning head only after the
> whole trusted command re-proves that head.
>
> Semantic idempotency attaches to the durable business effect. A retry after a
> committed but lost response returns the original episode, policy disposition,
> receipt, and handoff even if the retry crosses the policy boundary. An attempt
> that never committed may retry the entire command against the current source
> order. Replay, repair, restore, import, and projection rebuild never infer a
> different result from current policy or timestamps.
>
> Ordinary policy absence or explicit Off is an expected no-admission result and
> creates no incident. A stale concurrent policy observation aborts and receives
> a bounded whole-command retry. If the server proves an asserted-active policy
> generation but its optional cadence evidence remains missing, corrupt,
> unsupported, incomplete, or contradictory after ordering is resolved, cadence
> must not strand My Access: the otherwise valid D43 request still commits with a
> typed **cadence not admitted** source disposition and minimized durable
> operational evidence, emits no cadence/reminder handoff, and can never age in
> later. This safe non-admission is attached only to that new source receipt; it
> is not a historical negative-marker backfill.
>
> The first activation reads or writes no existing pending request, performs no
> current-work census or recipient fanout, and creates no backfill, baseline,
> schedule, occurrence, missed-reminder state, task, item, notification, or
> message. D48 rejects Apply current, Include pending, original-age evaluation,
> import, exception, override, and hidden compatibility enrollment. If future
> ministry evidence ever proves a current-work need, it requires a separate
> D36/D37-style consequence preview and founder decision; it is not prebuilt.
>
> D48 preserves the governing domain boundaries. Phase 12 owns policy
> publication, source order, request creation, cadence admission, source receipt,
> lifecycle, and any later occurrence. D44 owns current personal responsibility.
> ADR-0183 Tasks Hub and ADR-0027 in-product attention are projections and create
> no second task or reminder authority. Phase 17 may later compile an admitted
> semantic occurrence; Phase 6 owns communication intents and provider evidence.
> A Delivery Plan, preference, task age, unread state, provider, analytics event,
> or Inngest function cannot create, change, repair, or infer cadence admission.
> Inngest may eventually execute identifier-only post-commit work and remains
> replaceable.
>
> D48 creates no new capability. A future policy save must use D44's **intended**
> Phase 12 management boundary: a current same-Tenant Active Tenant Assignment
> independently authorized for Tenant-wide `permissions.manage_grants` and the
> registered policy-management purpose, through an expected-head trusted server
> command. Current broad MVP staff capabilities and shell role gates are
> migration inputs, not precedent. Tenant, actor, policy/source heads, command
> identity, ordering result, disposition, and audit attribution are derived from
> trusted server context. A caller-supplied expected D43 source/request head is
> only a checked concurrency precondition and grants no authority.
>
> Future persistence must be non-null Tenant-scoped, use same-Tenant composite
> relationships and restrictive deletion, preserve immutable history, and apply
> least grants plus equivalent RLS across tables, views, functions, RPCs, browser
> revocation, service-role, and BYPASSRLS paths. Mutation policy must protect both
> row selection and resulting state (`USING` and `WITH CHECK`) so an allowed
> update cannot move a row across Tenant, purpose, policy, request, or actor
> boundaries. Rollout uses deny-compatible readers before writers, no historical
> admission backfill, mixed-version proof, and a roll-forward/kill path that stops
> new admissions without rewriting committed episode history.
>
> D48 authorizes no runtime field/table/enum, OpenSpec implementation scenario,
> Phase 17 key/manifest row, task or notification field, event, queue, cron,
> Inngest function/sleep, telemetry pipeline, feature flag, migration, setting,
> UI, or hidden placeholder now. Phase 17 remains 20 Target Live candidates and
> 20 Reserved keys. Source-specific identity/access and outbound-communications
> OpenSpec requirements become mandatory before eventual activation, after D49,
> D50, exact evidence-backed values, later edit/Off semantics, content, channels,
> rollout, and D46 proof are resolved.
>
> The eventual first-enable experience belongs in **People & access → Access
> requests** and reuses the repository's Base Maia/Base UI form grammar. It has
> one compact impact statement before explicit Save/Cancel:
>
> **Applies only to access review requests created after you save.**  
> **Requests already waiting aren't included.**  
> **This doesn't set a due date or change access.**
>
> It shows no current-request count, backlog grid, checkbox, secondary current-
> work action, channel promise, schedule preview, or confirmation ceremony. Save
> success is durable inline status—not a toast-only claim—and says **Saved for
> future access review requests. Requests already waiting have not changed.** A
> stale head shows the current server summary and preserves the user's local
> choice for deliberate resubmission; an ambiguous response first recovers the
> authoritative receipt. The later implementation must prove keyboard and
> screen-reader operation, visible focus, forced colors, target size, 320-pixel/
> 400-percent reflow, localization, RTL/CJK, low bandwidth, and programmatically
> announced persistent status without focus theft.
>
> D48 deliberately does not decide how later non-Off edits, Off publication,
> policy removal, clock changes, or re-enable affect already-admitted episodes.
> D49 decides recipient binding, route churn, and proved-zero versus indeterminate
> membership. D50 decides the clock/calendar/anchor/useful-lateness model. None
> is implemented by implication.

The strongest alternative is **a separate deliberate Apply to current requests
operation with a fresh baseline**. It is technically valid and consistent with
D36/D37's approach to consequential current-work migration, but it adds a new
authorized command, complete-cohort preview, baseline identity, concurrency,
idempotency, audit, partial-failure recovery, rollback, and UX surface before
there is evidence that a courtesy reminder must reach old work. D44's complete
lane, task, and required in-product attention already preserve recovery. The
automatic original-age alternative remains rejected because it can create a
surprise burst and turns old timestamps into a hidden urgency policy.

This is current, evidence-supported product practice rather than copied vendor
behavior. SailPoint explicitly states that changed reminder/escalation/timeout
configuration affects only requests created after the change and pending
requests retain submission-time configuration. Microsoft Entra separates the
current review instance from future recurrence data. HubSpot makes existing-
record enrollment an explicit publish choice; Salesforce transition events,
Blackbaud form revisions, and Stripe Price/version behavior likewise separate
new work from deliberate migration of active records. PostgreSQL documents that
complex concurrent business rules need stronger ordering than an incidental
Read Committed snapshot and that serialization failures require whole-
transaction retry. WCAG status guidance supports persistent programmatic save
feedback without moving focus. These sources validate the boundary and UX
shape; none dictates Core's schema, cadence value, authorization, or executor.

assertions, 60 research acceptance criteria, lifecycle/race/failure matrices,

authorization, RLS, tenant, UX, migration, executor, and proof boundaries in:

## D49 — When should the one reminder bind its D44 recipients?

### Why this needs your decision

Suppose Ana and Ben are Access request coordinators when a genuinely new D43
request is created. Before its possible source reminder occurrence, Ana leaves
the Tenant and Carla becomes a coordinator. Carla already receives the normal
D44 source-backed task and required responsibility-update attention for this
current work. D49 must decide whether the one courtesy occurrence belongs to
Ana and Ben, Ben and Carla, or an audience that continues changing as each
delivery surface acts.

This is a source responsibility decision, not a notification preference. The
wrong boundary can disclose sensitive access work to former staff, omit the
people now able to act, duplicate pressure on Carla, let different channels
address different people, or make retries non-explainable.

Every option preserves one occurrence per exact request episode, the complete
shared Access requests lane, the existing D44 task/current assignment as work
truth, requester exclusion, same-Tenant purpose-bound authorization, and no
second Tasks Hub task. Every later irreversible presentation or provider
submission must freshly reauthorize and may only suppress/narrow an already
sealed member set—never add, replace, broaden, or reroute it. Complete proof of
no eligible member is `proved_zero` and may seal an empty terminal result;
incomplete or contradictory proof is `indeterminate`, releases nothing, never
falls back, and may retry only the same source occurrence until a separately
defined usefulness fence ends it. D49 activates no reminder, clock, or channel.

### Option 1 — seal the current D44 cohort at the source reminder occurrence — recommended

At the one possible source reminder occurrence, Phase 12 atomically resolves
and seals the exact unordered zero-to-three-member cohort from the then-current
D44 responsibility generation. Ana is excluded because her assignment ended;
Ben and Carla may be included because they currently own the work. The source
records that evaluated generation/member evidence once. Later in-product or
external delivery rechecks current assignment, authorization, destination,
preference/consent, and suppression and may only narrow the sealed set.

**UX/impact:** attention follows current responsibility, never former staff,
and every channel has one stable, auditable audience. The shared lane remains
the recovery path for `proved_zero`. The explicit tradeoff is that Carla may
receive both her normal D44 reassignment attention and this courtesy occurrence;
D49 acknowledges that risk but does not add another eligibility rule before the
clock decision.

### Option 2 — bind the request-creation D44 cohort, then narrow only

The source preserves Ana and Ben's request-creation generation. At the possible
occurrence, Ana is suppressed because she is no longer eligible, Ben may remain,
and Carla is never added even though she now owns the work.

**UX/impact:** this gives the simplest historical explanation and avoids a
second nudge for Carla. It can also miss every person currently able to act, and
a request created in lane-only mode can never gain a reminder recipient.
Mandatory narrowing avoids contacting former staff but cannot repair a stale
creation-time audience. This is the strongest alternative.

### Option 3 — continuously re-resolve current responsibility through delivery

Each in-product, email, push, chat, or retry path independently resolves the
current D44 route. Added coordinators can enter one channel while removed
coordinators disappear from another.

**UX/impact:** this maximizes freshness per attempt but lets one occurrence mean
different audiences, couples source responsibility to provider timing, and
makes privacy, audit, and idempotent recovery brittle. A provider-accepted
message cannot be recalled after a route change.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — seal one atomic current D44 cohort at the
source reminder occurrence, then narrow only.** It best matches Core's
authoritative current-responsibility model while retaining a stable,
cross-channel audience. Microsoft Entra, SailPoint, and Okta show why stable
review-instance membership and explicit reassignment are defensible; Core's
D44 source model adds the stronger requirement that former staff are excluded
and current replacements remain actionable. Option 1 reconciles both. Option 2
is quieter after reassignment but can omit every current owner. Option 3 makes
delivery infrastructure a routing authority and is too mutable.

Which D49 recipient-binding policy should Core record: **Option 1 — seal the
current D44 cohort at the source reminder occurrence, then narrow only**,
**Option 2 — bind the request-creation D44 cohort, then narrow only**, or
**Option 3 — continuously re-resolve current responsibility through delivery**?
You may amend any option.

### D49 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — at the one possible Phase 12 source reminder
occurrence, bind the people currently responsible under D44 once and permit
every later presentation or delivery path only to narrow that audience.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

> D49 selects one **Access-review reminder recipient cohort** for one exact
> D48-admitted D43 request episode and one permanent courtesy-reminder slot.
> “Current coordinators” means the exact complete D44 responsibility generation
> for that request after requester exclusion and current same-Tenant scope,
> ceiling, floor, source-visibility, and decision-authority proof. It never means
> every configured route member, a role, task assignee, request-creation member,
> cached roster, worker query, notification audience, provider lookup, or person/
> profile/email identifier.
>
> “At the source occurrence” means the successful authoritative Phase 12 seal
> commit. It is not a nominal wake instant, browser/server/worker time, HTTP
> arrival, task or item creation, render, provider preparation, submission, or
> retry. A concurrent D43 terminal transition, D44 route/application change,
> assignment end/recreation, capability/floor change, requester proof, or
> authorization epoch must have one serial result with the bind or force a
> complete retry. No projection or executor guesses the winner.
>
> One durable product occurrence identity survives every attempt. On complete
> proof, one trusted system/source command atomically seals that slot with exact
> request, D48 policy/admission, D44 route/application/responsibility heads,
> authorization epoch, one canonical unordered member result, member count and
> digest, immutable receipt/audit, and identifier-only durable handoff. A
> nonempty result has one to three unique members; each member binds both the
> exact D44 recipient-generation identity and exact same-Tenant Active Tenant
> Assignment. Profile, person, role, email, display name, group, manager,
> original grantor, Owner, Administrator, support user, and arbitrary eligible
> staff are not member or fallback identities.
>
> D49 and D44 policy/application publication must share one stable Tenant,
> environment, and D44-purpose serialization namespace—or an equivalently
> proven serializable predicate—even when no optional D44 policy or current
> recipient-generation row exists. If the occurrence wins while the source is
> completely lane-only, it seals terminal proved zero. If first coordinator
> configuration wins, D49 evaluates that complete current responsibility
> generation. `SELECT FOR UPDATE` on a missing optional row, a worker mutex, or
> eventual projection cannot define the order.
>
> The terminal recipient results are `sealed_members` and
> `sealed_proved_zero`. Complete proof of no eligible member seals proved zero,
> releases no descendant, consumes this one occurrence slot, and cannot be
> reopened by later coordinator configuration, policy change, retry, worker,
> replay, restore, or support action. Partial, stale, timed-out, unavailable,
> corrupt, contradictory, duplicate, over-limit, or otherwise incomplete proof
> is `recipient_resolution_indeterminate`: an unreleased nonterminal state, not
> a closed disposition. It atomically appends body-free immutable attempt
> evidence, releases no member or handoff, chooses no known subset, never guesses
> zero, and retries only the same occurrence identity. A successful retry may
> seal only the complete D44 cohort current at that successful commit or proved
> zero; only a later D50 source/usefulness fence may end it without release.
>
> Permanent occurrence uniqueness excludes policy revision, D44 route or
> recipient generation, member set/count/digest, task/item, channel, provider,
> executor, run, claim, and retry identities. None can mint another source
> occurrence. Same-identity/same-input replay returns the original receipt and
> member result; changed membership under a sealed identity conflicts and is
> quarantined rather than merged, replaced, or retried as a new occurrence.
>
> A sealed member is the maximum candidate audience and never an authorization
> grant or continuing-visibility promise. Every later source read/action,
> in-product presentation, and provider submission re-proves current source
> actionability, requester exclusion, exact assignment, exact authorization,
> purpose, and privacy. A member may continue only through a proved gap-free D44
> responsibility-continuation chain from the exact sealed recipient generation.
> Definite removal, assignment end, authorization loss, source end, or requester
> exclusion terminally suppresses that member from all remaining effects;
> remove-then-readd, restored eligibility after definite loss, a successor
> generation, or a recreated assignment cannot revive them.
>
> Channel-specific preference, consent, destination, readiness, or suppression
> may terminally narrow only that channel member and cannot alter the source
> cohort or another channel. An indeterminate downstream proof is not definite
> removal: it releases nothing and may retry only the same sealed member inside
> later usefulness rules. No adapter may add, substitute, broadcast, independently
> re-resolve D44, or borrow another channel's audience. Provider-accepted
> delivery cannot be recalled; current authorization still hides protected
> local detail.
>
> D49 does not reassign work. D44 remains current responsibility and creates the
> existing task plus its ordinary initial or responsibility-update attention.
> A coordinator newly admitted before the reminder occurrence may receive that
> normal D44 attention and also enter the D49 cohort; the meanings remain
> distinct. The reminder creates no second Tasks Hub task, task-reminder row,
> due date, assignee mutation, completion, priority, snooze, unread reset,
> engagement transfer, SLA, escalation, decision default, request/grant/access
> mutation, or another occurrence. Task state never repairs D49.
>
> Human policy publication and automatic occurrence authority are separate.
> Publishing D44/D47 Tenant policy uses a current authorized human and the
> registered `permissions.manage_grants` management purpose. The D49 occurrence
> is a registered code-owned system/source command caused only by the exact
> admitted current request, policy, and later-ratified source-time fact. Tenant,
> source heads, system actor kind, semantic command identity, and audit
> attribution are trusted-server-derived; it neither requires nor fabricates a
> live human policy-manager actor. Every human recipient read or D43 action
> independently requires that person's current exact authority.
>
> Future occurrence/member persistence must use non-null Tenant scope,
> same-Tenant composite request/policy/generation/assignment relationships,
> closed state/cardinality/digest constraints, immutable append-only history,
> restrictive deletion, browser base-table revocation, least grants, forced or
> equivalent RLS, mutation `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, hardened functions/RPCs,
> and owner/service-role/BYPASSRLS/worker/support/migration parity. Ordinary
> recipients see only their own currently authorized item, not peers, member
> counts, denial causes, protected D43 explanation, provenance, delivery state,
> or audit history. Events, logs, caches, analytics, exports, providers, and AI
> receive only purpose-minimized facts under their separately authorized seam.
>
> Phase 12 owns the occurrence slot, source recipient seal, result state, and
> receipt. D44 owns current responsibility. ADR-0183 owns the existing task.
> ADR-0027/Phase 17 own later presentation and Phase 6 owns communication intent,
> provider evidence, and channel-specific narrowing. Inngest may later wake or
> reconcile identifier-only claims but never owns membership, source state,
> permanent idempotency, cancellation, audit, or repair.
>
> D49 activates no reminder and adds no capability, relation, table, column,
> enum, key, plan, binding, preference, destination, channel, provider template,
> event, queue, job, cron, Inngest function, feature flag, telemetry, cache,
> migration, setting, UI, or hidden placeholder now. D50 clock/calendar,
> evidence-backed values, source usefulness, later Off/edit/re-enable behavior,
> stable content, channels, retention, rollout, and complete D46 activation proof
> remain separately gated.

The strongest alternative remains **request-creation cohort plus later
narrowing**. It gives the simplest historical explanation and reduces the
chance that Carla receives normal D44 reassignment attention and a courtesy
reminder close together. It loses because departed creation-time recipients or
a lane-only creation can leave every current responsible person outside the
reminder even after an authorized replacement takes the work. Continuous
delivery-time resolution remains rejected because it lets channels and provider
timing become responsibility authority.

Modern evidence supports the corrected boundary, not a copied vendor workflow.
Microsoft Entra snapshots users/resources/reviewers at each review-instance
start and does not silently add later owners to that instance. Okta resolves
reviewers at campaign launch and makes reassignment an explicit, auditable
operation. SailPoint similarly models assignment/reassignment separately.
GitHub's reminder products evaluate current pending review responsibility,
illustrating the value—and different semantics—of occurrence-time responsibility.
AWS's transactional-outbox guidance requires the source write and handoff to be
atomic and downstream consumption idempotent. PostgreSQL requires deliberate
serialization and whole-transaction retry for business invariants and identifies
RLS owner/BYPASSRLS exceptions. WCAG status guidance supports persistent,
programmatically available feedback without intrusive focus movement. None of
these sources proves ministry demand, Core's cardinality, or a reminder value;
D47's representative-evidence gate and default-Off posture remain mandatory.

Future cadence UX adds no recipient picker or duplicate roster. Its compact
read-only summary is:

**Recipients**  
**Access request coordinators responsible when the reminder occurs.**

One optional disclosure says:

**Later changes may stop delivery, but won't redirect that reminder. If no one
qualifies, the request stays in Access requests.**

It shows no names, avatars, live count, channel icons, delivery guarantee,
task claim, second Save control, or internal words such as cohort, generation,
seal, proved zero, or indeterminate. An authorized **Manage coordinators** link
reuses D44. Eventual recipient copy remains neutral—**An access review is still
waiting. Review current status and available actions in People & access.**—and
never claims prior notice, delay, fault, urgency, Due/Overdue, or access change.
No D49 UI exists today.

## D50 — What clock should make the one reminder occurrence eligible?

### Why this needs your decision

Hope Mission's admitted request commits Friday at 16:30 in the Tenant's
`America/New_York` zone while Carla works in Bangkok. A weekend and daylight-
saving transition follow; Ana leaves, Carla becomes responsible, the Tenant's
configured zone is later changed, and a worker wakes after the source instant.
D49 now fixes who can be sealed when the source occurrence successfully commits,
but it cannot say which temporal fact makes that occurrence eligible.

This is source truth, not merely scheduler configuration. The answer determines
whether “day” means 24 elapsed hours or a local calendar transition, whether DST
or a Tenant zone change can reinterpret admitted work, whether D44 reassignment
resets attention, and whether replay produces the same instant. D50 does not
choose a numeric cadence, useful-lateness window, Off/edit/re-enable behavior,
content, delivery time, or channel.

Every option preserves one source occurrence per exact D43 episode, D48
prospective admission, D49 occurrence-time cohort binding, trusted database
time, no task/date authority, no Due/Overdue/SLA meaning, and no worker,
provider, route, read, or notification timestamp as source truth.

### Option 1 — elapsed duration from the authoritative D43 source-creation commit — recommended

Phase 12 pins the later code-owned elapsed duration with the request/admission
source inputs and derives one absolute UTC not-before instant from the trusted
D43 creation commit. If a later approved value is described in days, each day
means exactly 24 elapsed hours. Tenant/browser/worker/recipient/provider zones,
DST, weekends, zone edits, D44 reassignment, task engagement, and executor delay
never reset or reinterpret that source instant.

**UX/impact:** this is the smallest deterministic model for one optional
non-deadline courtesy nudge. It is easiest to replay, migrate, test, and explain
as **after the request has been waiting for the selected interval**. The tradeoff
is that eligibility can occur outside local office hours; later channel quiet-
time and usefulness rules may narrow presentation without changing source time.

### Option 2 — Tenant-local calendar window from the D43 source creation

Phase 12 pins an IANA Tenant zone and calendar-rule generation with the admitted
request, maps creation to that civil calendar, and resolves the future local
window with explicit DST gap/overlap, tzdb-change, zone-edit, weekend, and
historical-interpretation rules. A working-day/holiday calendar would be the
more complex evidence-gated extension of this model, not an implicit default.

**UX/impact:** it can match familiar office-day expectations and produce a
consistent Tenant-local window. It also adds policy/versioning, DST, political
tzdb change, multi-region, holiday, localization, and repair complexity that a
non-deadline courtesy nudge has not yet justified. This is the strongest
alternative if representative ministries require a civil-calendar promise.

### Option 3 — elapsed duration from the current D44 responsibility generation

The source clock begins or resets when current D44 responsibility changes, so
Carla receives a fresh interval after assuming the request.

**UX/impact:** this reduces a reminder close to reassignment. It also lets route
churn postpone the occurrence indefinitely, allows governance edits to influence
temporal behavior, complicates replay, and makes D44 responsibility a second
clock owner contrary to the D43/D47/D49 source boundary.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — one elapsed duration from the immutable D43
source-creation commit, resolved to an absolute UTC instant and never reset by
D44 changes.** PostgreSQL's UTC instant behavior is deterministic, while IANA
documents that civil-time rules change through political decisions and require
updated tzdb generations. For a courtesy nudge with no deadline or promised
office date, importing that civil-calendar machinery now would be needless
technical debt. Option 2 remains available if representative ministry evidence
proves users need a Tenant-local promise; Option 3 violates source ownership.

Which D50 temporal model should Core record: **Option 1 — elapsed duration from
the authoritative D43 source-creation commit**, **Option 2 — Tenant-local
calendar window from request creation**, or **Option 3 — elapsed duration from
the current D44 responsibility generation**? You may amend any option.

### D50 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — elapsed duration from the authoritative D43
source-creation commit, after current research and repository fit are verified.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

The request-owned elapsed model is the modern, least-brittle permanent choice
for this single optional courtesy occurrence. The phrase “commit timestamp,”
however, cannot mean a physical PostgreSQL commit timestamp. PostgreSQL's
ordinary current-time functions have transaction/statement/call semantics and
physical commit-time tracking is optional. The corrected source anchor is a
fresh database-derived instant captured once at the authoritative request write
inside the D43 source-creation transaction after D48 has serialized the policy/
request race and proved the winning non-Off policy. It becomes authoritative only if that
transaction commits.

> For every D48-admitted D43 request episode, Phase 12 atomically retains one
> immutable trusted source-created absolute instant, the exact admitted code-
> owned cadence-choice identity and revision, its bounded positive whole
> elapsed seconds, and one finite absolute UTC **Access-review reminder
> eligibility instant** derived from those inputs. Exact committed replay
> returns the same evidence and instant. An aborted attempt creates no
> authoritative time; an ambiguous retry first recovers any committed receipt.
>
> D48 ordering and D50 time remain distinct. The source-created instant is
> captured only after the winning serialization result is known, so a
> transaction that began before first activation but commits after it cannot
> inherit an earlier transaction-start time. “Source-creation commit” means
> the successful business transaction—not PostgreSQL physical commit time,
> generic `created_at`, UUID order, HTTP arrival/response, or browser,
> application-process, task, notification, worker, provider, cache, analytics,
> import, restore, or support time.
>
> D50 is exact elapsed time. If an activated future choice uses the
> word **day**, one day is exactly 86,400 elapsed seconds. Calendar-day/month
> interval fields, civil or working calendars, IANA/session/Tenant/recipient
> zones, DST, weekends, holidays, tzdb changes, and local display do not enter
> source arithmetic. The implementation must compare absolute instants using
> exact bounded seconds; it must not use PostgreSQL `interval 'N days'`, a
> mutable current-policy join, JavaScript date arithmetic, or query-time age.
>
> One product-owned occurrence claim becomes eligible only at the inclusive
> boundary where a fresh authoritative database instant is at or after the
> stored not-before instant. Early executor wake creates and releases nothing.
> Late wake neither moves the instant nor authorizes catch-up or a second
> occurrence; the later cancellation/usefulness decisions govern whether the
> same unreleased occurrence can still close. D49 resolves the complete current
> D44 cohort at the actual successful source-seal commit, not retroactively at
> the nominal not-before instant.
>
> Source-created, not-before, wake/claim, D49 seal, presentation, provider-
> submission, and delivery-evidence instants are different facts with separate
> attribution. Policy, Tenant-zone, D44 route/recipient, task/engagement,
> deployment, restore, provider, and executor changes never recompute D50
> evidence. Current D43 actionability, D48 admission, D49 proof, current
> authorization, cancellation, and usefulness must still pass before any
> descendant. Product claims, permanent semantic uniqueness, the atomic
> identifier-only handoff, and durable business audit remain in Core; Inngest
> may later sleep/wake/reconcile but owns none of those facts.
>
> Missing, unsupported, contradictory, nonpositive, overflowing, nonfinite, or
> otherwise unprovable optional duration/time evidence cannot block the valid
> D43 access-review request. It follows D48's safe non-admission path and
> releases no temporal candidate or handoff. No worker, support tool, import,
> AI, or direct database repair may invent/rebase the source time.
>
> D50 creates no numeric choice, policy row, `remind_at`, task date/reminder,
> Due/Overdue/SLA/deadline, countdown, schedule/time-zone picker, message key,
> Delivery Step, preference, channel, schema, migration, OpenSpec requirement,
> event, job, Inngest function, feature flag, telemetry, or UI now. D51 and
> later decisions still govern policy Off/edit/re-enable cancellation, exact
> values, useful lateness, content, presentation, channels, and rollout.

The strongest alternative remains a pinned Tenant-local civil calendar. It
would be appropriate only if representative ministry research demonstrates a
real promise about local dates or working days. IANA's current database is
updated as political bodies change offsets and daylight-saving rules, and
PostgreSQL documents that adding one calendar day can differ from adding 24
hours. Importing zone, DST, holiday, and historical-rule authority without that
need would create complexity rather than user value. Restarting on D44 changes
is rejected because a routing edit would become a hidden snooze and could defer
the occurrence indefinitely.

The complete future source-policy UI remains one quiet Base Maia form under
**People & access → Access requests**. Its timing row reads **After the request
has been waiting for [selected interval]**. Persistent supporting copy remains
**This does not set a due date or change access.** One progressive **How timing
works** disclosure says **Timing starts when a new access review request is
created and runs continuously, including weekends. Time-zone and coordinator
changes do not restart it.** D48's **Applies only to access review requests
created after you save** consequence remains visible before explicit Save.
Ordinary staff see no countdown, candidate timestamp, promised send time,
business-day statement, worker status, or internal source/clock terms. A D42-
authorized provenance/audit view may separately label localized **Request
created**, **Reminder eligible**, **Recipients set**, and **Submitted** instants;
localization is display-only and never round-trips into source truth.

No D43–D50 runtime currently ships. Generic Tasks Hub `due_at`/`remind_at`,
contribution approval age scans, workflow retry/lease timestamps, Tenant
time-zone settings, Support business calendars, and widespread generic
`created_at DEFAULT now()` fields are current migration inputs, not D50
precedent or authority.

instant ownership, elapsed-second arithmetic, immutable source evidence,

negative architecture rules, production-shaped tests, and named zero-tolerance
monitors in:

## D51 — What should turning the cadence Off do to already-admitted work?

### Why this needs your decision

Hope Mission has three D48-admitted requests when Priya, an authorized policy
administrator, turns the courtesy cadence Off:

- the first has not reached its immutable D50 not-before instant;
- the second has reached it, but D49 recipient resolution is still
  indeterminate and has released nobody; and
- the third has a sealed D49 cohort, but no in-product presentation or external
  provider submission has crossed its irreversible boundary.

Priya later turns the cadence back On. D50 makes the original source instant,
duration evidence, and not-before instant immutable, but it deliberately does
not decide whether Off cancels current optional work, whether an interval edit
rebases it, or whether re-enable revives it. This is a source lifecycle and UX
decision—not a notification toggle detail.

Every option preserves the D43 request, existing Tasks Hub task, required D44
initial in-product attention, access, audit history, one-occurrence limit, and
non-retractability of any provider-accepted effect. No option turns Off into
request completion or access removal.

### Option 1 — immediate irreversible narrowing — recommended

Off atomically terminates every not-yet-sealed candidate and unresolved D49
recipient resolution admitted under the prior policy and suppresses every not-
yet-irreversible descendant of a sealed occurrence. An external effect already
accepted by its provider remains historical and cannot be recalled. A non-Off
interval edit and later re-enable apply only to genuine future D43 request
episodes; neither rebases, resumes, catches up, nor resurrects canceled work.

**UX/impact:** **Off** truthfully means no further courtesy-reminder effect from
current optional work. The confirmation can show one fresh authorized aggregate
impact—not names or protected request details—and say **Reminders that haven't
been sent will stop. Turning this back on later applies only to new requests.**
This is monotonic, explainable, rollback-safe, and avoids a resume burst.

### Option 2 — prospective Off only

Off excludes only future requests. Every already-admitted request continues
under its pinned D50 facts until it seals, ends, or reaches a later usefulness
fence.

**UX/impact:** preserves the simplest historical snapshot rule but conflicts
with the ordinary expectation that turning a reminder setting Off stops
pending reminders. Staff could receive reminders after an administrator saw
and saved Off, requiring prominent warning copy and ongoing support explanation.

### Option 3 — pause and resume current work

Off pauses all pending candidates and descendants. Re-enable resumes them or
recalculates their remaining delay under the new policy.

**UX/impact:** sounds reversible but creates hidden mutable clock state,
catch-up bursts, duration-version ambiguity, complex concurrency and migration,
and a second path to the one semantic occurrence. It is the most brittle
option.

### Recommendation and exact question

**My recommendation is Option 1 — immediate irreversible narrowing.** It gives
Off the least surprising safe effect, preserves D50's immutable clock and D47's
one-occurrence invariant, keeps widening prospective under D48, and avoids
pause/resume state or catch-up debt. It also cleanly separates policy choice
from non-retractable provider history.

Which D51 lifecycle should Core record: **Option 1 — Off immediately and
irreversibly stops every not-yet-irreversible effect, while edits/re-enable are
future-request-only**, **Option 2 — Off is future-request-only and existing
admissions continue**, or **Option 3 — pause and resume/recalculate current
work**? You may amend any option.

### D51 resolution

**Founder direction:** Option 1 — immediate irreversible narrowing, after
current research, repository fit, technical-debt, brittleness, and UX/UI review.

**Disposition after adversarial review: Accept with required amendments.**

The ordinary product meaning is right: turning an optional cadence Off must
stop every remaining reminder effect Asym can still prevent, and later turning
it on must not resurrect old work. The unqualified wording was not safe,
however. Provider acceptance is too late to be the first external boundary; a
request can already be in flight or have an ambiguous lost response. A policy
head alone is also insufficient because harmless non-Off interval edits advance
that head but must not cancel already admitted D50 packages.

The corrected decision is **immediate source-fenced irreversible narrowing**:

> Every successful Active-to-Off publication appends one immutable Phase 12
> policy revision and atomically advances a separate monotonic cancellation
> epoch with the expected Tenant/environment/policy-kind head, business audit,
> semantic receipt, and identifier-only outbox intent. Exact retry and an
> already-Off no-op do not advance it again. Non-Off interval edits do not
> advance the epoch; re-enable retains the advanced epoch. Both apply only to
> genuine D43 source creations ordered after their policy boundary under D48's
> shared serialization. They never recompute D50, resume, revive, catch up, or
> mint another occurrence for prior work.
>
> Each admitted request pins the current cancellation epoch. D49 source seal
> and every later registered channel-specific irreversible-effect admission
> re-prove that pin. If Off wins first, the prior occurrence or descendant can
> never cross its boundary, including an unresolved D49 occurrence; re-enable
> cannot retry it. If a source/effect boundary wins first, its immutable history
> remains truthful even if projection or provider evidence arrives later. The
> losing complete command conflicts/retries; no stale worker can guess an
> order.
>
> For in-product reminder attention, the boundary is the atomic role-safe
> release that makes the exact item queryable, not human read. Off-first
> releases nothing. Release-first preserves history while the reminder-
> occurrence Off end may remove active/unread presentation under ADR-0027
> without fabricating read, dismissal, archive, or deletion. The unchanged D43
> request and task remain active when their own source says so.
>
> For the currently governed email step, Off races Phase 6's product-owned
> provider-submission attempt fence committed before the first byte may leave
> Asym—not provider acceptance. **Prepared definitely unsubmitted** is still
> suppressible. After attempt admission, dispatch remains **Submission may have
> begun** while the independent provider outcome remains **None**, **Accepted**,
> **Definitely rejected**, or **Indeterminate** as evidence permits. After Off,
> reconciliation/webhooks may reduce that existing evidence, but no same-key
> follow-up call, retry after rejection, replacement attempt, blind resend,
> rekey, or recall claim is legal. Core never infers provider-acceptance order
> from a provider timestamp. Every later push, Slack, Teams, Google Chat, or
> other step must register and prove its own product-owned admission/finality/
> recovery boundary rather than inherit email assumptions or a generic
> cancellation engine.
>
> The Off transaction is O(1) in current request count. It does not enumerate,
> count, lock, or synchronously update requests, D49 members, tasks, items,
> intents, provider records, or workflow runs. Bounded indexed reconciliation
> may source-end/materialize projections later, but source truth changes at the
> policy commit and every read/claim remains fence-aware.
>
> Off changes no D43 request, grant, EffectiveAccess, holder decision, D44
> responsibility, existing source-backed task, or access. It creates no second
> or cancellation task, task mutation, cancellation notification, bell item,
> unread reset, email, push, chat, digest, escalation, or provider message.

The future complete policy editor remains one route-addressable Base Maia form
under **People & access → Access requests**. Off is a local radio/card draft,
not an instant switch, autosave, save-on-blur, or optimistic mutation. Selecting
Off reveals one inline consequence review in the same form; the ordinary Save
action becomes **Turn off courtesy reminders**, beside **Cancel**:

> **Turning off courtesy reminders**
>
> This stops every pending reminder Asym can still prevent. Earlier in-product
> reminder history may remain, and a reminder already being sent may still
> arrive. Turning reminders on again applies only to new access review requests.
> Requests, tasks, and access do not change.

There is no nested modal, typed phrase, confirmation checkbox, second
confirmation, recipient name, protected request detail, current-work count/list,
or provider-internal status. A stale save preserves the draft and reloads the
current head. Lost-response recovery reads the semantic receipt before offering
retry. Success is persistent and programmatically announced, not toast-only.
Keyboard, screen-reader, focus return, 320-pixel/400-percent reflow, target
size, forced colors, reduced motion, RTL/CJK, localization, mobile touch, and
low-bandwidth recovery remain release gates.

The strongest alternative—prospective Off only—is simpler but violates staff's
reasonable expectation that Off stops optional pending attention. Pause/resume
is rejected because it creates mutable remaining-time state, policy-version
ambiguity, backlog bursts, resurrection paths, and scheduler/fanout debt.
SailPoint supports prospective ordinary policy edits; Microsoft Entra separates
stopping a current instance from a future series; HubSpot skips actions while
Off without automatic replay; Inngest documents that cancellation cannot stop
an executing step; Phase 17 already separates pre-I/O, ambiguous submission,
provider outcome, and delivery evidence. These are comparators, not imported
authority: Core's source fence follows its governing ADRs and OpenSpec.

D51 creates no runtime, schema, migration, OpenSpec delta, policy row, epoch
field, message key, Delivery Step, channel, event, job, Inngest function,
feature flag, telemetry, or UI now. At D51 recording, useful-lateness expiry for
an otherwise-current occurrence remained the next decision; D52 now settles it
below.
