### Source and repository status

Current `develop` still has one optional nonunique Payload Tenant
`primaryDomain`, a Tenant-level resolver using `overrideAccess:true` and slug
fallback, `siteId: null`, global/static canonical inputs, and no product Vercel
Domains integration or D72 workspace. Phase 23 PR #1340 was verified
`OPEN/BLOCKED` on 2026-08-30. These are migration facts, not D72 authority.

The inherited Phase 5 p99 ≤15 ms admission-projection value is a launch budget,
not verified current capacity. It becomes a supported claim only after the exact
production topology, catalog, cache state, workload, sample, and duration prove
it. Once a public-role command commits, D7's hard 30-second desired/observed
containment bound applies; DNS preparation may remain honestly pending longer.

### Required proof and monitors

D72 activation remains off until the repository proves D72-R1–R18 and AC1–AC40,
including cardinality, global hostname claim, hostile Host/forwarded headers,
route-owner precedence, D16 one-hop root, real-browser fragment suppression,
zero Giving/protected redirect, canonical-generation closure, IDN, RLS/grants/
privileged paths, provider ambiguity/rates, adverse fencing, cache isolation,
migration/mixed versions/rollback, 320px/400%/screen-reader/keyboard/touch, weak
network, maximum catalog, and representative ministry-staff comprehension.

Ten D72 monitors name exact thresholds, owners, and responses for primary
cardinality, cross-scope binding, Redirect content, ineligible-route redirect,
redirect chain, fragment carry, primary-output generation mismatch, public-role
projection divergence beyond 30 seconds, host lookup budget, and platform-host
public output. Any wrong-Tenant binding, two primaries,
Redirect duplicate content, Giving/protected redirect, chain, or platform-host
Tenant content is an incident rather than monitorable residual behavior.

### Final decision status

D72 qualifies for ADR treatment because public-origin cardinality is hard to
reverse, surprising in the presence of provider aliases, and selected from real
trade-offs. It is recorded in
[ADR-0193](../../adr/0193-one-primary-site-domain-with-redirect-site-domains.md),
the glossary, Phases 2/5/12, ADR-0028/0030, the Web Studio living spec, and the
roadmap. No runtime, schema, migration, Supabase policy, Vercel setting, OpenSpec
delta, ticket, deployment, or production state changed.

## D73 — What should happen to the former primary website domain?

### Plain-language context

Changing a Primary Site Domain is not an ordinary text-field edit. It changes
the public origin used by every new website address, locale homepage, canonical
link, `hreflang` relation, sitemap, feed, social-sharing URL, and cache identity.
The former domain may still appear in search results, bookmarks, partner sites,
printed newsletters, campaign materials, and QR codes.

Keeping it as a website redirect protects ordinary link continuity. Stopping its
website use prevents Core from creating that website redirect relationship—
important for a ministry changing domains because of unwanted attention or
safety concerns—but cannot erase independent routes or external evidence.
Neither Vercel nor current code can choose that trade-off for the Tenant.

This decision concerns the former domain's **website role**. Existing Giving,
protected, callback, or other source-owned routes never move merely because the
Primary changes. They remain direct, become unavailable, or receive successors
only under their existing owners.

### Concrete example

Hope Relief is changing:

- Current Primary Site Domain: `www.hoperelief.org`
- Fully proved replacement: `www.hopeglobal.org`

The old domain appears on printed annual reports and links to:

`https://www.hoperelief.org/lang/en-us/stories/water-project`

For a routine rebrand, visitors should probably reach the same story at the new
domain. But if Hope Relief is separating a sensitive ministry from unwanted
public attention, redirecting the old address would reveal the relationship it
intended to end. Existing Giving addresses on the old hostname remain governed
by D9–D15 and are shown separately in the impact review.

### Safeguards every option keeps

- The replacement first proves exact Tenant/environment/Site, ownership, DNS,
  TLS, provider assignment, trusted admission, production rendering, locales,
  canonical closure, and safety.
- The old Primary remains authoritative until one explicit authorized successor
  command; Vercel completion never performs the change.
- The command advances exactly one Primary Site Domain and compatible D1/D66
  public-origin generations atomically—never zero, two, or a mixed cohort.
- Redirect targets are server-derived, same-Site final destinations. Staff never
  enter an arbitrary URL.
- Giving/protected/auth/callback/API/provider routes retain their source-owned
  behavior and cannot be hidden inside a blanket provider redirect.
- Historical documents, gifts, receipts, attribution, audit, and frozen URLs are
  never rewritten.
- Pre-commit failure changes nothing; uncertain/post-commit outcomes reconcile
  the same durable command rather than inviting repeated clicks.
- No Asym/provider public fallback, automatic domain force-transfer, scheduled
  change, timer, typed confirmation phrase, or generic redirect policy is added.
- Search recrawl is monitored separately and never defines command completion.

### Option 1 — require one explicit former-domain website choice during cutover (recommended)

The change review asks one required, initially unselected question:

> **What should happen to website visits at www.hoperelief.org?**
>
> **Redirect eligible website visits — recommended**  
> Current public website pages with a safe matching destination open directly
> at `www.hopeglobal.org` while Hope Relief controls and secures the old domain.
> Giving and protected addresses keep their separately listed outcomes.
>
> **Stop website use on the old domain**  
> Core will stop serving or redirecting this Site's website pages on the old
> domain. Existing website links may stop working. Independently managed
> addresses and external evidence listed below do not change.

The impact review separately lists any Giving/protected routes whose owners keep
their existing direct behavior or block the transition. The choice and Primary
successor commit as one domain-role transition. A retained redirect can later be
removed deliberately through the domain lifecycle.

**Why this is strong:** it supports the normal rebrand and the sensitive-ministry
case without guessing, adding a policy engine, or forcing a second workflow. The
common continuity choice is clearly recommended but never preselected.

**Tradeoff:** staff make one additional decision during a rare, high-consequence
change and must understand that “website visits” does not include every route.

### Option 2 — always retain the former primary as a Redirect Site Domain

Every successful Primary change automatically makes the former Primary
**Redirects website visits** while ownership, DNS, TLS, route, and safety proof
remain current.

**Why this is strong:** it is the smallest continuity rule, minimizes broken
ordinary links, and closely matches mainstream CMS defaults.

**Tradeoff:** it publicly connects old and new identities and creates ongoing
domain-renewal/DNS/TLS obligations even when the change is safety-motivated.

### Option 3 — always stop the former domain's website role

Every successful Primary change makes the former domain inactive for website
visits. Staff can later activate it deliberately as a Redirect Site Domain.

**Why this is strong:** it gives a predictable Core website-role stop, minimizes
retained website attack surface, and is safest when the Tenant plans to
relinquish or separate the old domain after resolving independent uses.

**Tradeoff:** it knowingly strands ordinary links, search continuity, bookmarks,
printed materials, and QR codes during routine rebrands and adds another action
to restore continuity.

### Recommendation

**Option 1 — require one explicit former-domain website choice during cutover.**
Google's current site-move guidance recommends mapping equivalent URLs, using
direct server-side permanent redirects, updating internal links/sitemaps, and
keeping valid redirects for at least a year—and potentially indefinitely for
visitors. That makes **Redirect eligible website visits** the right recommendation
for a routine move, but not a safe universal mandate for a missions organization
whose domain change may be privacy- or safety-motivated.

The UX remains one consequence-led review with current/proposed domains, an
unselected two-choice RadioGroup, a separate route-owner impact section, Back/
Cancel, and one final **Make {new hostname} primary** action. It creates no
global policy, schedule, expiry, approval workflow, or routing editor.

Primary evidence:

- [Google — Site moves and URL changes](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)
- [Shopify — Domain types](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/domains/domain-type)
- [Squarespace — Primary domains](https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/205812368-Setting-a-primary-domain)

### Exact question

When staff make a fully proved domain the new Primary Site Domain, should Core
use **Option 1 — an explicit per-change former-domain website choice**,
**Option 2 — always retain the former Primary as a Redirect Site Domain**, or
**Option 3 — always stop its website role**?

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — explicit per-change choice**, conditioned on up-to-date modern
practice, current Vercel behavior, edge-case safety, and excellent staff,
Tenant, and donor UX.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** Mainstream hosted products generally
automatically retain every connected former domain as a redirect. Shopify,
Squarespace, Wix, and WordPress.com therefore support making continuity the
recommended result. Core deliberately improves on that default because a
missions organization can have a valid safety/privacy reason not to create a new
old→new public identity link.

The informal wording is not accepted literally:

- **Redirect eligible website visits — recommended** replaces **Keep old links
  working**, because D9–D16 and every route owner remain stronger.
- **Stop website use on the old domain** stops the Site website role only. It
  does not stop Giving/protected routes, detach the hostname, change DNS, or
  erase search, archives, certificate records, backlinks, external caches, or
  copies.
- Every exact Primary successor—including apex/`www`—uses the choice. A prior
  browser-cached inverse redirect can make an automatic companion swap loop;
  redirect/cache history must prove promotion safe.
- The hard gate is complete only over finite code-owned Domain/public-head/
  route/security registries. Known messages, documents, QR codes, analytics/
  search properties, backlinks, and external placements are explicitly
  incomplete advisory evidence. D73 adds no URL crawler.

The complete 22-category concern analysis, D73-R1–R18, AC1–AC40, ten named
monitors, synthesis, and proof gate are in the
[D73 adversarial review](./phase-24-d73-explicit-former-primary-disposition-adversarial-review.md).

### Corrected decision

Every authorized replacement of an existing Primary Site Domain with another
exact fully proved Tenant hostname requires one initially unselected
former-primary **website-role** disposition:

1. **Redirect eligible website visits — recommended.** Current public website
   `GET`/`HEAD` routes whose owners prove a final equivalent destination redirect
   directly to the new Primary. The Tenant continues controlling, registering,
   renewing, connecting, and securing the former hostname.
2. **Stop website use on the old domain.** Core stops serving or redirecting the
   Site's website pages on the former hostname. Ordinary requests reaching Core
   receive the applicable neutral no-brand result. Existing links may stop
   working, and Core does not claim to erase external evidence.

The choice applies to every exact hostname change. There is no automatic
apex/`www`, same-domain, provider, migration, or AI answer. A current/historical
Redirect Site Domain may become Primary only when immutable redirect/cache
history proves promotion cannot create a stale response or inverse loop.

### Owner and privacy boundary

D73 changes only the Site website role. Each finite registered source owner
returns exactly one current `direct`, `unavailable`,
`unchanged_with_owner_successor`, or `blocks_primary_change` outcome. Giving,
checkout, Issued Giving Addresses, auth, callbacks/returns, APIs, protected
actions, webhooks, provider results, control, and every other source-owned route
run first and keep that outcome. D73 never redirects, stops, transfers, reissues,
reinterprets, or terminalizes them.

The review truthfully states when these routes can still identify the Tenant or
ministry. A former host without a Site website role says **Not used for
website** while any favorable independent route may remain. **Not public** is
reserved for complete owner proof that no favorable Core public route remains.

The server compiles a complete hard gate from finite code-owned Domain, exact
current D1/D66 public-head, route, and security/origin registries. Known CMS
placements, messages, documents, QR codes, analytics/search properties,
backlinks, printed material, and external integrations remain bounded,
permission-filtered advisory evidence labelled incomplete. No crawler,
universal content graph, inferred equivalence, or cross-owner workflow is added.

### HTTP, browser, and origin behavior

Stable equivalent former-host website resources may use owner-approved `308
Permanent Redirect`. Former-host `/` composes D16's current final Default Site
Locale homepage and uses `307 Temporary Redirect` because that destination may
change. Every favorable redirect:

- targets the direct final current destination in one hop;
- uses `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`;
- uses the owner-approved explicit empty-fragment form;
- preserves only owner-allowlisted nonauthoritative query context;
- sets no application cookie and emits no client analytics; and
- never handles unsafe methods, missing/unproved routes, or source-owned intent.

A host/target generation mismatch withholds the redirect and fails safely.
Existing Redirect Site Domains derive their new direct final target from the
same current Primary generation. Previously cached browser/provider redirects
cannot be recalled; incompatible history blocks instead of guessing.

### Authority, transaction, and Vercel boundary

Core privately proves the replacement's exact Tenant/environment/Site,
ownership, DNS, TLS, Vercel assignment, trusted host admission, rendering,
public locales, route/security impacts, redirect history, and compatible D1/D66
origin successors. One reauthorized semantic command uses expected Domain and
public-generation heads. In one short stable-order local transaction it inserts
the immutable Domain/public-origin successor cohort, receipt, audit, and outbox
and advances every exact head—or changes nothing. It advances no unrelated
draft, content, translation, Navigation, Giving, message, money, or source-owned
state.

Provider calls occur outside the transaction. Vercel supplies project-domain,
deployment, DNS, TLS, rate, and webhook evidence only. D73 configures no Vercel
whole-domain redirect; uses no `--force`; performs no move/detach/account/
registrar/DNS change; and never interprets an Instant Rollback/deployment revert
as product rollback. Vercel `/.well-known` control remains provider-owned.

Pre-commit failure changes nothing. Lost acknowledgement reconciles the original
receipt and suppresses blind retry. The new Primary can be authoritative while a
retained former effect says **Needs attention**; completion and receipts itemize
the exact authoritative and lagging effects. Reverting is a fresh successor,
never Undo or automatic fallback.

### Staff, Tenant, and donor experience

The qualified row exposes **Make primary**. One focused route-addressable Base
Maia review—not a wizard or provider dashboard—shows:

1. Site and production context;
2. stacked **Current** and **New** safe hostname values;
3. new-origin, public-locale, and existing Redirect consequences;
4. **What this change does not move** with authorized owner outcomes;
5. incomplete known external/placement guidance;
6. the unselected two-choice RadioGroup; and
7. **Cancel** plus **Make `www.hopeglobal.org` primary**.

Desktop Sheet versus full page remains evidence-owned; mobile is full-viewport
single-column. Submitting without a choice produces and focuses one visible
group error. Stale heads/impacts clear the choice and require review again. IDNs
show safe Unicode plus canonical ASCII, bidi-isolated and LTR for technical
values. No provider IDs/errors, status/cache controls, hidden counts, manual
canonical/redirect inputs, typed hostname, reason, second approval, schedule,
timer, or SEO certification appear.

After acknowledgement, the review returns to a durable **Changing primary
website address — You can leave this page** operation card. Success, partial,
unknown, and needs-attention receipts survive navigation and itemize Primary,
former website disposition, unchanged owner outcomes, and current recovery.
Visitor behavior works without JavaScript or an interstitial and contains no
Asym/platform branding, content flash, duplicate analytics, or homepage
fallback.

### Source and repository status

Current `develop` still has one mutable optional Payload Tenant
`primaryDomain`, a Tenant-level `overrideAccess:true` resolver with slug
fallback, `siteId: null`, global canonical inputs, host-blind static redirects,
and no D72/D73 schema, command, Vercel integration, or staff experience. Branch
HEAD and freshly fetched `origin/develop` were both
`7abd2c11ffd4ed70c6775c4fd6f51c996e4350dd`; Phase 23 PR #1340 was reverified
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at head `9069dcad67f9630323474ca5ee8bcc85ca7bf0f6`.

D73 remains intended documentation only. Runtime activation is gated on
D73-R1–R18, AC1–AC40, inherited D72/D9–D16/D66 proof, reconciled Phase 23
generation authority, consolidated Phase 24 OpenSpec, and exact design,
migration, provider, browser, authorization, capacity, accessibility, usability,
and rollback evidence.

### Final decision status

D73 qualifies for ADR treatment: the external/cache/privacy consequences are
hard to reverse, Core deliberately differs from mainstream automatic behavior,
and continuity versus identity separation is a real trade-off. It is recorded
in [ADR-0194](../../adr/0194-explicit-former-primary-website-disposition.md),
the glossary, ADR-0193, Phases 2/5/12, ADR-0028/0030, the living spec, and the
roadmap. No runtime, schema, migration, Supabase policy, Vercel setting,
OpenSpec delta, ticket, deployment, DNS record, or production state changed.

## D74 — After a domain stops every Core public use, who disconnects it from Core hosting?

### Plain-language context

Stopping a domain's website role and disconnecting it from Core hosting are
different actions. After D73, a former hostname can be **Not used for website**
while remaining attached to Core's Vercel project because an Issued Giving
Address, protected route, provider certificate path, or controlled neutral
response still needs it.

Disconnecting is stronger. Core asks Vercel to remove the hostname from its
project and eventually releases the current Site connection. It does not cancel
the Tenant's domain registration or edit registrar DNS. If DNS still points to
Vercel afterward, visitors may receive a browser/provider error rather than
Core's controlled neutral response.

Vercel exposes project-domain removal as a distinct operation and separates it
from account/domain removal. Its documentation also warns that ordinary
remove/re-add project moves can create downtime. Detachment is therefore not a
harmless cleanup detail.

Primary evidence:

- [Vercel — Removing a project domain](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/remove-a-domain)
- [Vercel — Transferring domains](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/transfer-your-domain)

### Concrete example

Hope Relief changed its Primary to `www.hopeglobal.org` and stopped website use
at `www.hoperelief.org`. Every source owner now proves that the old hostname has
no Primary/Redirect website role, current Site content, Giving address, auth,
callback, protected, provider-return, or other Core public use. Hope Relief wants
to move it to an independently hosted historical archive.

Who should remove `www.hoperelief.org` from Core's Vercel project and release its
current Site connection?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- Current Primary, Redirect, or independently used hostnames cannot disconnect.
- Every finite source owner must prove no current Core public behavior depends
  on the host; missing/stale/contradictory/unknown evidence blocks.
- Core acknowledges its adverse host-admission fence before provider removal.
- Provider work is outside the authoritative transaction, durable, idempotent,
  and reconciled; unknown does not mean disconnected.
- Caller input never supplies provider team/project/domain IDs, target account,
  or force-transfer behavior.
- The effect removes only Core's exact project-hosting association. It does not
  sell, expire, transfer, unregister, or edit Tenant DNS/registration.
- Immutable history and every D9–D15 address reservation survive.
- Release never automatically attaches the hostname to another Tenant, Site,
  environment, or provider project; reuse requires fresh complete proof.
- No timer, scheduled cleanup, provider quota, or metric authorizes deletion.
- Safety/ownership loss may fence immediately but does not silently authorize
  provider detach or claim release.

### Option 1 — separate Tenant self-service disconnection after complete clearance (recommended)

Once every owner proves the hostname clear, authorized Tenant staff see **Not
public · Still connected to Core** and one **Disconnect from Core** action. A
short consequence review explains that Core will remove the hosting connection
and release the current Site claim only after provider confirmation; domain
registration/DNS remain the Tenant's responsibility, historical reservations
remain, and future Core use requires fresh setup.

**Why this is strong:** it preserves Phase 24 self-service, Tenant control, and a
prepared move to another host without adding a workflow or provider dashboard.

**Trade-off:** an unused provider association may remain until staff deliberately
clean it up.

### Option 2 — automatically disconnect after every owner proves clearance

When the last Core use ends, Core automatically fences, removes the provider
association, and releases the current Site claim.

**Why this is strong:** minimizes orphaned provider associations, certificate
maintenance, quota consumption, and cleanup work.

**Trade-off:** “nothing currently uses this” does not prove the Tenant is ready
to disconnect. Automation can surprise staff, replace a controlled neutral
response with a provider error, and make reconsideration require full setup.

### Option 3 — Asym support performs provider disconnection

Tenant staff stop public roles and then request support to verify clearance and
detach the hostname.

**Why this is strong:** rare provider conflicts, account ownership, registration
complications, and ambiguous external outcomes receive expert handling.

**Trade-off:** creates a support bottleneck and tribal knowledge for an ordinary
self-service outcome that Core can prove mechanically.

### Recommendation

**Option 1 — a separate, owner-cleared Tenant self-service Disconnect from Core
action.** It cleanly separates stopping Core behavior from an external provider
removal, gives the Tenant the final choice, and keeps support as the recovery
path rather than the standard workflow.

The normal sequence is:

```text
Stop all public Core behavior
        ↓
Prove every finite source owner is clear
        ↓
Tenant explicitly chooses Disconnect from Core
        ↓
Fence acknowledged; provider removal reconciles
        ↓
Release current Site claim; retain history/reservations
```

### Exact question

After a nonprimary hostname has stopped every Core public use and all source
owners prove it clear, should Core use **Option 1 — a separate Tenant self-
service Disconnect from Core action**, **Option 2 — automatic provider
disconnection**, or **Option 3 — support-only disconnection**?

### Founder answer

> Separate Tenant self-service disconnection after complete owner clearance.
> Make the Tenant/staff UX excellent, well considered, and consistent with the
> product and repository.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** Current hosted-product practice supports a
separate self-service action, and Vercel confirms that project-domain removal is
different from account/domain removal. Automatic disconnection remains too
surprising; support-only remains too burdensome. The original wording and
technical boundary needed correction:

1. “Complete owner clearance” means no _current positive dependency on Core
   hosting_. Immutable history, audits, D9–D15 reservations, provider-control
   paths ending with detachment, and the current neutral adverse response
   survive without falsely blocking.
2. Ordinary staff copy uses **Disconnect from this Site** and **Disconnect
   domain**, not delete, release, transfer, unregister, remove from Vercel, or
   the platform-centric **Disconnect from Core**.
3. One short transaction first records a durable operation and monotonic
   Disconnecting barrier. Every public admission cohort acknowledges the
   adverse host generation before provider removal begins.
4. A Vercel DELETE/webhook is not completion. Current authenticated readback
   must prove every applicable Core-controlled project-domain, alias, branch,
   redirect, and wildcard association for the exact host absent.
5. Only then does a second short transaction end the current Site-binding
   interval and platform-wide occupancy claim. Canonical hostname identity,
   history, attribution, audits, and protected address reservations remain.
6. DNS, registration, renewal, email, Vercel team/account ownership, unrelated
   hosts, subsequent claimant authorization, and transfer are separate
   authorities.

The final disposition is documented in
[ADR-0195](../../adr/0195-owner-cleared-tenant-domain-disconnection.md) and the
[D74 adversarial review](./phase-24-d74-owner-cleared-domain-disconnection-adversarial-review.md).

### Corrected decision recorded

An authorized current human with `sites.disconnect_domains` may disconnect one
exact nonprimary Tenant-controlled custom hostname from one Site only after the
complete finite owner registry proves no current positive hosting dependency.
The capability is separately protected but included in the standard Domain
Manager bundle, so normal use needs neither a second role nor support approval.

The first reauthorized expected-head command binds exact Tenant/environment/
Site, canonical hostname, current claim/binding/provider generations, owner
digest, capability epoch, actor, and semantic idempotency identity. One short
transaction enters a monotonic Disconnecting barrier and writes the receipt,
audit, and outbox. No network call occurs under lock. Every favorable host,
role, route, publication, and reattachment writer rejects the barrier.

After the adverse host fence is read back, a sealed worker removes only the
exact Core-controlled Vercel routing associations and reconciles authenticated
current absence. Timeout, lost response, `429`, `5xx`, `403`, malformed data,
missing/late/duplicate event, or residual association retains the adverse fence
and current claim and shows **Disconnection needs attention**. Staff do not
resubmit or attach elsewhere. Only proved absence permits the final transaction
to end the current binding/occupancy interval.

D74 affects one exact custom hostname. It never cascades to apex/`www`, parent,
child, sibling, wildcard, another Site/environment/Tenant, Donor Portal host, or
platform/provider hostname. It never deletes/moves the Vercel account domain,
uses `--force`, changes DNS/nameservers/MX/CAA/DNSSEC/email, cancels registration/
renewal, transfers ownership, erases history/reservations, or authorizes future
reuse. A later connection is fresh setup under D75.

### Exact staff experience

The Domain row progresses through four plain states:

1. **Not used for website · Other uses remain** — show one permission-safe
   **Review current uses** handoff; no disconnect action.
2. **Not public · Connected for hosting** — show **Disconnect from this Site**.
3. **Disconnecting** or **Not public · Disconnection needs attention** — durable
   status, no cancel or second submission.
4. **Disconnected** — retain a permission-filtered history row and receipt.

The eligible shared Base UI AlertDialog is compact:

> **Disconnect `www.hoperelief.org` from Hope Relief Website?**
>
> Hope Relief Website is already not public at this domain. Disconnecting removes
> its remaining website-hosting connection. It does not cancel or transfer the
> domain, change DNS or renewal, affect email, or delete Site content and history.
>
> If DNS still points to the current hosting service afterward, visitors may see
> a browser or hosting-provider error until you update it. Protected address
> reservations remain. Using this domain here again requires fresh setup.

The actions are **Keep connected**—initial focus—and **Disconnect domain**. No
wizard, Sheet, route matrix, typed hostname, checkbox, reason, second approver,
timer, bulk action, raw provider error, fake percentage, or toast-only result is
added. The action remains usable and truthful at 320 CSS pixels, 400% zoom,
keyboard, screen reader, touch, forced colors, long localization, RTL/bidi, IDN,
weak-network, refresh/resume, and session-expiry conditions.

### Source and repository status

Current `develop` still has one mutable optional Payload Tenant
`primaryDomain`, Tenant-only `overrideAccess:true`/slug fallback resolution,
`siteId: null`, global canonical inputs, host-blind redirects, and no D72–D74
Domain schema, Vercel adapter, command, RLS, or staff experience. Freshly fetched
HEAD and `origin/develop` were both
`7abd2c11ffd4ed70c6775c4fd6f51c996e4350dd`; Phase 23 PR #1340 remained
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at `9069dcad67f9630323474ca5ee8bcc85ca7bf0f6`.

D74 is accepted documentation intent only. No runtime, schema, migration,
Supabase policy, Vercel setting, provider request, DNS record, OpenSpec delta,
ticket, deployment, or production state changed.

## D75 — Who may connect a previously disconnected hostname to a new Core Site?

### Plain-language context

D74 safely ends one current Site connection; it does not decide who may use the
hostname next. A disconnected domain may later be:

- reconnected to another Site in the same Tenant;
- sold or transferred to a different ministry that uses another Tenant; or
- acquired by a new registrant after the former owner lets it expire.

Historical Core facts must remain private and protected, especially old Issued
Giving Addresses. But prior Core history should not become permanent ownership
authority that lets a former Tenant hold a legitimately transferred domain
hostage.

Current Vercel practice uses a fresh DNS TXT challenge when a domain is linked
to another team/account. Cloudflare for SaaS likewise separates hostname-
ownership validation from certificate validation and traffic cutover. OWASP
warns that dangling custom-domain DNS can enable takeover, so fresh proof and a
clean nonpublic start are required; a prior Core proof can never be replayed.

Primary evidence:

- [Vercel — Claim domain ownership](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/claim-domain-ownership)
- [Vercel — Domain linked to another account](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/domain-linked-to-another-account)
- [Cloudflare — Custom-hostname validation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/domain-support/hostname-validation/)
- [OWASP — Subdomain takeover prevention](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Subdomain_Takeover_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

### Concrete example

Hope Relief disconnects `www.hoperelief.org` from its former Site.

Six months later either:

1. Hope Relief wants that exact hostname on a different Site in the same Tenant;
   or
2. New Mercy has legitimately acquired the domain and controls its authoritative
   DNS through a different Tenant.

New Mercy enters the hostname in **Add domain**. Core can see private historical
evidence and permanent old Giving-address reservations, but New Mercy must not
learn Hope Relief's name, Site, routes, dates, content, staff, or provider
account. Should fresh current DNS control proof be enough to create a clean
private candidate, or should historical cross-Tenant use add human review?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- D74 must be complete: exact provider absence is acknowledged, the former
  current binding/claim interval ended, and no current/pending/ambiguous use
  remains.
- The claimant proves one fresh, expiring, single-use DNS challenge bound to the
  exact canonical hostname, requesting Tenant/environment/Site, provider adapter,
  request identity, and purpose. Prior proof cannot replay.
- DNS ownership proof and certificate/TLS proof remain separate; neither alone
  activates a website role.
- The new binding begins as a private nonpublic candidate. Later Primary/
  Redirect activation still requires D6/D66/D72 readiness and explicit action.
- The candidate inherits no former Tenant/Site content, Brand Version,
  Navigation, locale, public generation, role, redirect, permission, analytics,
  cookie, cache, service worker, provider object, or operational status.
- D9 clean-start behavior and every D10 permanent Issued Giving Address
  reservation remain. Old protected paths stay unavailable without revealing
  why or who used them.
- Availability and failure are non-enumerating: the claimant sees only
  **Continue domain setup**, **Domain isn't available for setup**, or **We
  couldn't confirm availability**.
- Current hostname occupancy stays platform-wide unique. No `--force`, wildcard
  inference, suffix substitution, automatic transfer, former-Tenant approval,
  public fallback, or auto-activation is allowed.
- A failed claim changes nothing and does not notify or disclose a former Tenant
  by default.

### Option 1 — fresh-proof clean-start self-service for every Tenant (recommended)

After confirmed D74 release, any authorized Tenant may prove current external
control and create a new private candidate. Same-Tenant and cross-Tenant claims
use the same rule. Hidden history and reservations constrain outcomes but former
ownership is neither disclosed nor an approval dependency.

**Why this is strong:** it follows current SaaS ownership-proof practice,
supports legitimate transfers and expired-domain acquisition, prevents former-
Tenant hostage behavior, and keeps normal domain setup self-service.

**Trade-off:** Core must prove strict structural non-inheritance and permanent
reserved-path precedence across every cross-Tenant/privileged path. That is a
real implementation gate, not a support judgment.

### Option 2 — same-Tenant self-service; governed cross-Tenant review

Fresh proof creates a private candidate immediately within the former Tenant. A
different Tenant passes the same proof but then receives a privacy-preserving
platform review before candidate creation. Reviewers see only the minimum
current control, release, collision, reservation, and safety evidence.

**Why this is strong:** planned internal Site reorganization remains fast while
the rarest cross-Tenant transitions receive additional scrutiny and an explicit
audit boundary.

**Trade-off:** a human often cannot improve on complete current DNS/provider/
claim proof, so the queue can delay a legitimate new registrant and introduce
tribal approval criteria. The former Tenant must never receive a veto.

### Option 3 — explicit cross-Tenant handoff when possible; exception review otherwise

Same-Tenant reuse remains fresh-proof self-service. For a planned sale or
ministry transfer, the current Tenant creates a short-lived one-time handoff
that the named receiving Tenant combines with its own fresh DNS proof. An
unplanned new registrant with no handoff uses a privacy-preserving platform
exception review.

**Why this is strong:** deliberate organizational transfers have excellent
continuity and strong bilateral evidence without exposing history, while
surprise claims still receive scrutiny.

**Trade-off:** it adds a handoff lifecycle, expiry/revocation, recipient identity,
and exception queue; it cannot cover expired domains or transfers where the
former Tenant is unavailable. It is justified only if real tenants need planned
cross-Tenant transfers often enough.

### Recommendation

**Option 1 — fresh-proof clean-start self-service for every Tenant.** External
domain control can legitimately change, and complete current proof plus strict
non-inheritance is a stronger permanent boundary than a person interpreting
private history. It also gives the best staff UX:

```text
Prior D74 release confirmed
        ↓
New claimant proves fresh current DNS control
        ↓
Create a private clean-start candidate
        ↓
Retain hidden history and permanent address protections
        ↓
Later explicit readiness and activation
```

Option 2 is the strongest conservative alternative if representative security/
support evidence proves a human review catches risks the structural proof
cannot. Option 3 is best only if planned cross-Tenant transfers become a real,
measured workflow rather than a plausible one.

### Exact question

After D74 has completely disconnected a hostname and ended its former current
claim, should Core use **Option 1 — fresh-proof clean-start self-service for
every Tenant**, **Option 2 — same-Tenant self-service with governed cross-Tenant
review**, or **Option 3 — explicit cross-Tenant handoff with exception review**?

### Founder answer

> Option 1 — Fresh-proof clean-start self-service for every Tenant. Make sure
> the Tenant/staff UX is excellent, well thought out, and consistent with the
> product and repository UX/UI.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** Current Shopify and Vercel practice
strongly supports proof-based self-service without former-account access. Core
must nevertheless own a stricter Tenant boundary because several Core Tenants
may share one Vercel team/project; Vercel `verified` cannot identify which Core
Tenant is entitled to a hostname.

The selected answer is recorded with these corrections:

1. Fresh proof means **current DNS control**, not legal ownership, acquisition,
   registrant identity, or provider verification.
2. Every Tenant uses the same ordinary **Add domain** path; there is no reconnect
   workflow, former-Tenant approval, routine support review, or new capability.
3. A private verification attempt reserves nothing and causes no provider call.
   Typing cannot squat a hostname.
4. Core always issues one server-generated, 256-bit, seven-day, exact-host,
   single-use DNS TXT challenge. Screenshots, HTTP/CNAME/traffic, certificates,
   provider status, and prior proof cannot satisfy it.
5. Immediately after trusted server DNS observation, one short transaction
   consumes the challenge, proves D74 final/no current claim, acquires the one
   platform-wide current claim, creates a new private binding generation, and
   records receipt/audit/provider outbox—or changes nothing.
6. Former bindings remain immutable. No former positive Site/content/brand/
   locale/role/route/permission/provider/integration/donor/auth/cache/client
   state follows; D9–D15 adverse reservations remain and run first.
7. Core proof, provider verification/assignment, TLS, DNS routing, Site
   readiness, and Primary/Redirect activation remain six separate states. D75
   success is only **Domain verified · Not public**.

The decision is documented in
[ADR-0196](../../adr/0196-fresh-proof-clean-start-site-domain-claims.md) and the
[D75 adversarial review](./phase-24-d75-fresh-proof-clean-start-domain-claim-adversarial-review.md).

### Corrected decision recorded

Any current authorized human with `sites.manage_domains` may start or resume one
private verification attempt for an exact custom hostname and destination Site.
The attempt stores no global reservation, binding, provider association, public
role, or former-owner notification. Same-Site duplicate input resumes the
current attempt; another verification invalidates the old challenge before
issuing a new value. Other Tenants/scopes remain invisible.

Core's opaque TXT challenge binds the exact canonical ASCII hostname, Tenant,
environment, Site, immutable attempt/challenge generation, and purpose. It is
valid for seven calendar days, with exact expiry/timezone shown, and is forever
invalid after success, expiry, cancellation, rotation, or a meaning change. A
trusted server-side DNS verifier observes it; the browser/caller cannot assert
success. Staff may remove the consumed Core record. A later provider or
certificate record carries its own clearly stated retention rule.

Because DNS cannot join a transaction, proof acceptance is never stored for a
later claim. After lookup, the claim command reauthorizes and locks/rechecks the
exact identity/attempt/scope, D74 final receipt, current challenge, and no current
claim; then it consumes proof, inserts a new private binding generation, acquires
the global current claim, and writes receipt/audit/outbox atomically. Two valid
claimants have one constraint-enforced winner. A loser learns only **Domain
isn't available for setup**.

Only after claim may a sealed worker attach Vercel hosting. It derives provider
scope server-side, never uses `--force`/move/account delete/transfer, honors live
rate/reset headers, and reconciles through authenticated readback. If provider
proof is separately required, the same setup surface shows a second **Verify
with the hosting provider** step without raw account identifiers.

Successful D75 proof creates no public origin or donor behavior. Every later
public request, session/cookie/context, and cache binds the new Tenant/Site/
binding generation; old-generation state is rejected. Launch reusable custom
Site hosts register no root-scope service worker. Core guarantees no prior Core
authority is inherited but does not claim to erase browser/DNS/search/archive/
certificate/Internet history or rely on `Clear-Site-Data` as isolation.

### Exact staff experience

The Site name remains visible in **Site → Domains**, with one primary **Add
domain** action. **Add a domain to Hope Relief Website** is route-addressable and
resumable; desktop may use the existing record-detail Sheet only if usability
evidence supports it, while mobile is full viewport. It is one current-step
detail—not a modal, wizard, provider dashboard, or second product.

The first view has one visible field:

> **Domain name**  
> Enter a domain such as `www.hope.org`. This starts a private setup for Hope
> Relief Website. It will not publish the Site or copy content or settings from
> another Site.

Common HTTPS URL paste is accepted; Core visibly confirms the exact extracted
hostname. Protocol/path/query are not claimed. Invalid/reserved/IP/port/
credential/wildcard/public-suffix/provider/IDNA inputs receive specific inline
errors without clearing the entered value.

The resumable **Verify domain control** detail shows:

- exact TXT **Type**, **Name**, and **Value**;
- separately labelled Copy actions and one polite copied-status message;
- **Valid until {absolute time, timezone}**;
- **Last checked {time, timezone}**;
- bounded automatic checks and one coalesced **Check again**; and
- **I can't edit DNS** guidance to ask the domain's DNS administrator—never a
  screenshot/support bypass.

Plain states are **Verify domain**, **Waiting for DNS**, **Checking DNS**,
**Verification expired · Start new verification**, **We couldn't check this
domain · Try again**, **Domain isn't available for setup**, and **Domain verified
· Not public**, followed by D72's hosting/readiness states.

Success says:

> **Domain verified · Not public**  
> `www.hoperelief.org` is connected to Hope Relief Website as a new private
> setup. Nothing from another Site was copied or restored. You can leave this
> page while secure hosting is prepared.

Technical values use Geist Mono, LTR/bidi isolation, safe wrapping, and complete
copy values without truncation. Base Maia/Zinc semantic surfaces, visible focus,
44px mobile targets, 320px, 400% zoom, keyboard, screen reader, forced colors,
long localization, RTL, IDN, weak network, refresh/resume, and session expiry
are release tests. No raw Vercel error, spinner lock-in, countdown, fake
percentage, repeated live announcement, decorative status card, or toast-only
result is added.

### Source and repository status

Current `develop` still has a nullable nonunique Payload Tenant `primaryDomain`,
Tenant-only `overrideAccess:true`/slug fallback, `siteId: null`, global canonical
inputs, host-blind redirects, broad transitional staff permissions, and no D72–
D75 Domain identity, verification attempt, global claim, binding generation,
provider adapter, RLS, or staff flow. Freshly fetched HEAD and `origin/develop`
were both `7abd2c11ffd4ed70c6775c4fd6f51c996e4350dd`; Phase 23 PR #1340 remained
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at `9069dcad67f9630323474ca5ee8bcc85ca7bf0f6`.

D75 is accepted documentation intent only. No runtime, schema, migration,
Supabase policy, provider request, DNS record, capability registry, OpenSpec
delta, ticket, deployment, or production state changed.

## D76 — How should an already-connected domain move between Sites in the same Tenant?

### Plain-language context

D75 covers a hostname only after D74 has fully disconnected it and ended its
former current claim. Staff will also encounter a more ordinary multi-Site job:
the hostname is still safely connected to another Site belonging to the same
Tenant.

Forcing staff through Disconnect → Add domain would deliberately remove a
working hosting connection, repeat verification/provider setup, and create an
avoidable error window. Silently reassigning the row would be worse: the wrong
Site could appear under a trusted address, the source Site could lose its only
Primary, and Giving/auth/callback/protected routes could move accidentally.

Core's target public websites share the `apps/donor` hosting surface rather than
using one Vercel project per Site. An ordinary Site-to-Site move is therefore
primarily one Core Domain/public-generation successor—not necessarily a Vercel
project move. Vercel nevertheless exposes a project-domain move event/API, while
its remove/add guidance warns of possible downtime. This supports a separate
prepared move command where topology requires it, with Vercel still subordinate
to Core authority.

Primary evidence:

- [Vercel — Project-domain API](https://vercel.com/docs/rest-api)
- [Vercel — Activity log and project-domain-moved](https://vercel.com/docs/activity-log)
- [Vercel — Project moves and downtime](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/how-to-move-a-domain-between-vercel-projects-with-zero-downtime)

### Concrete example

Hope Relief currently uses `stories.hoperelief.org` as the **Primary website
address** for **Field Stories**. Staff want that exact hostname to serve **Main
Website** instead.

Both Sites belong to Hope Relief. Main Website is privately previewed and ready.
Visitors must continue seeing Field Stories until the exact cutover; the
hostname must never serve both Sites, expose Main Website early, fall through to
another Tenant, or show an Asym/Vercel page.

If it is Field Stories' Primary, the move must also give Field Stories another
eligible Primary. Otherwise staff must separately complete Site retirement
before moving; D76 cannot hide retirement or suspension inside Move domain.
Giving, authentication, callback, and protected routes remain independently
owned and cannot be swept along.

### Safeguards every option keeps

- Only a current human authorized for both exact Sites in the same Tenant and
  production environment may proceed.
- Source identity appears only to a viewer authorized to see it; otherwise the
  result remains permission-safe.
- The current exact-host global claim and trusted control/provider posture must
  still be valid. An ordinary same-Tenant move does not repeat DNS work; Core
  asks for fresh verification only when that posture is stale, unverified, or
  ambiguous.
- Source disposition, destination readiness, locales/origins, protected routes,
  cookies/caches, branding, and public-generation impacts are reviewed before
  any effect.
- Content, Brand Version, Navigation, locale, role, redirect, permission,
  analytics, cookie/session, provider object, Giving, and auth meaning never
  move implicitly.
- The hostname retains one same-Tenant current occupancy and at most one
  favorable Site. Active public Sites retain exactly one Primary; an adverse
  Moving generation may create a bounded neutral gap during the final switch.
- Cross-Tenant movement is unavailable here; it requires D74/D75 or the later
  contested-claim decision.
- Registration, DNS, renewal, email, and unrelated hostnames remain unchanged.
- No `--force`, remove/re-add simulation, bulk/scheduled/drag-and-drop move, raw
  provider control, guessed fallback, or automatic role selection is allowed.
- Launch requires both Sites on the current shared donor Vercel project and
  performs no provider mutation. A future provider-per-Site topology requires a
  separate decision rather than an implicit adapter branch.

### Option 1 — prepared self-service Site-to-Site cutover (recommended)

The source Domain detail offers **Move to another Site**. If authorized staff
instead enter the hostname from a destination Site, Core shows **Already
connected to Field Stories** with **Open Field Stories** and **Move to this
Site**. Both entry points open the same route-addressable move review; they are
not separate workflows.

One focused review revalidates the current claim and shows source/destination
Sites, required source replacement, initially unselected destination role,
destination readiness, public-origin/locale and route-owner effects, and
unchanged consequences. It requests fresh external proof only when present
control posture is no longer trustworthy. The final action is **Move
`stories.hoperelief.org` to Main Website**; no typed confirmation is required.
One durable human command installs/read-backs an adverse Moving barrier and then
advances the complete immutable binding/public-generation cohort. Launch makes
no provider call. The source stays authoritative until the barrier begins.

**Why this is strong:** best staff and visitor UX, no needless provider detach
or ownership churn, no wrong-Site exposure, and one explicit audited high-
consequence transition. It truthfully permits a bounded neutral gap rather than
promising literal zero downtime.

**Trade-off:** requires D73's finite owner registry to compile a bounded two-Site
plan, plus shared-head concurrency/admission fencing and production-shaped
cutover proof. It must remain one exact Domain successor—not become a generic
migration workflow.

### Option 2 — always disconnect, then add as new

Staff clear the source Site's uses, complete D74, return to the destination, and
use D75 Add domain.

**Why this is strong:** one very simple lifecycle and an unmistakable claim-
release boundary; no separate move command or two-Site transaction.

**Trade-off:** repeats proof/hosting work and intentionally creates avoidable
downtime for an ordinary same-organization reconfiguration.

### Option 3 — support-coordinated live moves

Nonpublic moves use D74/D75. For a hostname that must stay live, Tenant staff
prepare the destination and Core revalidates the current claim, requesting
fresh external proof only if its control posture is stale; platform support
then invokes one governed product cutover command.

**Why this is strong:** preserves continuity while limiting the most complex
early operation to trained operators and a narrow rollout cohort.

**Trade-off:** creates scheduling delay, support dependency, and potential tribal
knowledge. Support still needs the same safe product command—never manual
Vercel changes or database repair—so most implementation complexity remains.

### Recommendation

**Option 1 — prepared self-service Site-to-Site cutover.** Moving a domain
between a Tenant's own Sites is a core Phase 24 job, not speculative
infrastructure. Simulating it through destructive disconnection gives staff and
visitors a worse result.

The bounded flow is:

```text
Add domain
    ↓
Already connected to Field Stories
    ↓
Move to this Site
    ↓
Revalidate current claim; reverify only if stale
    ↓
Review source + destination consequences
    ↓
Adverse barrier, then explicit generation-safe cutover
```

Option 2 is the strongest simplicity-first alternative. Option 3 is a sensible
staged-rollout alternative if early production evidence shows the self-service
impact review is not yet reliable enough.

### Exact question

When a hostname is already connected to another Site in the same Tenant, should
Core use **Option 1 — a prepared self-service Site-to-Site cutover**, **Option 2
— always disconnect then add as new**, or **Option 3 — support-coordinated live
moves**?

### Founder answer

> Option 1 — Prepared self-service Site-to-Site cutover. Make sure this is
> current modern best practice, and make the Tenant/staff UX excellent, well
> thought out, and consistent with Core's product and repository UX/UI.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** Authenticated same-owner movement is the
current modern pattern. Vercel explicitly recommends Move rather than DNS claim
when both scopes remain accessible, and it separates domain ownership from
project assignment. WordPress.com also provides a direct same-account move to
another Site with explicit target selection and confirmation. Repeating
registrar/DNS work for every same-Tenant Site change would add friction without
proving the destination is safe.

The original choice required these corrections:

1. Launch D76 is a **Core-only provider no-op**. Every public Site currently
   shares the one `apps/donor` Vercel project; calling Vercel Move, alias,
   remove/add, redirect, branch or force APIs would add a second routing
   authority without changing the actual hosting topology.
2. Ordinary moves revalidate current control but do not repeat DNS proof. A new
   challenge appears only for a disconnected host, scope/ownership change,
   missing provenance, `verified: false`, loss/conflict or material ambiguity—
   never merely because old proof has aged.
3. A move never mutates the old binding's Site. Core appends a new immutable
   Site-scoped claim/binding generation and advances one private global
   current-host head while same-Tenant occupancy remains continuous.
4. Destination Primary/Redirect/Not-public meaning is initially unselected. A
   source Primary must have a different eligible replacement if its Site stays
   public. Destination first go-live composes D6; destination Primary replacement
   composes D73. D76 cannot silently pause or retire either Site.
5. Distributed admission cannot switch every region in one Postgres commit.
   One human command installs and acknowledges a monotonic adverse **Moving**
   barrier, then atomically advances the complete source/destination Domain and
   public heads and admits only the exact target generation.
6. Core promises no wrong-Site or mixed-generation response—not mathematically
   absolute zero downtime. During the short acknowledged cutover barrier,
   uncertain requests may receive a neutral, no-brand, `no-store` unavailable
   response.
7. D73's finite critical-path/owner registry is reused. Content, Brand,
   Navigation, locale data, Giving, auth, callbacks, protected routes, cookies,
   sessions, Stripe, DNS, registration, renewal, email and provider project do
   not move implicitly.

The decision is documented in
[ADR-0197](../../adr/0197-prepared-same-tenant-site-domain-cutover.md) and the
[D76 adversarial review](./phase-24-d76-prepared-same-tenant-site-domain-cutover-adversarial-review.md).

### Corrected decision recorded

A current human with `sites.manage_domains` on both exact Sites may prepare one
same-Tenant, same-production-environment hostname move. Current
`sites.activate_domains` on both is required to commit. No new move capability,
routine second approver, support queue or provider permission is created.

The immutable review plan pins hostname, source/destination binding and public
heads, source replacement when required, initially unselected destination role,
applicable D6/D73 choice, finite owner-manifest digest, current control posture,
the exact shared donor-project topology, complete target preview, and expected
effects. Any effect-bearing drift requires review again.

One command first records the durable move and establishes the adverse host
barrier. After required cohort readback, a stable-lock-order transaction appends
the target binding, closes source, advances the private hostname head and both
Sites' exact Domain/public heads all-or-none. Target serving begins only after
its exact admission/readback succeeds. Failure before authority swap changes
nothing or re-admits only the proved unchanged source; after authority swap,
recovery is forward-only and moving back is a new reviewed successor.

The hostname remains globally occupied by the same Tenant. D74/D75, Vercel
project movement, provider aliases, DNS/TLS/registrar work and all money owners
are outside the effect. A future provider-per-Site topology requires a separate
ADR rather than an untested adapter branch.

### Exact staff experience

The source Domain row exposes **Move to another Site**. If staff instead enter
the hostname from another authorized Site's **Add domain** flow, Core says:

> **Already connected to Field Stories**  
> `stories.hoperelief.org` is currently used by another Hope Relief Site. You
> can review a move to Main Website without disconnecting it first.

Actions are **Open Field Stories** and **Move to this Site**. A viewer without
source access sees only **Already connected elsewhere in Hope Relief** and that
access to both Sites is required. A cross-Tenant conflict remains **Domain isn't
available for setup**.

Both entry points open one resumable full-page Base Maia review—not a Sheet,
AlertDialog, wizard, matrix or provider dashboard:

> **Move `stories.hoperelief.org`**  
> **Field Stories → Main Website**

Its compact PageShell sections are:

1. current and destination Site roles;
2. **Before this domain can move**, with finite authoritative checks and one
   cause-owned action per blocker;
3. initially unselected destination role: **Primary website address**,
   **Redirects website visits**, or **Not public on this Site**;
4. source Site after the move, including a replacement Primary when required;
5. destination former-primary disposition when required;
6. complete protected-route outcomes and explicitly incomplete known external
   placements;
7. **What changes** and **What does not change**; and
8. production-faithful private preview.

Normal copy says:

> Visitors will continue using the same address. Core does not expect a DNS
> change or new verification. The move becomes public only after both Sites and
> the complete public cutover pass their checks.

The safe secondary action is **Keep on Field Stories**. The final action is
**Move `stories.hoperelief.org` to Main Website** or, when D6 first activation
is included, **Move domain and make Main Website public**. The page is the
confirmation; there is no typed hostname, checkbox, reason, schedule, countdown,
second approver, support ticket or second dialog.

Durable states are **Needs preparation**, **Ready to move**, **Plan changed ·
Review again**, **Moving domain**, **Move not started**, **Move needs attention**,
and **Moved to Main Website**. During the barrier:

> **Core is switching this address.** Visitors may briefly see an unavailable
> page, but Core will not show the wrong Site. You can leave this page.

Success names the exact new Site, source replacement, target role and unchanged
source-owned outcomes, and confirms that DNS, email, registration, provider
project, Site content and gifts were not changed or copied.

The UI retains Base Maia/Base UI/Zinc, PageShell, shared RadioGroup/fields/
buttons, textual status, visible focus and restrained motion. Release evidence
covers 320px, 400% zoom, 44px touch targets, keyboard, screen reader, forced
colors, long localization, RTL/IDN, weak networks, refresh/resume, session
expiry, duplicate clicks and lost acknowledgement.

### Visitor, donor and browser truth

Before the barrier, requests use the complete Field Stories generation. During
the barrier, uncertain requests receive only the neutral temporary-unavailable
response. After target admission, requests use the complete Main Website Site,
Brand, locale, Navigation, canonical/search metadata, owner routing, security
and cache generation. A pre-admitted request may finish under its complete old
generation; no response or write may mix generations.

The hostname does not change, so old cookies and other browser state can still
be sent. Tenant-scoped sessions survive only when independently valid;
Site/binding-scoped context must validate the new immutable generation. Root-
scope reusable-host service workers remain prohibited, and stale cache is never
an accepted wrong-Site response.

Pre-admitted forms, checkouts, gifts, recurring commitments and tasks stay
pinned to their original Site, purpose, designation, currency, cadence and
idempotency authority or require explicit refresh. D76 creates no Stripe,
ledger, settlement or accounting mutation.

### Source and repository status

Current `develop` still has Payload Tenant `primaryDomain`, forwarded-host/
slug resolution, `siteId: null`, host-blind redirects, broad staff permissions,
one donor Vercel project, and no D72–D76 runtime authority. Freshly fetched
`HEAD` and `origin/develop` were
`7abd2c11ffd4ed70c6775c4fd6f51c996e4350dd`; Phase 23 PR #1340 remained
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at `9069dcad67f9630323474ca5ee8bcc85ca7bf0f6`.

D76 is accepted documentation intent only. No runtime, schema, migration,
Supabase policy, Vercel/Stripe/DNS request, capability registry, OpenSpec delta,
ticket, deployment or production state changed.

## D77 — How much URL continuity must staff resolve before a domain moves?

### Plain-language context

D76 moves a hostname, but a hostname carries many addresses—not only its home
page. If `stories.hoperelief.org` moves from Field Stories to Main Website, old
visitors may request:

- `/about`
- `/stories/water-project`
- `/give/water`
- `/auth/callback`

Main Website may coincidentally use some of the same paths. Without a deliberate
rule, the exact same external URL could silently acquire different content,
donor purpose, authentication behavior or Site attribution even though the
hostname never redirected.

D9 already rejects guessed whole-Site continuity and permits ordinary URL
successors only after exact owner proof. D10 permanently protects Issued Giving
Addresses. D76 therefore needs a bounded route-readiness rule, but it must not
become an Internet crawler or a page-by-page migration project.

Current Google guidance says to map an old URL to a relevant equivalent, avoid
irrelevant homepage redirects, return a real `404`/`410` where no replacement
exists, and avoid redirect chains. This is search guidance—not Core authority—
but it supports the same visitor-truth rule.

Primary evidence:

- [Google — Site moves and URL mapping](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)
- [Google — Meaningful 404 behavior](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/troubleshoot-crawling-errors)
- [OWASP — Server-owned redirect mappings](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Unvalidated_Redirects_and_Forwards_Cheat_Sheet.html)

### Concrete example

Field Stories currently serves:

- `stories.hoperelief.org/about`
- `stories.hoperelief.org/stories/water-project`
- `stories.hoperelief.org/give/water`

Main Website has its own `/about` page and a different clean-water Giving
entry. `/give/water` must never start the new gift. But should staff review every
ordinary Page, only important collisions, or intentionally carry no ordinary
continuity?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- Core maintains a small, versioned, code-owned critical-path owner inventory;
  missing, stale, contradictory or unknown critical evidence blocks.
- Issued Giving addresses and protected routes retain only their independently
  authorized exact meaning; no override exists.
- Auth, callback, API, checkout, locale-root and other protected owners supply
  their own dispositions.
- Same slug/title/content/Site relationship or AI similarity never proves
  equivalence.
- No wildcard, catch-all, homepage fallback, query/cookie/body carry, redirect
  chain or arbitrary external destination is created.
- Core examines current Core-owned manifests only; it never claims to inventory
  the Internet, backlinks, QR codes, browser caches, sent messages or print.
- Unmapped/ineligible old addresses fail with the neutral result, never
  destination content by accident.
- Every result is generation-bound, authorization-filtered and committed only
  with the D76 cutover.

### Option 1 — critical-path gate plus exception-led ordinary-route review (recommended)

Every critical route owner must be green. Core then compares authoritative
source and destination ordinary-route manifests and surfaces only:

- exact path collisions;
- routes with an already owner-qualified same-resource successor;
- current redirect/loop conflicts; and
- material externally issued placements already known to Core.

Unmapped ordinary source paths default to neutral `404`. Eligible continuity is
published only by the owning Page/route domain under D9's exact-proof rule.
Staff see counts and actionable exceptions—not a giant route table—and the move
consumes the complete current digest.

**Why this is strong:** protects donor/auth meaning, preserves legitimate Page
continuity and keeps staff effort proportional to real risk.

**Trade-off:** requires a deterministic manifest comparison and owner adapters,
though it reuses the existing critical inventory rather than adding a router or
crawler.

### Option 2 — complete route-by-route disposition before move

Every current source route must be explicitly marked **Keep exact continuity**,
**Redirect to proved equivalent**, or **Retire to Page not found** before the
cutover proceeds.

**Why this is strong:** maximum visitor/search continuity and a complete
human-readable migration record.

**Trade-off:** larger Sites face substantial review fatigue, and staff may
mechanically approve mappings they do not understand. It risks turning one
domain move into a full CMS migration product.

### Option 3 — strict clean ordinary-route cutover

The move carries no ordinary Page continuity. Every source ordinary path is
retired for the new binding and returns neutral `404`; Main Website uses only
its independently published paths unless a route owner later publishes a
separately proved successor.

**Why this is strong:** simplest and strongest isolation boundary, with almost
no move-time route UX or inference risk.

**Trade-off:** breaks legitimate bookmarks/search traffic and creates avoidable
communications work even when an exact Page successor is already known.

### Recommendation

**Option 1 — critical-path gate plus exception-led ordinary-route review.** It
preserves Core's earlier principle: maintain a **small, well-defined critical-
path inventory**, let each source own meaning, show staff only actionable
exceptions, and default uncertain ordinary history to a truthful `404`. It gives
donors the strongest protection and staff the best balance of clarity and effort
without another resolver or workflow engine.

### Exact question

Before a same-Tenant hostname cutover, should Core use **Option 1 — a critical-
path gate plus exception-led ordinary-route review**, **Option 2 — complete
route-by-route disposition**, or **Option 3 — a strict clean ordinary-route
cutover**?

### Founder answer

> Option 1 — Critical-path gate plus exception-led ordinary-route review. Make
> sure this is current modern best practice, gives Tenant staff excellent Core-
> consistent UX/UI, does not over-engineer or create technical debt/brittleness,
> and improves the deterministic manifest-comparison/owner-adapter trade-off
> while reusing the existing critical inventory.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** Current Google, Vercel, CMS, HTTP,
security, Postgres/Supabase, and accessibility evidence supports the bounded
middle: exact genuine successors, truthful real not-found where no replacement
exists, no irrelevant homepage fallback or chains, and exception-first staff
work. Comparable products' pattern/wildcard facilities do not override Core's
D9/D10 and proposed Phase 23 exact-owner contracts; D77 deliberately ships no
pattern DSL.

The founder answer required these corrections:

1. **Contract reuse, not current runtime reuse.** Current `develop` has neither a
   critical owner registry nor an authoritative ordinary-route manifest. D77
   depends on the accepted D72–D76 and reconciled Phase 22/23 foundations.
2. **No D77-specific owner adapters.** Critical families reuse the one D73/D76
   typed owner port. Ordinary Pages use one D1/Public Site Generation manifest.
   D77 adds only a pure deterministic comparison and permission-safe projection.
3. **The critical inventory is family-sized.** Core must maintain a small,
   versioned, code-owned inventory of money/protected-effect, auth/callback/API,
   origin/root/locale/admission, and safety/cache owner families—not concrete URL
   rows. CI fails an unregistered framework route family.
4. **Source-only not-found is explicit and durable.** Mere absence would let a
   later destination Page silently reuse the old URL. The new binding generation
   therefore carries an owner-declared negative effect/reservation until a
   separately authorized successor/reuse decision.
5. **Different-Page cross-Site equivalence is not smuggled into D77.** Proposed
   Phase 22/23 contracts allow automatic continuity only for the same immutable
   Page under narrower scope. Exact different-Page collisions block or not-found
   until D78 and the Page owner establish an accepted proof contract.
6. **Authority and advice are separate.** Critical/ordinary route heads and
   effects form the move authority digest. Known messages, QR files, analytics,
   backlinks, print, bookmarks, search, and other external placements remain an
   explicitly incomplete advisory snapshot.
7. **One runtime and provider no-op.** Phase 5's owner-aware router consumes one
   compiled indexed effect before content/cache. D77 creates no resolver,
   redirect table, crawler, workflow, plugin, wildcard, query/body/cookie carry,
   or Vercel/project rule.

The decision is recorded in
[ADR-0198](../../adr/0198-critical-path-gated-exception-led-domain-move-route-review.md)
and the [D77 adversarial review](./phase-24-d77-critical-path-exception-led-domain-move-route-adversarial-review.md).

### Corrected decision recorded

Before one D76 same-Tenant hostname cutover, every applicable family in Core's
small code-owned D72–D77 critical inventory supplies one complete current typed
outcome. Missing, hidden, stale, contradictory, unregistered, unknown, or
blocking authority stops the move; permission filtering changes only detail,
never readiness.

One pure canonical comparison consumes the complete immutable source and
destination effective-host manifests and classifies:

- critical owner result;
- source-only ordinary address → durable real not-found effect;
- target-only ordinary address → retain exact target owner effect;
- exact collision → owner action or block/not-found;
- already owner-qualified successor → consume exact current relation;
- redirect/history/duplicate/canonical conflict → block; and
- unknown/incomplete → block.

D77 creates no mapping or public effect. The D76 plan pins the authority digest,
manifest/head IDs, owner/canonicalizer versions, and current effects and rechecks
them before the Moving barrier and target admission. Advice has a separate
incomplete snapshot/digest. Effect-bearing drift is **Plan changed · Review
again**; advisory churn never creates authority.

### Exact staff experience

D77 adds one section to D76's existing route-addressable full-page Base Maia
review—not a new workspace, Sheet, dialog, wizard, route table, or provider
console:

> **Existing web addresses**  
> Core checked the current addresses it manages for Field Stories and Main
> Website. This does not include every bookmark, printed QR code, backlink,
> browser cache, sent message, search result, or external campaign.

When blocked:

> **2 issues must be resolved before this domain can move.**

The compact text summary—not decorative statistic cards—shows:

- **Critical addresses:** Ready, or a permission-safe blocker;
- **Ordinary Page conflicts:** only unresolved actionable exceptions;
- **Continuity already prepared:** collapsed count;
- **Former addresses:** collapsed count that will show **Page not found**; and
- **Known places to update:** explicitly incomplete advice.

Only blocker/review sections open by default. Authorized long lists use stable
server keyset paging/search and preserve route/filter/position. Safe outcomes do
not require acknowledgement. No select-all, bulk approval, CSV, AI mapping,
wildcard/regex, arbitrary target, HTTP code, manifest digest, provider setting,
or second confirmation appears.

An authorized ordinary collision row says:

> **`/about` · Different Page at this address**  
> Field Stories and Main Website publish different Pages here. Core will not
> decide that they serve the same visitor purpose.  
> **Review Page continuity**

An unauthorized viewer sees only:

> **A protected address needs another owner**  
> An authorized staff member for that address must resolve it before the domain
> can move.

No hidden path, title, purpose, identity, count, or Site leaks. Owner actions
open the exact source surface; returning resumes D76 and re-verifies the current
digest. There is no **Mark fixed** or toast-only resolution.

When ready:

> **Web addresses are ready for this move.**  
> Every critical owner has a current outcome. Three ordinary addresses already
> have approved continuity; 148 former addresses will safely show Page not found.

Copy never claims all links moved, nothing will break, or Core inventoried the
Internet. Release evidence covers 320px/400% reflow, keyboard, screen reader,
visible focus, forced colors, reduced motion, 44px targets, long localization,
RTL/IDN/path wrap/copy, weak network, refresh/back/resume, session expiry,
duplicate action, lost response, error focus, and one polite meaningful status
announcement.

### Visitor, donor, HTTP, and provider truth

Before D76, D77 has no public effect. Before the barrier, source remains complete;
during uncertainty, only the no-brand `no-store` temporary-unavailable envelope
is allowed; after admission, the target's exact binding/public/route-effect
generation runs before content/cache.

Source-only historical ordinary paths use D9's real, non-enumerating, no-brand,
no-store `404`, never `200`, homepage, same-slug target, or historical
explanation. Authority outage is temporary unavailable, not false absence.
Giving, checkout, auth, callback, API, forms, provider paths, protected actions,
root/locale/sitemap/robots/`/.well-known`, and unsafe methods remain independently
owned. Only an already qualified internal ordinary successor may serve/redirect,
and a redirect is direct final clean `GET`/`HEAD` with no arbitrary context carry.

D77 performs zero Vercel, DNS, TLS, project, redirect, rewrite, bulk-redirect,
cache, certificate, or deployment mutation. A shared-project provider rule would
be cross-Tenant coupling and a second authority. D77 creates no Stripe, gift,
recurring, ledger, settlement, receipt, or accounting effect.

### Source and repository status

Freshly fetched `HEAD` and `origin/develop` remained
`7abd2c11ffd4ed70c6775c4fd6f51c996e4350dd`. Phase 22 PR #1323 remained
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at `70c50e8c97556c43be5543332fb0993b468b90ab`; Phase 23 PR #1340 remained
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at `9069dcad67f9630323474ca5ee8bcc85ca7bf0f6`.

Current runtime still uses Tenant-only mutable Page slugs, latest-published
Payload reads, CMS catch-all, raw Navigation hrefs, global canonical metadata,
host-shaped caches, host-blind static redirects, one donor Vercel project, and no
D72–D77 authority. D77 is accepted documentation intent only. No runtime, schema,
migration, Supabase policy, OpenSpec delta, ticket, Vercel/Stripe/DNS request,
deployment, or production state changed.

## D78 — What proof may let a different ordinary Page continue an old address?

### Decision title

**Different-Page ordinary URL succession across Sites**

### Plain-language context

D77 can detect an exact ordinary Page collision, but it deliberately cannot
decide whether two different Page records mean the same thing to a visitor.

This question applies only to ordinary public Pages. Giving, checkout,
authentication, callbacks, APIs, forms, files, member-care/sensitive routes,
missionary/project Pages with stricter owners, and arbitrary external URLs remain
excluded.

Core has two current directions that need deliberate reconciliation:

- D9 permits a different ordinary content successor only after exact owner proof
  of the same visitor task, subject, substantive purpose, locale, audience, and
  safety class.
- Proposed Phase 22/23 contracts automatically redirect only another route of
  the same immutable Page identity; Phase 23's bounded repair remains same-Site/
  same-locale.

Google recommends mapping an old URL only to its genuine corresponding Page and
returning a real not-found result when no replacement exists. That supports the
visitor-truth goal but does not define ministry purpose or authorize Core
equivalence.

Primary evidence:

- [D9 exact-equivalence contract](./phase-24-d9-retired-address-disposition-adversarial-review.md#d9-r6--exact-equivalent-content-proof)
- [Google URL mapping](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)
- [Phase 22 PR #1323](https://github.com/Asymmetric-al/core/pull/1323)
- [Phase 23 PR #1340](https://github.com/Asymmetric-al/core/pull/1340)

### Concrete example

Field Stories currently publishes:

`stories.hoperelief.org/about`

Main Website independently publishes another Page at `/about`. It has a
different immutable Page ID and updated design/wording, but both Pages may
explain Hope Relief's identity, mission, leadership, and contact expectations to
the same public audience in the same locale.
