Should an authorized Page publisher be able to prove the Main Website Page is
the exact successor, or must continuity require the original Page identity or a
visibly different destination URL?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- Ordinary public Pages only; every protected/specialized owner remains excluded.
- Same Tenant, production environment, exact locale, public audience/safety
  class, visitor task, subject, and substantive purpose are mandatory.
- Both exact Page releases, routes, Sites, locale heads, and public generations
  must be current and inspectable.
- Same path, slug, title, copied blocks, content hash, template, Site relation,
  analytics, search rank, or AI similarity never proves equivalence.
- One currently authorized human must hold the Page-continuity capability and
  access both Pages; no bulk, automation, support override, or autonomous AI.
- Source and destination appear side-by-side with public URLs and production-
  faithful visitor previews; effect-bearing change invalidates the decision.
- Default/rejection remains the D77 real not-found result; no homepage fallback.
- A redirect, when an option permits it, is one direct server-owned permanent
  clean-`GET`/`HEAD` result to a stable internal Page route, with no chain or
  arbitrary context carry.

### Option 1 — same immutable Page identity only

The old address may continue only when the destination publishes another
eligible generation of the same stable Page identity. A copied or independently
recreated Page is a different resource and cannot receive the old address.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it has the clearest invariant, least
subjective review, simplest database/proof model, and strongest alignment with
the stricter Phase 22 route contract.

**Trade-off:** legitimate Site reorganizations or rebuilt equivalent Pages lose
continuity unless Core first gains a separate governed Page-move/shared-identity
capability. Visitors may get avoidable not-found responses even when staff can
clearly establish the same public task.

### Option 2 — explicit owner-qualified equivalent Page successor (recommended)

A different Page identity may continue the old address only after an authorized
Page publisher completes D9's structured side-by-side proof and deliberately
records one immutable source→target successor relation. It proves the same
visitor task, subject, substantive purpose, locale, audience, and safety class;
it is neither inferred nor reusable for another address.

If the target retains the same external path, the relation authorizes direct
service only with the complete new binding generation. If the target path
differs, the Page owner publishes one direct permanent redirect.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it preserves legitimate visitor/search
continuity through real CMS/Site reorganizations while keeping the risky semantic
judgment explicit, narrow, owner-scoped, auditable, and unavailable to protected
routes.

**Trade-off:** human semantic judgment remains a real footgun. Structured
criteria, exact capability, side-by-side preview, no bulk/AI, current-head CAS,
and independent tests must be release gates.

### Option 3 — different Page identity requires a distinct destination URL

A different Page may be approved as the substantive successor, but it must first
publish at a different destination path. The historical address then redirects
to that new path; a different Page never directly inherits the identical public
URL.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it makes identity change visible in
routing history, avoids silent direct address reuse, simplifies incident
explanation, and still preserves visitor/search continuity.

**Trade-off:** it forces a new URL and permanent redirect maintenance even when
the unchanged public `/about` address is clearly the best experience. Staff and
visitors pay extra complexity for technical identity visibility.

### Recommendation

**Option 2 — explicit owner-qualified equivalent Page successor.** It best
reconciles D9's already accepted ordinary-content direction with D77's concrete
cross-Site gap. It follows careful migration practice without importing search
similarity as authority and preserves the fewest reasonable steps for staff and
visitors.

Keep it deliberately narrow: one source Page, one target Page, one address
relation, one structured side-by-side review, one authorized human decision, one
immutable receipt, and no bulk, AI, wildcard, protected route, arbitrary target,
or redirect console.

Option 1 is the strongest simplicity/safety alternative if immutable resource
identity must always outrank visitor-purpose continuity. Option 3 is the
strongest visible-separation alternative.

### Exact question

When two different ordinary Page records appear to serve the same public purpose
across a Site-to-Site Domain move, should Core use **Option 1 — same immutable
Page identity only**, **Option 2 — an explicit owner-qualified equivalent Page
successor**, or **Option 3 — require a different destination URL and direct
redirect**?

### Founder answer

> Option 2 — Explicit owner-qualified equivalent Page successor. BUT, make sure
> this is modern best practice that is up to date. Make sure the tenant/staff UX
> and UI is excellent and consistent with the product. Research deeply; do not
> over-engineer, create technical debt, or introduce brittleness.

### Adversarial review result

**Disposition: Accept with required amendments.**

The choice is modern and appropriate only when Core does **not** store a broad
claim that two Pages are equivalent. Modern search and CMS products consistently
separate automatic continuity for the same content identity from explicit
mapping to a different item. Google permits a consolidation redirect only when
the target genuinely carries the old content and otherwise expects a real
not-found result. HubSpot, WordPress, Webflow, and Shopify automatically preserve
same-item URL changes while treating different-item mapping as a separate human
decision. Blackbaud and Neon One confirm the nonprofit migration need, but their
generic URL/wildcard/bulk controls are too broad for Core's route-owner, tenant,
Giving, and shared-project boundaries.

The corrected domain fact is an **Ordinary Page Successor Qualification**:

1. **One old address, one different General Page.** D78 launch applies only to
   `general_page`→`general_page`. Articles, Site/locale roots, Phase 22 Pages,
   Giving, auth, callbacks, APIs, forms, files, protected/provider routes, and
   external URLs remain excluded.
2. **Directional, not equivalent identity.** The relation is source-address→
   target-Page, non-symmetric, non-transitive, non-bulk, and never a Page merge,
   copy, move, sync, inheritance, or reusable equivalence flag.
3. **Hard facts before judgment.** Core proves same Tenant/environment, exact
   locale, General Page family, public audience, Publication Reach, compatible
   safety, exact current releases/routes/Sites/public generations, and stable
   internal target.
4. **One human semantic decision.** One current Page owner compares the exact
   former and proposed public releases and answers whether a person using the old
   address receives the same public subject, substantive purpose, and intended
   task.
5. **No semantic machinery.** Path, slug, title, copy provenance, blocks, body
   hash, template, taxonomy, analytics, backlinks, search, or AI never proves or
   preselects the answer. D78 adds no purpose taxonomy, score, diff engine,
   recommender, LLM, reason field, comments, assignment, or approval workflow.
6. **Existing authority only.** Phase 12 proves the Page owner's exact source
   route-continuity/publication effect plus target read/publication scope.
   Domain permission alone is insufficient. D78 creates no role, capability
   bundle, invite, or access workflow.
7. **One focused review.** D77 fixes the pair before cutover; after cutover
   **Historical addresses** may reopen only that same immutable relation. One
   route-addressable **Review Page continuity** full page shows consequence and
   hard facts first, then former/proposed production-faithful previews on
   demand. Wide panels stack former-first on mobile/400 percent zoom.
8. **One real choice.** An initially unselected RadioGroup offers **Use Main
   Website's About Page for this address** and **Keep this address unavailable**;
   **Save this address decision** commits. No checkbox, modal, target picker,
   URL/status field, bulk action, or provider language appears.
9. **Prepared is not public.** D78 saves an immutable owner outcome and receipt
   only. D76 may activate pre-cutover proof; after cutover only the exact
   preserving D1 publication transaction may consume a same-relation candidate receipt while
   every pinned head still matches. Drift says **Page changed — Review again**;
   no stale choice follows. D80 neither consumes nor activates a D78 receipt.
10. **Role-aware visitor result.** A target Primary with the same address may
    serve directly. A Redirect Site Domain or different target path composes one
    direct final internal `308` for clean `GET`/`HEAD` to the Primary. No query,
    fragment meaning, body, cookie, auth, attribution, return state, chain, or
    arbitrary URL carries. Not-public/private/moving/disconnected/unknown roles
    produce no favorable Page result.
11. **One authority and safe storage.** The existing Page route owner stores
    stable Page references, exact heads, criteria version, server-derived actor,
    append-only outcome/receipt/audit/outbox, and one current source disposition
    under same-scope constraints, least grants, RLS, and privileged parity. It
    is not a D78 redirect store or resolver.
12. **Safe temporal ceiling.** Before cutover, the qualification covers only the
    exact reviewed target public revision/generation. ADR-0200/D79 governs later
    releases after activation through one explicit opaque Page Purpose
    Continuity Version. Target ineligibility or unknown authority becomes D9
    not-found/temporary unavailable, never another guessed Page.

### Staff and visitor example

For `stories.hoperelief.org/about`, the review says:

> **Review Page continuity**  
> Decide whether this one old address should show Main Website's About Page
> after the domain moves. The safe alternative is Page not found.

It labels the two exact releases **Former Page — Field Stories** and **Page at
this address after the move — Main Website**. It explains:

> Choose the successor only if a visitor receives the same public subject,
> substantive purpose, and intended task. Updated wording or design can be
> appropriate. A related Page, homepage, category, or different action is not.

After saving the favorable choice, D77 persistently shows:

> **Successor prepared for this domain move.** Nothing is public yet.

After D76 activation, visitors see only Hope Relief's current Page under Hope
Relief branding, one direct internal navigation result when necessary, or the
existing neutral Page-not-found envelope. They never see Asym/Vercel branding,
an equivalence explanation, or a migration interstitial.

### Repository and implementation posture

Current `develop` cannot implement this decision: Pages remain Tenant-only
mutable-slug records, public reads choose mutable latest-published content, the
CMS catch-all serves those rows directly, canonical metadata is global, and
host-blind static redirects remain. Proposed Phase 23 ADR-0147/US23-003/
OpenSpec also restrict different-Page repair to the same Site/locale and preserve
queries. They MUST be explicitly amended for D78's narrow cross-Site and no-
context-carry case. Proposed ADR-0167's copied Page remains a fresh independent
identity; Phase 22 ADR-0125 remains stricter and unchanged.

D78 performs zero Vercel project/bulk/deployment/middleware redirect, DNS, TLS,
provider, Stripe, checkout, gift, recurring, ledger, content, Page-copy,
notification, or public mutation. Runtime rollout is reader/adverse-first with
no inferred legacy backfill. Physical table and capability-key names remain
design-owned; the invariants are fixed.

The permanent decision is recorded in
[ADR-0199](../../adr/0199-owner-qualified-exact-ordinary-page-succession.md) and
the [D78 adversarial review](./phase-24-d78-owner-qualified-ordinary-page-successor-adversarial-review.md).

### Source and repository status

Freshly fetched `HEAD` and `origin/develop` remained
`7abd2c11ffd4ed70c6775c4fd6f51c996e4350dd`. Phase 22 PR #1323 remained
`OPEN/BLOCKED` at `70c50e8c97556c43be5543332fb0993b468b90ab`; Phase 23
PR #1340 remained `OPEN/BLOCKED` at
`9069dcad67f9630323474ca5ee8bcc85ca7bf0f6`.

No runtime, schema, migration, Supabase policy, OpenSpec delta, ticket, provider
request, deployment, or production state changed. D78 is accepted documentation
intent only.

## D79 — How should Page continuity survive later target Page updates?

### Decision title

**Later-release validity for an approved different-Page successor**

### Plain-language context

D78 proves one exact target Page release at the moment staff review and activate
the Domain move. But Pages naturally change afterward.

Some changes are routine and should not break a trusted link: correcting a phone
number, improving accessibility, updating staff names, or refreshing design.
Other changes can invalidate the promise behind the old address: turning an
About Page into a volunteer signup, changing the organization subject to one
campaign, changing the public audience, or changing the intended visitor task.

If every typo requires the complete D78 comparison again, staff will learn to
click through mechanically or delay useful updates. If approval lasts forever,
the historical address can silently drift to a different meaning. This question
chooses the narrow temporal rule without building an AI material-change
classifier or a second publication workflow.

### Concrete example

Ana approves Main Website's About Page as the successor for:

`stories.hoperelief.org/about`

Two months later, Luis publishes two changes:

1. he corrects Hope Relief's phone number and improves heading structure; then
2. he rewrites the Page as **Join a short-term mission team**, led by a signup
   action rather than organization information.

Should the old address require the full D78 review after both releases, stay
valid only while a small versioned public-purpose contract is unchanged, or
continue for the stable Page identity until an owner explicitly ends it?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- The source address, original qualification, actor, reviewed releases, and
  every later correction remain immutable history.
- Normal Page publication still proves current Tenant, Site, locale, family,
  audience, Publication Reach, safety, route, capability, and public generation.
- Target unpublish, Trash, safety withdrawal, locale/role loss, or authority
  outage immediately prevents a favorable fresh response.
- A change to another Page identity always requires a fresh D78 qualification.
- No AI, content hash, similarity score, traffic, analytics, timer, support
  override, or provider state decides validity.
- Giving, auth, APIs, forms, protected routes, Articles, and Phase 22 Pages stay
  excluded.
- Unknown or contradictory validity fails safely and never guesses another
  target.

### Option 1 — pin every qualification to one exact target release

Every new target Page release ends favorable continuity. Staff must complete the
full D78 side-by-side review again before the old address can continue.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it has the strongest direct evidence,
the simplest invariant, no purpose-profile model, and no judgment about which
edits are material. Every served release was explicitly reviewed against the
former Page.

**Costs and downstream effects:** typo, accessibility, contact, image, and
layout changes repeatedly interrupt continuity. The safe outcome is clear, but
review fatigue may make approvals mechanical or discourage routine improvement.
Pages with several separately qualified old addresses multiply the work.

### Option 2 — stable Page identity plus a small versioned public-purpose contract (recommended)

The successor remains valid across ordinary content/design releases only while
one Page-owner contract keeps the exact public audience, Publication Reach,
safety class, visitor task, subject, substantive purpose, locale, family, and
route eligibility unchanged. A material contract change blocks favorable continuation and requires
a fresh D78 decision; routine copy/design changes do not.

The contract is not a taxonomy or classifier. It is a small immutable Page-
owner statement used only when a Page carries different-identity predecessors,
versioned through the existing Page publish consequence review. No AI reads body
text to decide whether it changed.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it protects public meaning without
making every typo a migration event. It aligns validity with the facts D78
actually proved and keeps the route relation attached to stable Page identity.

**Costs and downstream effects:** Core must define a truthful, minimal contract
and make intentional repurposing visible. If staff can change body meaning while
leaving the contract untouched, it becomes ceremony; authoring copy, tests, and
representative ministry usability proof must make that failure obvious. This is
more model than Options 1 or 3, so it must stay predecessor-only and bounded.

### Option 3 — stable Page identity continues until an owner explicitly ends it

After D76, ordinary releases of the same target Page automatically retain the
old-address relation. A Page owner can explicitly end continuity, and current
adverse safety/publication facts still win.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it matches familiar CMS behavior for a
stable Page, creates the least staff friction, and adds no purpose model or
repeat approval. A normal About Page remains one Page through normal evolution.

**Costs and downstream effects:** a Page can drift or be deliberately repurposed
without any structural signal. The original D78 receipt remains historically
true but no longer protects present visitor meaning. Preventing misuse would
rely mainly on editorial discipline and audits rather than an impossible state.

### Recommendation

**Option 2 — stable Page identity plus a small versioned public-purpose
contract.** It best balances donor/visitor continuity, staff efficiency, and
technical safety:

- routine edits remain routine;
- material subject/purpose/task changes become explicit;
- the existing Page owner and publish consequence review remain the only
  mutation boundary;
- no AI, diff engine, ontology, or separate workflow is required; and
- the old address cannot silently acquire unrelated meaning forever.

Option 1 is the strongest proof-minimal alternative when eliminating every
materiality model matters more than staff friction. Option 3 is the strongest
workflow-minimal alternative when stable Page identity and editorial discipline
are trusted to carry meaning.

### Exact question

When an approved D78 target General Page later publishes a new release, should
Core use **Option 1 — require the full D78 review after every release**,
**Option 2 — continue only while a small versioned public-purpose contract stays
unchanged**, or **Option 3 — continue for the stable Page identity until an
owner explicitly ends it**?

### Founder answer

**Option 2 — stable Page identity plus a small versioned public-purpose
contract; routine edits continue, material purpose changes require fresh
qualification.** Use it only if current evidence and Core's governing contracts
support it; otherwise change it. Keep the staff/tenant experience excellent and
avoid overengineering, brittleness, and technical debt.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** The stable-identity/versioned-continuity
direction is correct for Core, but a tenant-authored “public-purpose contract”
would be the wrong implementation.

Current official CMS evidence supports stable document identity, separate draft/
published state, revision history, and staff-managed same-resource URL
continuity. W3C treats URI consistency as an owner policy judged against user
expectations; Google requires old URLs to reach accurate corresponding
destinations and warns against irrelevant redirects. GOV.UK supports user-need-
oriented content governance. Exact immutable Core receipts and the D79 effective-
release choice are repository-specific safeguards. None of the reviewed official
sources establishes a reliable automatic material-change classifier or a
mandatory Page-purpose field that governs redirect validity.

If D78 were only a same-Page slug redirect, the strongest answer would be stable
identity plus a passive notice. D78 is deliberately different: another Page
identity inherited one trusted historical address only after an exact human
same-subject/purpose/task judgment. Importing the looser CMS default would
silently conflict with ADR-0199. Core therefore keeps one narrower owner
decision without building purpose content.

The corrected domain fact is a **Page Purpose Continuity Version**:

1. **Sparse exact scope.** It exists only for one exact Tenant/environment/
   Site-owned `general_page` identity and BCP-47 locale after D76 activates a
   D78 predecessor. Prepared-only relations show passive exact-release context
   but have no continuity head/radio. Pages that never carried D78 have no
   field, prompt, head, query, or changed workflow; terminal history is retained
   inert rather than deleted/reused.
2. **Opaque owner assertion.** One immutable version means the Page owner
   universally asserts that every currently favorable historical address pinned
   to it still gives a person that address's same public subject, substantive
   purpose, and intended visitor task under D78's code-owned criteria. It
   stores no tenant-authored purpose statement, subject/task fields, Page
   family, taxonomy, tag, category, note, body, snapshot, hash, diff, score,
   threshold, analytics, embedding, or AI output.
3. **No shadow ownership.** Audience, Publication Reach, safety, locale, family,
   route, binding, canonical path, publication, and eligibility remain their
   owners' current facts. They are independently rechecked and never copied into
   writable continuity state.
4. **Exact pre-cutover evidence remains.** Before D76 activates a relation, any
   target release/generation drift still stales D78 and requires the full fixed-
   pair review. A Page publisher cannot carry a changed preview into a cutover
   merely by saying its purpose stayed the same.
5. **One choice only on affected effective publication.** After activation,
   every candidate whose exact Page Editorial Revision or meaning-bearing
   localized/Reusable Section/shared/global/reference dependency digest changed
   uses one initially unselected RadioGroup in the existing D1 Publish
   consequence review:
   - **This update keeps what this Page is for** — reuse the current continuity
     version; or
   - **This update changes what this Page is for** — this candidate cannot
     publish through this Page identity. D80 may create a fresh independent
     private Page from the exact acknowledged candidate; it creates or advances
     no source continuity version, and the source head and D78 relations remain
     unchanged.
6. **Routine work stays routine.** Draft save, autosave, preview, compare,
   selection, abandonment, and failed validation have no effect. A delivery-
   only D1 rebuild with the exact meaning-bearing dependency digest and
   continuity head unchanged needs no human choice. A changed meaning-bearing
   indirect dependency cannot bypass D79 merely because the Page row is
   unchanged. Core adds no semantic field-diff classifier or autosave timing.
7. **One existing consequence review.** The **keeps** choice is an input to D1
   Publish; **changes** reveals D80's private new-Page continuation instead. It
   is not a checkbox, modal, second save, workflow, task, assignment, comment,
   approver, or capability. Selection does not submit, navigate, move focus, or
   publish.
8. **Several historical addresses, one universal Page choice.** One choice can
   preserve the current version only when the publisher can review the complete
   currently favorable relation set and asserts the D78 test remains true for
   every relation. Any failed/unreviewable relation disables **keeps** for the
   cohort. It cannot create/renew a relation; fresh favorable D78 remains one
   immutable source address at a time.
9. **No material continuity advance.** Selection, candidate state, and D80
   private-target creation never advance the source head. The target starts
   with no continuity version or D78 relation. Restoring old content, returning
   a path, or copying a Page does not restore authority.
10. **Fresh review reuses D78.** A stale relation opens the same fixed source-
    address/target-Page comparison with current exact evidence—or one exact D1-
    admitted production-ready candidate digest—and both-Page authority. A D78
    candidate receipt remains prepared-only until the ordinary D1 publication
    that releases that exact target candidate; D80 neither consumes nor
    activates a D78 relation. There is no target search, arbitrary URL, redirect
    console, bulk approval, or new workflow.
11. **Adverse current truth wins.** Unpublish, Trash/delete, safety withdrawal,
    incompatible audience/Reach, locale disablement, route-owner conflict, or
    unknown state prevents favorable fresh delivery independently of the
    continuity version.
12. **Server and database enforcement.** Append-only versions plus one current
    head use same-scope composite integrity, restrictive deletes, non-null D78
    version pins, expected heads, unique semantic command identity, equality-
    leading indexes, least grants, RLS `USING`/`WITH CHECK`, privileged-path
    parity, and one short set-based transaction with no network call. Caller
    input never supplies authoritative Tenant/Site/Page/actor/head facts.
13. **One compiled public effect.** Phase 5 reads only D1's current direct Page,
    direct final permanent redirect, or neutral not-found route effect. It never
    joins purpose versions, D78 history, Page bodies, CMS versions, or provider
    state per request.
14. **No provider or money mutation.** D79 writes no Vercel project, Domain,
    DNS/TLS, redirect/rewrite, middleware, deployment, cache rule, Stripe, gift,
    ledger, currency, message, or notification state.
15. **Honest cache limit.** Core can govern fresh requests and its own cache
    generations, but cannot recall a permanent redirect already cached by a
    browser or external intermediary. No staff or donor copy promises otherwise.

### Staff workspace and Publish experience

Only an affected Page gains one calm main-column panel immediately after the
existing document-state strip. It is not hidden in the desktop-only Inspector:

> **Historical addresses · 3**
>
> Three older web addresses currently lead to this Page. When publishing,
> choose whether the update keeps what this Page is for.
>
> **Review historical addresses**

Prepared, active, needs-review, adverse, and unavailable states use distinct
copy; none is mislabeled active. Exact count, source paths, Sites, titles,
receipts, and previews appear only with existing aggregate/detail read authority.
Otherwise the panel says **Historical addresses connected** and **Some details
require another owner** without a hidden count. The complete private digest
still governs publication and restricted cached content never flashes.

The normal D1 Publish review shows a permission-safe consequence, current
published effective release, exact candidate effective release, links to the
last D78 criteria/basis receipt and authorized predecessor list, on-demand
production-faithful previews, and one plain example before the RadioGroup:

> Wording, design, contact, staff-name, image, and accessibility improvements
> can keep the same purpose. Changing an About Page into a volunteer signup is
> a different purpose.

For several predecessors, helper text adds:

> Your choice applies to every currently active historical address in this
> review. Choose **keeps** only if a person using each address would still find
> that address's same public subject, purpose, and visitor task. If any one does
> not—or required detail is unavailable—**keeps** is unavailable.

Neither option is preselected. There is no second confirmation or donor-facing
notice. The existing Publish action remains the single commit. Until D80 decides
the material-change transaction, a candidate choosing **changes what this Page
is for** cannot publish with unrequalified predecessors; the current public
generation remains safe.

The panel/review follow PageShell/Base UI/base-maia/Zinc patterns with semantic
heading/RadioGroup, visible focus, 44-pixel targets, persistent non-toast status,
320-CSS-pixel/400-percent reflow, forced colors, reduced motion, keyboard/screen
reader behavior, long localization/RTL, bidi-isolated wrapping URLs, weak-
network summary-first rendering, back/refresh/resume, duplicate-submit and lost-
acknowledgement recovery.

Visitors and donors see no workflow or platform vocabulary. An eligible old
address reaches the current tenant-native Page directly/in one final clean
`GET`/`HEAD` result; an ineligible historical address receives the governing
D9/D72/D77 role-aware, platform-neutral, non-enumerating no-brand/no-store
envelope. No Asym, Vercel, Tenant/Site, purpose, or migration branding appears
in that adverse result.

### Required repository reconciliation

- ADR-0199 and D78-R13 replace the exact-release _post-activation_ ceiling with
  the D79 continuity-version rule while retaining exact pre-cutover proof.
- D78 gains one post-cutover fixed-pair re-entry from **Historical addresses**;
  its current Domain-move-only entry/success copy is insufficient.
- Proposed Phase 23 ADR-0145/D1 treat continuity as a Page publication/route
  semantic dependency, not a third editable Page document. D1's effective Page
  release digest includes exact meaning-bearing localized/Reusable Section/
  shared/global/reference dependencies; placement-only and delivery rebuilds
  do not create semantic ceremony.
- Proposed ADR-0152 Reusable Section publication therefore cannot bypass D79:
  a changed meaning-bearing shared revision obtains the Page-owner consequence
  in D1 or keeps affected D78 routes adverse pending review.
- Proposed ADR-0150 continues to reject Page-family-per-purpose and open tenant
  schemas; proposed ADR-0156/0157 keep autosave separate and pin schedule-time
  choice/current heads; proposed ADR-0167 copies no public authority; proposed
  ADR-0168 keeps audience/Reach separate; proposed ADR-0174/Phase 12 add no
  capability; proposed ADR-0175 may project but never own/repair continuity.
- Phase 5, Phase 12, glossary, living spec, roadmap, consolidated Phase 24 PRD/
  OpenSpec/design/tasks/tickets/tests/release evidence carry D79-R1–R24,
  AC1–AC44, invariants, monitors, and the provider-no-op boundary.

The permanent decision is recorded in

and the

## D80 — What should Publish do when a changed Page purpose affects historical addresses?

### Decision title

**Atomic public outcome for a materially repurposed successor Page**

### Plain-language context

D79 lets routine edits stay routine. When staff explicitly say a Page now serves
a different subject, purpose, or visitor task, the old D78 promise cannot carry
forward. Core must choose what one Publish action does with the Page and every
historical address still pinned to the earlier purpose version.

This is not only a workflow choice. A permanent redirect may already be cached
outside Core. Core can change the result for fresh requests to the old address,
but it cannot force a browser that cached `old URL -> current canonical URL` to
ask the old host again. Keeping the repurposed content at that canonical URL may
therefore expose it through previously cached redirects even after Core marks
the old route unavailable.

That evidence creates a non-negotiable eligibility fence. If any affected
predecessor ever emitted a cacheable permanent redirect to this Page's current
canonical URL—or Core cannot prove otherwise—in-place repurposing cannot preserve
D78's visitor-meaning guarantee. Options 1 and 2 are then unavailable and Core
must use a new Page identity/route. Options 1 and 2 remain real choices only for
a completely proved direct-only cohort with no such redirect history.
Eligibility comes from immutable Core binding/public-generation route-effect
history, not browser telemetry, analytics, CDN observation, or a staff checkbox.
Missing history is unknown and therefore follows the cacheable-history fence.

The decision must balance three good goals:

- staff can publish legitimate urgent Page changes;
- old trusted links never receive unrelated meaning through fresh Core routing;
  and
- Page/resource identity and externally cached redirects remain honest.

### Concrete Hope Relief example

Main Website's About Page currently has seven historical addresses, including:

`stories.hoperelief.org/about`

Luis changes the Page from explaining Hope Relief's mission, leadership, and
contact information to helping prospective volunteers choose and apply for a
short-term mission team. In D79's Publish review he chooses:

> **This update changes what this Page is for**

None of the seven old addresses has been freshly qualified for the new purpose.
For this example, immutable Core route-effect history proves that all seven have
always been served directly at the same path and none emitted a cacheable
permanent redirect to Main Website's canonical About URL. All three options are
therefore eligible. If that proof instead showed any cacheable redirect—or were
unknown—Core would deterministically require Option 3 before asking staff.

Should Core publish the new content in place and make fresh old-address requests
not-found, block publication until every old address has a disposition, or guide
Luis to publish the new purpose as a new Page identity and route?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- No fresh Core request from a historical address may serve the new purpose
  without current exact D78 qualification.
- For eligible in-place Options 1/2, one command uses the exact candidate
  effective-release digest, successor continuity version, complete private
  affected relation set, expected heads, actor effect, and policy versions or
  changes nothing. Option 3 instead creates a fresh Page draft/identity and
  leaves the old Page's published release, route, and continuity head unchanged.
- Drafts/autosaves/previews have no public effect; scheduled execution
  reauthorizes and revalidates current heads.
- Restricted source detail/count stays hidden, but hidden relations remain in
  the private authoritative closure.
- D78 renewal remains one address at a time; no bulk equivalence approval.
- Unknown, partial, stale, unauthorized, or lost-response state fails safely and
  resumes through the durable receipt.
- Giving, auth, APIs, forms, callbacks, files, protected/Phase 22 routes, source
  context carry, arbitrary/external targets, and unsafe methods remain excluded.
- No AI/classifier/diff/timer/traffic/support/provider state decides meaning.
- No Vercel/DNS/TLS/Stripe/money mutation or donor-facing interstitial is added.
- Staff are told that already cached external permanent redirects cannot be
  recalled.

### Option 1 — for a proved direct-only cohort, publish in place and stop fresh old-address routing

The final review states the exact consequence. One transaction publishes the
new Page/purpose generation and compiles every unrequalified predecessor pinned
to the old version to **Page not found** for fresh Core requests. Staff can run
fresh D78 reviews afterward. The option is unavailable if any affected route
ever emitted a cacheable permanent redirect to the current canonical URL or the
history is unknown.

Example final action:

> **Publish new purpose and stop fresh Core routing from 7 historical addresses**

The exact count appears only with aggregate-count authority; otherwise the
action says **affected historical addresses** while the complete private closure
still commits atomically.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** the current Page owner is not held
hostage by old links or unavailable source owners. The server state is complete,
atomic, easy to explain, and uses the already accepted safe not-found outcome.
It is the least new product surface.

**Costs and downstream effects:** bookmarks and search links to the historical
addresses break until reviewed; staff must prioritize any high-value known
placements. The option is correctly absent rather than caveated when redirect
history makes in-place safety unprovable.

### Option 2 — for a proved direct-only cohort, block until every address has a disposition

Core keeps the candidate private until every predecessor has either a fresh
D78 qualification for the new purpose or an explicit not-found outcome. A
favorable pre-publication decision reuses D78 against the exact D1-admitted
production-faithful candidate and remains prepared-only; it activates only in
the same Page/continuity/route transaction that publishes that digest. The Page
Publish review becomes a complete migration checklist. This option is likewise
unavailable when cacheable redirect history exists or is unknown.

Example final action after all seven decisions:

> **Publish new purpose with all historical addresses resolved**

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** every fresh server-side route has an
intentional outcome at the moment of publication, which minimizes accidental
broken links and gives staff the strongest continuity planning.

**Costs and downstream effects:** one Page can be blocked by many old addresses,
restricted source owners, expired sessions, or urgent safety/legal corrections.
Staff may mechanically choose results merely to unblock Publish. The option is
correctly absent rather than caveated when redirect history makes in-place
safety unprovable.

### Option 3 — publish the new purpose as a new Page identity and route (recommended)

Core guides staff to **Create as new Page** from the candidate. That action
copies the candidate content into a new private Page draft with a fresh identity
and distinct proposed canonical path. It leaves the current Page's published
release, current purpose, canonical route, continuity head, and D78 relations
unchanged. Publishing the new Page later uses its ordinary independent Page
flow. Any future unpublish/retirement of the old Page is a separate explicit
Page-owner decision under its existing lifecycle; there is no undefined “long
enough” timer. D79 continuity and D78 relations never copy.

Example:

- existing resource: `/about` — mission, leadership, contact; and
- new resource: `/serve/short-term-teams` — choose and apply for a team.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** a genuinely new public subject/purpose/
task becomes a genuinely new Web resource. It best follows stable-URI/resource
semantics, preserves staff and donor expectations, avoids misleading cached
redirects, and keeps histories/routes clear. The copy action can reuse the
candidate content without retyping while still creating fresh identity.

**Costs and downstream effects:** staff must choose a new route, later publish
the new Page, update Navigation/internal links, and maintain or separately
retire the old Page. Some
changes that staff call “material” may not deserve two Pages; forcing this for
every case could create clutter and cleanup work. The UX must make the route and
old-Page consequence one clear review, not a multi-step wizard.

### Recommendation

**Option 3 — publish a genuinely different purpose as a new Page identity and
route.** It is the only eligible option when any affected historical address
has cacheable redirect history or that history is unknown, and it best aligns
Page identity, canonical URL, D78
meaning, and already cached redirects without pretending Core can revoke
external cache state. A concise **Create as new Page** flow can carry the draft
content, show the old/new route consequences once, and leave the current Page
publicly unchanged.

For a completely proved direct-only cohort, Option 1 is the strongest low-
friction alternative when the current canonical resource may legitimately
evolve in place. Option 2 is the strongest planned-cutover alternative when
uninterrupted fresh-request continuity matters more than publishing speed. No
option may ask staff to “accept” a known cached-redirect meaning violation.

### Exact question

When staff choose **This update changes what this Page is for**, should Core use
**Option 1 — for a proved direct-only cohort, publish in place and stop fresh
historical routing**, **Option 2 — for a proved direct-only cohort, block until
every historical address has an explicit disposition**, or **Option 3 — create
a new Page identity and route for the new purpose**? Any cacheable redirect
history—or unknown history—makes Options 1/2 unavailable rather than a staff
override.

### Founder selection

The founder selected **Option 3 — create a new Page identity and route** on
2026-08-31, subject to current-practice verification, excellent Core-consistent
staff/donor UX, and a full adversarial review.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** A genuinely different public subject,
substantive purpose, or intended visitor task is a different Web resource. A
fresh Page identity and distinct proposed route is the strongest answer for URI
meaning, donor expectations, cached redirects, staff history, and Core's
accepted D78/D79 contract.

The review removed the conditional direct-only branch. Redirect history can
prove that a cached-redirect risk exists, but it cannot prove that every browser,
intermediary, bookmark, search result, printed link, or visitor expectation is
safe. Keeping Options 1/2 as runtime branches would add deterministic history
comparison and staff eligibility rules without solving the canonical-resource
problem. D79 **keeps what this Page is for** remains the correct low-friction
lane for routine Page evolution; once the authorized publisher explicitly
chooses **changes**, D80 universally continues as a new Page.

This is a Core product judgment supported—not literally prescribed—by current
W3C URI-consistency principles, RFC 9110 cacheable permanent-redirect semantics,
Google corresponding-target/soft-404 guidance, independent-draft behavior in
current CMS products, and the repository's stricter Page/route promise.

### Corrected D80 decision

1. **No in-place material publication.** A D79 material candidate cannot
   publish through the existing Page identity, current canonical route, or any
   historical address. No route-history/direct-only/traffic/cache/staff-override
   exception exists.
2. **No continuity advance.** The existing Page does not publish, so D80 creates
   or advances no source Page Purpose Continuity Version. Its head and every D78
   relation remain unchanged. The target inherits none.
3. **One exact private target.** **Move saved changes to new Page draft** creates a fresh
   independent `general_page` under the same exact Tenant, environment, Site,
   and locale from one acknowledged Page-owned candidate, with fresh Page,
   locale-lineage, block/anchor, Working Revision, and D2 Placement identities.
4. **Explicit address.** Staff review Page title, eligible Parent Page or **Top
   level under the current Site root**, and local web-address segment while
   seeing the complete tenant-branded URL. D80 never creates/reassigns the Site
   root or copies source children/breadcrumbs. D2 and database constraints
   decide normalized route availability. No overwrite or silent numeric suffix
   is allowed.
5. **Bounded transfer reuse.** D80 reuses proposed D23's finite versioned
   transfer compiler, repair classes, owner adapters, expected-revision fencing,
   atomic creation, and semantic receipt through one narrow same-Site policy.
   It does not widen **Copy to another Site...**, expose generic duplicate, or
   trust Payload `duplicateFromID`.
6. **Independent content.** Eligible Page-owned editorial/SEO content copies;
   Page-local IDs/anchors and self-references remap; Reusable Sections
   materialize locally; other references/Media revalidate. Unknown or unsafe
   members block or become bounded explicit repairs. A nonseparable shared/
   global owner change blocks with its existing owner action; D80 creates no
   dependency-fork engine.
7. **Authority does not copy.** Route/predecessor history, D78/D79, Navigation,
   incoming-link authority, schedule, publication, search/cache/sitemap/
   analytics, lifecycle, audience/Reach/safety, permissions, actor/provider,
   operational, and money truth never transfer.
8. **Source public state is invariant.** The source's published release,
   canonical/historical routes, public generation, continuity/D78, Navigation,
   search/cache, and donor result remain unchanged. Later retirement, move, or
   fresh relation work is separate.
9. **Source private state needs one final choice.** The exact candidate remains
   conserved in the target transfer result and exact protected source history;
   it cannot remain an unlabelled ordinary publishable source draft or be
   silently destroyed. ADR-0202/D81 appends the clean source result and fences
   its leases in the same transaction.
10. **All-or-none command.** One sealed preflight and short expected-head
    transaction creates complete target identity/revisions/path claim/repairs/
    inert provenance/receipt/audit/outbox plus D81's protected checkpoint,
    necessary clean source successors/head advances, and lease fences, or none.
    It contains no network/provider call. Exact replay returns one target;
    changed input conflicts; concurrency has one safe winner.
11. **Existing authorization.** The command reuses current source read/edit/
    release and target Page create/edit/placement effects with trusted server-
    derived scope. It adds no permission, role, invite, assignment, approval,
    support override, or access workflow.
12. **Zero public/provider/money effect.** Creation publishes, unpublishes,
    redirects, canonicalizes, navigates, deploys, charges, or messages nothing;
    it calls no Vercel/Domain/DNS/TLS/CDN/Stripe/bank/currency/gift/ledger/form/
    email system. Only later ordinary target D1 publication can create a public
    route.
13. **One D33 capacity authority.** Before a private cohort activates, D33
    governance ratifies a new whole Production Capacity Profile version and
    matching exact Vercel Qualification Attachment. Its Minimum, Typical, and
    Measured maximum cohorts include one named D80 handoff scenario with
    separate numeric cells and a Capacity Evidence Package. D80 invents no
    independent profile, cell authority, or vague performance claim.

### Staff workspace and donor experience

Selecting D79 **changes** performs no mutation and reveals one main-column
continuation inside the existing D1 consequence review—no wizard, nested modal,
focus jump, second confirmation, provider terms, or donor interstitial:

> **This update needs a new Page**
>
> Keep **About** at its current address for its current purpose, and create a
> separate private Page draft for this new purpose. Nothing will be published
> now.

> **Current Page · Stays live as-is**<br>
> About<br>
> `https://hoperelief.org/about`
>
> **New Page draft · Not live**<br>
> Main Website · English (US)

The only editable target fields are **Page title**, **Parent Page** with **Top
level** explicitly meaning under the current Site root, and **Web address** with
full proposed URL. Consequence
copy states that the independent draft is created from saved changes while the
old Page, historical addresses, Navigation, incoming links, schedule, and
public search stay unchanged. It also states that the moved Page-owned changes
leave About's draft, separately managed content stays unchanged, and the exact
candidate remains protected in History. The primary
action is **Move saved changes to new Page draft**; secondary is **Back to
editing**.

Save-required, checking, ready, repair, blocker, shared-owner, schedule,
collision, drift, permission loss, moving, uncertain outcome, failure, and
success each have persistent cause-owned text. Errors retain inputs and focus
the summary/field; uncertain results reconcile the receipt before retry. After
fresh target read/edit and lease proof, success navigates to the target, focuses
its heading, and persistently shows exact Site, domain, locale, **Draft — not
live**, repairs, **Open About**, and the precise source moved-changes result. If
that post-commit target check fails, Core persists a detail-free committed
confirmation instead of navigating.

The surface uses PageShell/Base UI/base-maia/Zinc, one DOM/reading order,
semantic labels/status, visible focus, 44-pixel targets, forced colors, reduced
motion, copyable bidi-isolated URLs, keyboard/screen reader, 320-CSS-pixel/400-
percent reflow, long/CJK/RTL, and summary-first weak-network behavior.

Donors see no D80 state. Until the independent Page later passes D1, the old
tenant-native Page and all existing route behavior remain the only public
result. No Asym, Vercel, Tenant/Site, draft, transition, or purpose vocabulary
appears publicly.

### Required repository reconciliation

- ADR-0200/D79 must replace every deferred **D80 advances the continuity head**
  placeholder with **D80 creates a new private Page and leaves the source head
  unchanged**.
- ADR-0199/D78 post-cutover relation consumption remains an ordinary D1
  preserving-release concern; D80 neither consumes nor activates a D78 relation.
- Proposed ADR-0145/0146/0150/0152/0156/0157/0167/0174/0177 and Phase 23
  OpenSpec must add the narrow create-and-replace handoff and D33 workload cell
  while preserving D23's different-Site/source-unchanged product command.
- Phase 2/5/12, living spec, roadmap, glossary, consolidated Phase 24 PRD/
  OpenSpec/design/tasks/tickets/tests/release evidence carry D80-R1-R26,
  AC1-AC50, invariants, monitors, and the provider/money no-op boundary.
- D77's existing small critical-path owner inventory remains small and
  unchanged; D80 adds no route-history owner adapter or public resolver.

The permanent decision is recorded in
[ADR-0201](../../adr/0201-material-purpose-changes-create-independent-pages.md)
and the
[D80 adversarial review](./phase-24-d80-material-purpose-new-page-adversarial-review.md).

## D81 — What should remain as the active draft on the original Page?

### Decision title

**Private source Working Revision after a material-purpose Page handoff**

### Plain-language context

D80 safely creates a separate private Page from the exact saved candidate
through its finite fresh-identity transfer compiler and
leaves the current public Page unchanged. One private question remains: the old
Page has one visible active draft backed by separate Editorial and Placement
Working heads. Leaving the same new-purpose candidate
there as an ordinary draft invites someone to try publishing it again. Replacing
it without clear evidence could surprise staff when the candidate also contains
a routine correction intended for the old Page.

Every option below is safe at the public boundary. All preserve every safely
transferable saved Page-owned meaning in the new Page, explicitly disclose any
repairable omission, and preserve the exact untransformed candidate in an
immutable named source checkpoint; none publishes, deletes history, transfers
D78/D79, or changes the old public Page. The choice is only which private
revision is active when staff return to the old Page.

### Concrete Hope Relief example

Luis's About draft changes the Page into a short-term-team application, but it
also corrects Hope Relief's phone number. D80 creates the private Page
`/serve/short-term-teams`. When Luis later opens **About**, should it be clean at
the current live About content, still show the transferred candidate behind a
publication fence, or ask Luis which of those two outcomes he wants during each
handoff?

### Safeguards every option keeps

- The new Page contains D80's complete validated transfer result and remains
  **Draft — not live**; the exact untransformed source candidate stays in
  source History.
- The old candidate remains immutable, named, comparable, and recoverable in
  source history; no work is silently lost.
- The old Page's public release, route, continuity head, D78 relations,
  Navigation, schedule, search/cache, and donor result remain unchanged.
- No source draft can publish the material candidate without returning through
  a new current D79 review.
- One expected-head transaction creates the target and chosen source-private
  result or neither; exact replay cannot duplicate it.
- Core does not semantically split fields or guess which phone/image/text edits
  belong on both Pages. Staff who need that outcome can go back, publish the
  preserving correction first, then prepare the new purpose.
- No new permission, assignment, approval, notification, background cleanup,
  or target-publication coupling is added.

### Option 1 — Move the saved candidate and clean the original atomically (recommended)

The handoff checkpoints the exact candidate, creates the new Page, and appends
one new source Working successor for each changed Editorial/Placement axis from
the exact current D1-pinned About release. An unchanged axis receives no no-op
revision. About's sealed Page-owned Working heads return to their exact D1
public pins while separately managed content remains unchanged. History
shows **Moved saved changes to a new Page draft**. Any target link or comparison
resolves only to the receipt-bound initial target Working Revision after fresh
exact target-resource and target-version/history read checks; current-target
read alone is insufficient. Otherwise it gives a non-enumerating
unavailable result. It never opens the target's current draft or creates a live
source-to-target dependency. Luis may manually reapply the phone correction
from that comparison.

Example primary action:

> **Move saved changes to new Page draft**

If selected, the D80 consequence list also states:

> After creation, these moved Page-owned changes are no longer active on About.
> Separately managed content stays unchanged. Every safely transferable saved
> Page change remains in the new Page; any repairable omission is listed, and
> the exact original version remains protected in About History.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it gives staff the cleanest mental
model, prevents duplicate active drafts and repeat-publish mistakes, needs no
new transferred status/cleanup workflow, and is all-or-none. It is not data
loss: its admitted meaning exists in the new Page and the exact original exists
in protected source history.

**Cost:** a routine correction mixed into the candidate is not automatically
kept active on About. Staff must split it before handoff or reapply it from the
clear comparison afterward. That is explicit human work rather than an unsafe
semantic merge.

### Option 2 — Keep a clearly blocked transferred draft until staff restores it

The new Page is created, while About retains the candidate as its active private
revision under a new explicit non-publishable state:

> **Moved to Short-term team application · Not publishable here**

Persistent actions are **Continue on new Page** and **Restore About to its live
version**. The exact transferred digest cannot enter ordinary Publish on About.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it maximizes visible preservation and
avoids an immediate reset of the source editor, but it keeps the _entire_
candidate blocked; no part remains independently editable or publishable on
About.

**Cost:** it creates a new transferred-draft state, publish fence, recovery UI,
retention/cleanup rules, reporting, tests, and potentially long-lived duplicate
work. It is safer than an ordinary draft but carries real product and operating
cost.

### Option 3 — Ask one explicit clean-or-keep choice for each handoff

The same D80 review adds one initially unselected source-draft choice:

- **Clean About after moving these changes**; or
- **Keep the full saved draft visible on About, but block it from publishing.**
  To publish a correction on About, first restore About to its live version and
  reapply that correction separately.

The chosen outcome participates in the sealed plan and one transaction. Core
never changes it later automatically.

**Why this is a genuinely good option:** it combines Option 1's clean default
path with Option 2's control for genuinely mixed drafts, and it makes the source
effect impossible to miss.

**Cost:** every material handoff gains another consequential question; staff may
not understand why keeping is useful, behavior differs per occurrence, and Core
must still implement/operate Option 2's transferred state for the minority who
select it. The added choice can become ceremony.

### Recommendation

**Option 1 — move the saved candidate and clean the original atomically.** It is
the smallest complete model, the clearest staff experience, and the least likely
to create technical debt or repeat-publish mistakes. Exact target content plus
immutable source history makes it recoverable without leaving two active copies.
The UI must state the consequence before commit and persist the post-success
source-history entry. It shows the receipt-bound target link/comparison only
when the current actor passes fresh exact target-resource and target-version/
history read authorization;
staff with mixed changes can use **Back to editing** and split them deliberately.

Option 2 is the strongest preservation-first alternative when keeping the full
candidate visibly present in the original editor matters more than lifecycle
simplicity. Option 3 is the strongest per-occurrence-control alternative, but
it pays most of Option 2's permanent cost and adds recurring ceremony.

### Exact question

When Core creates the new-purpose Page draft, should it use **Option 1 — move
the saved candidate and clean the original atomically**, **Option 2 — keep a
clearly blocked transferred draft until staff restores it**, or **Option 3 — ask
one explicit clean-or-keep choice for each handoff**?

### Founder answer

**Option 1 — move the saved candidate and clean the original atomically.** Use
it only if it reflects current proven practice; keep the tenant/staff UX
excellent and consistent with Core, and avoid overengineering, brittleness, and
technical debt.

### Adversarial disposition

**Accept with required amendments.** The direction is the best permanent fit,
but **clean** must mean append-and-advance—not delete, overwrite, rewind, or raw
provider restore.

Current CMS evidence supports each safety primitive, not a universal vendor
command. Payload's current **revert to published** keeps the old drafts and
creates a new version equal to published. Sanity explicitly warns that copying
a draft elsewhere leaves the original draft behind and can later lose or
publish unintended changes. PostgreSQL and Payload support the required one-
transaction composition. WCAG supports one reviewable/recoverable consequential
action without another confirmation on routine saves. Core therefore owns this
bounded synthesis:

1. The final action is **Move saved changes to new Page draft**, inside D80's
   existing review. There is no standalone duplicate, transferred state,
   cleanup workflow, modal, semantic merge, or new permission.
2. The exact source Editorial/Placement candidate pair becomes one logical
   handoff event named **Moved saved changes to a new Page draft**, grouping
   independently resource-scoped D12 checkpoint pins rather than fusing content
   axes. The D80 receipt stores only IDs, digests, causes, actor, time, and
   result references—not Page bodies.
3. For each source-owned axis that differs from the exact authoritative
   revision pinned by the same current D1 public generation, Core appends one
   clean private successor and advances that Working head. An already-clean
   axis receives no redundant revision. No compiled output, provider `latest`,
   or browser buffer can supply the baseline.
4. Editorial and Placement stay separate D12 resources. Navigation,
   Reusable/shared/global owners, schedule, D78/D79, publication, route/public,
   search/cache, provider, operational, and money facts do not reset or transfer
   implicitly.
5. The target is D80's deterministic fresh-identity transfer result, not a byte
   clone. Every manifest-admitted saved member is copied/materialized, explicitly
   omitted with a named repair, or blocks. The exact
   untransformed candidate remains independently recoverable in source History.
6. One short transaction creates the target and transfer artifacts, appends
   the source checkpoint and necessary clean successors, advances source heads,
   fences every old lease generation in the sealed source Editorial/Placement
   pair, and appends receipt/audit/outbox—
   or does none. Every qualified Payload write is awaited under the same
   request transaction; no provider/network call runs inside it.
7. Commit rederives actor/scope and rechecks source/target effects, Working and
   public heads, D79/D80 state, lease generations, schedule, manifest/schema,
   target route claim, and constraints. Exact replay adds no effect;
   different-input reuse conflicts. Unknown results freeze source edits and
   reconcile the durable receipt before retry. Existing authority includes the
   source Editorial edit effect and, when that axis differs, the exact source
   Placement edit/supersede effect; target Placement authority cannot mutate
   the source.
8. Browser/Data API roles get no direct mutation path. Same-scope composite
   keys, restrictive deletion, unique head/lease/route/command constraints,
   least grants, RLS `USING` and `WITH CHECK`, and privileged Payload/service/
   RPC parity are mandatory. RLS is never claimed to constrain a bypassing
   provider connection.
9. The source checkpoint is protected from ordinary rolling/provider pruning
   for the governing D12 recovery period, but is not immortal or outside
   authorized retention, privacy, deletion, anonymization, or legal-hold rules.
   D12's versioned `material_page_handoff` retention class records protection
   start, explicit owner-authorized release/prune evidence, governing holds,
   and tombstone/receipt outcome without inventing a day count. Target deletion
   or access loss never makes source recovery depend on the target.
10. Successful commit fences every current lease in the sealed source
    Editorial/Placement pair. A stale tab or browser back-cache becomes
    read-only and cannot autosave the moved candidate. Opening the target
    obtains a fresh ordinary D12 target lease; source authority never transfers.
11. D81 is side-effect-dark. It changes no source public generation, route,
    continuity, Navigation, schedule, search/cache, donor result, Vercel/DNS/
    TLS/deployment state, Stripe, currency, gift, ledger, form, message, or
    other money/integration fact.

### Final staff experience

D80's existing inline PageShell review shows the two consequences immediately
above the action:

> **New Page · Private draft**  
> Short-term team application  
> `https://hoperelief.org/serve/short-term-teams`
>
> **About · Stays live; these Page changes leave its draft**  
> `https://hoperelief.org/about`
>
> The safely transferable saved Page content and the new Page details shown
> above will become the private draft. Anything that cannot transfer safely is
> listed under Review after moving and remains in the exact protected source
> History. Nothing will be published. About stays live; these moved Page-owned
> changes are no longer active there. Separately managed content stays
> unchanged.
>
> If any of these changes still belong on About, go back and separate them
> before moving.

Actions are **Compare saved draft with live About**, **Move saved changes to
new Page draft**, and **Back to editing**. Pending autosave, drift, schedule,
route, permission, manifest, owner, or schema state blocks with one cause-owned
repair; the server still decides.

During commit, persistent status says **Creating the new Page and removing
these Page changes from About's active draft...**. An unknown response says
**Checking whether the changes were moved...** and exposes no blind retry. A
fresh target read/edit and ordinary target-lease check follows commit. If it
passes, success opens the target in the same tab, focuses its heading, and
persistently says:

> **Saved changes moved from About**  
> About stays live. These moved Page changes are no longer active there.
> Separately managed content was not changed. Nothing was published.

The target still shows exact Site, tenant-branded domain, locale, and **Draft —
not live**, plus permission-safe **Open About** and **View source history**.
History compares each authorized source axis in the exact candidate to its clean
successor. A target link can open only the receipt-bound initial target revision
after fresh exact target-resource and target-version/history read authorization;
current-target read alone is insufficient. If fresh target read/edit or lease
acquisition fails after commit, Core shows a detail-free committed confirmation
instead of navigating. There is no destructive one-click Undo.

The experience uses PageShell/Base UI/base-maia/Zinc, one semantic reading
order, native labels, visible focus, 44-pixel targets, forced colors, reduced
motion, keyboard/screen reader, 320-CSS-pixel/400-percent reflow, bidi-safe long/
CJK/RTL URLs/copy, summary-first weak-network rendering, persistent status, and
input preservation on error. Donors see no D81 state.

### Required repository reconciliation

- ADR-0201/D80 now uses **Move saved changes to new Page draft** and incorporates
  the protected checkpoint, clean successors, head advances, and lease fences
  in its one transaction.
- Proposed ADR-0156/OpenSpec must add the D81 logical handoff cause with
  independent per-axis checkpoint pins, versioned semantic-retention release
  predicate, and sealed-pair system-command lease fence without fusing
  Editorial/Placement or exposing raw restore.
- Proposed ADR-0167/D23 remains a different source-unchanged product command;
  D80/D81 reuses only its finite compiler inside a separately authorized
  same-Site create-and-clean command.
- Phase 12, D1/D2/D12/D23/D33, living spec, roadmap, glossary, consolidated
  Phase 24 PRD/OpenSpec/design/tasks/tickets/tests/release evidence carry

  no-effect proof.
- D33's named scenario covers the complete target/source transaction, checkpoint
